title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Beginner’s Guide: What to Do First
description: A spoiler-light Red Dead Redemption 2 beginner’s guide covering early progression, cores, camp, horses, exploration and the systems worth understanding first.
body:
Red Dead Redemption 2 is deliberately slow at the beginning. The opening chapters teach you how its world works, but they also hide a large number of systems behind menus, camp routines, character interactions and small pieces of feedback. New players can make the game feel harder than it is by rushing through those systems or trying to optimize everything immediately.

A better approach is to treat the early game as a period of orientation. Learn how Arthur’s health, stamina and Dead Eye cores work, get comfortable with your horse, use camp as a base rather than a chore list, and give yourself permission to explore once Chapter 2 opens the map more fully. The game rewards patience far more than speed.

For our broader assessment of Rockstar’s open-world western, read the [Red Dead Redemption 2 review](/stories/red-dead-redemption-2-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Arthur Morgan appears in stylized red-and-yellow Red Dead Redemption 2 promotional artwork with members of the Van der Linde gang riding in silhouette behind him.
imageCredit: Rockstar Games / Red Dead Redemption 2 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
The snowbound opening is more structured than the rest of Red Dead Redemption 2, and that is intentional. It introduces movement, camp routines, horse handling, tracking and the basic shape of missions before the world becomes much less directed.

If the opening feels restrictive, avoid treating it as the full game. Once the gang establishes a more permanent camp in Chapter 2, you gain far more freedom to explore, take side activities, visit towns and decide how quickly you want to push the story forward.
contentBlocks.heading: Let Chapter 1 Teach You the Basics

contentBlocks.text:
Arthur’s health, stamina and Dead Eye each have an outer meter and an inner core. The meter is the resource you spend in the moment, while the core influences how effectively that meter recovers and can also affect Arthur’s general condition.

You do not need to micromanage food every few minutes, but ignoring depleted cores for long stretches makes the game feel harsher. Eat, rest and use camp when Arthur is running low, especially before longer trips or story missions.
contentBlocks.heading: Understand the Difference Between Cores and Meters

contentBlocks.text:
A horse is more than transportation. As bonding increases, handling improves and additional interactions become available, which makes long journeys less awkward.

For a first playthrough, there is little reason to chase a perfect horse immediately. Pick one you like, keep it nearby, care for it when necessary and learn how saddles, stables and horse inventory fit into your travel routine. Consistency is more useful than constantly swapping mounts.
contentBlocks.heading: Keep One Horse and Build a Routine Around It

contentBlocks.text:
Camp is where many companion conversations, optional scenes and progression systems live. Returning regularly helps the gang feel like a group of characters rather than a menu between missions.

Contribute when you can, check in with people, and pay attention when new camp options appear. You do not need to maximize every upgrade immediately. Early money is often more useful when it supports the activities you are already doing rather than disappearing into upgrades you do not yet understand.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Camp as a Home Base, Not a Checklist

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 gradually introduces mechanics through story missions. If something in the world seems unavailable or strangely limited, the answer is often that a nearby Chapter 2 mission has not yet introduced it.

This is especially useful early on: alternate between main missions and exploration rather than spending hours trying to force every system open before the game has explained it.
contentBlocks.heading: Let Missions Unlock Systems Before You Over-Explore

contentBlocks.text:
Dead Eye slows combat and gives you more time to read a difficult encounter. For beginners, its main value is not showing off; it is creating enough breathing room to understand what is happening when several threats appear at once.

The system develops as the story progresses, so do not worry if early Dead Eye feels more limited than clips from later parts of the game. Use the version you currently have and let the campaign introduce the rest.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Dead Eye as a Planning Tool

contentBlocks.text:
The game autosaves, but a manual save before a long detour, expensive purchase or unfamiliar activity makes experimentation less stressful. RDR2 often lets small choices cascade into different outcomes, and having a clean checkpoint can be useful when you are still learning what the world considers important.

Use saves as insurance rather than a demand to perfect every event. Some of the game’s strongest moments come from unexpected consequences.
contentBlocks.heading: Manual Saves Make Experimentation Easier

contentBlocks.text:
The map is full of side stories, strangers, environmental details and optional activities, but trying to clear every icon in one sweep can flatten the experience.

A better rhythm is to choose a destination, travel there normally and allow the journey to interrupt you. That gives the open world space to produce the encounters and discoveries that make it memorable without turning exploration into a completion checklist.
contentBlocks.heading: Explore With a Purpose, but Leave Room for Distraction

contentBlocks.text:
The early game gives you many things to buy before you understand which ones matter to your playstyle. Resist the urge to empty your wallet every time a new shop or camp option appears.

Spend on practical needs first, then let your preferences become clearer. Red Dead Redemption 2 is long enough that you will have plenty of opportunities to improve your equipment, wardrobe, horse setup and camp later.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Spend Early Money Just Because You Have It

quickRead: Reach Chapter 2 before judging the game’s pace: that is where the world and most of its core systems open up.
Keep Arthur’s health, stamina and Dead Eye cores in good condition; depleted cores make the corresponding meters less effective.
Bond with one reliable horse instead of constantly replacing it, and use camp as a place to rest, resupply and advance companion stories.
Do not try to clear the map immediately. RDR2 is easier to enjoy when exploration, hunting, side stories and main missions develop together.
conclusion:
The best first hours in Red Dead Redemption 2 come from accepting its pace. Reach Chapter 2, learn the relationship between cores and meters, settle into one horse, and use camp and story missions to understand systems before trying to master them.

After that, let the world breathe. Follow a main mission when you want direction, wander when something catches your attention, and avoid turning Arthur’s journey into a race to clear the map. RDR2 rewards players who give its routines and characters enough time to become meaningful.

title: Why Red Dead Redemption 2’s World Still Feels Alive
description: An analysis of the systems, encounters, routines and environmental detail that make Red Dead Redemption 2’s world feel unusually reactive.
body:
Red Dead Redemption 2’s world feels alive because Rockstar rarely relies on one system to create the illusion. Wildlife, weather, towns, travel, camp life, ambient encounters, animation and environmental storytelling overlap until the player stops thinking about individual mechanics and starts reading the world as a place.

The effect is strongest when nothing dramatic is happening. A road, a shop, a campsite or an animal crossing can still feel observed and specific, which gives the larger story a world that seems to continue existing beyond the next mission marker.

For our broader assessment of Rockstar’s world and story, read the [Red Dead Redemption 2 review](/stories/red-dead-redemption-2-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Arthur Morgan appears in stylized red-and-yellow Red Dead Redemption 2 promotional artwork with members of the Van der Linde gang riding behind him.
imageCredit: Rockstar Games / Red Dead Redemption 2 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text: Red Dead Redemption 2 rarely announces the machinery behind its world. Instead, several systems operate close enough together that one event can feel unscripted even when parts of it are authored. A weather change affects the mood of a ride, wildlife crosses the route, an encounter interrupts the trip, and the next town is already busy with its own activity. The illusion comes from accumulation.
contentBlocks.heading: The World Is Built From Overlapping Systems

contentBlocks.text: Rockstar says the game contains around 200 species of animals, birds and fish across different habitats and climates. More important than the number is the behavioral variety: herds move across plains, predators hunt, scavengers respond to carrion and animals react differently to nearby threats. That makes wildlife feel integrated into the environment rather than scattered across it as collectibles.
contentBlocks.heading: Wildlife Behaves Like Part of the Landscape

contentBlocks.text: Settlements work because people appear to have reasons to be there. Shops open into functional interiors, workers occupy spaces that match their jobs, streets change character between locations, and small conversations suggest lives that do not begin when the player arrives. The simulation is selective, but it provides enough continuity for a town to feel inhabited rather than staged.
contentBlocks.heading: Towns Feel Occupied, Not Merely Decorated

contentBlocks.text: The gang’s camp acts as more than a mission hub. Characters move through chores, conversations, arguments, meals and quiet moments, giving the player a repeated social space that changes as the story develops. Returning to camp creates a rhythm of departure and return, which helps the wider map feel like somewhere the group actually lives within rather than merely crosses.
contentBlocks.heading: Camp Makes the World Social

contentBlocks.text: Long rides are not empty time. They allow weather, wildlife, strangers, landmarks and unexpected events to enter the player’s attention. Rockstar’s willingness to leave distance between major objectives gives those smaller details room to matter. The map feels larger not only because of its physical scale, but because travelling through it produces experiences that are not identical each time.
contentBlocks.heading: Travel Creates Space for Unplanned Moments

contentBlocks.text: Red Dead Redemption 2 spends unusual attention on mundane interactions. Mounting a horse, opening a drawer, preparing at camp or moving through mud is given enough animation and sound to suggest physical presence. That deliberateness can make the game feel slow, but it is also part of why objects and spaces seem tangible instead of instantly consumed by interface shortcuts.
contentBlocks.heading: Animation Gives Ordinary Actions Weight

contentBlocks.text: The world regularly places meaning away from the central route: abandoned structures, signs of previous activity, changes in architecture, small camps and landscape details that imply a story without formal exposition. These discoveries are valuable because they are not always converted into quests. Some exist simply to make the world feel older and larger than the player’s current objective.
contentBlocks.heading: Environmental Detail Rewards Looking Sideways

contentBlocks.text: Many open worlds push the player quickly between activities. Red Dead Redemption 2 often does the opposite. Its slower interaction and travel rhythms create time to notice changes in light, sound, weather and behavior. That pace is not universally appealing, but it is tightly connected to the game’s sense of place: the world becomes convincing because the player is repeatedly asked to inhabit it rather than skip across it.
contentBlocks.heading: Slowness Is Part of the Illusion

quickRead: Red Dead Redemption 2 creates a sense of life through overlapping routines, ambient encounters and environmental systems rather than one single simulation feature.
Camp conversations and changing relationships give the world continuity beyond missions.
Wildlife, weather, travel and small reactive details make ordinary movement through the map feel authored without being fully scripted.
conclusion:
Red Dead Redemption 2 feels alive because its systems reinforce one another. Wildlife behaves like part of an ecosystem, towns appear occupied, camp gives the story a social home, travel creates room for interruption and environmental detail rewards attention beyond the objective marker.

None of those systems alone would create the effect. Together, they produce a world that seems to have momentum before the player arrives and after they leave. That continuity is why its open world can still feel unusually convincing years later.
conclusionHeading: A living world is built from small consistencies

title: Why Super Mario Galaxy’s Gravity Mechanics Still Feel Brilliant
description: An analysis of how Super Mario Galaxy turns gravity, planetoids and camera perspective into memorable platforming ideas.
body:
Super Mario Galaxy’s gravity still feels brilliant because Nintendo did not treat it as a visual trick layered on top of familiar platforming. Gravity became the rule that organizes movement, level shape, camera perspective and surprise.

That decision gave the game a vocabulary other 3D Mario titles rarely use. A tiny planetoid can wrap a jump back toward the player, a wall can become a floor, and a route that looks impossible from one angle can make sense as soon as gravity shifts. The mechanic continually changes how space is read without changing Mario’s basic controls.

For the broader platforming context, read our [Super Mario Galaxy review](/stories/super-mario-galaxy-review-platforming-masterpiece-among-the-stars/) and [Super Mario Galaxy 2 review](/stories/super-mario-galaxy-2-review-platforming-ideas-at-full-speed/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario leaps between small planets in the gravity-bending worlds of Super Mario Galaxy.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Galaxy

contentBlocks.text: Nintendo’s own development interviews describe gravity as the defining idea for Super Mario Galaxy. Shigeru Miyamoto said he was looking for something that could make a 3D Mario world feel new again, while the development team built an early prototype around spherical terrain placed in space with gravity attached. The final game grows directly from that experiment.
contentBlocks.heading: Gravity Was the Core Idea From the Beginning

contentBlocks.text: A normal platforming field has obvious edges. A sphere can hide routes on its far side, let the player run underneath what was previously “ground,” and bring distant-looking landmarks back into reach. Nintendo’s designers specifically noted that travelling around a planet could reveal things hidden on the opposite side, turning compact stages into spaces that reward curiosity.
contentBlocks.heading: Spherical Worlds Make Small Spaces Feel Expansive

contentBlocks.text: One reason the mechanic remains approachable is that Mario does not need a completely new control scheme every time gravity changes. The world rotates its logic around him while running and jumping still feel recognizably Mario. That separation lets the level produce strange spatial ideas without forcing the player to relearn basic movement each time.
contentBlocks.heading: The Controls Stay Familiar While the World Changes

contentBlocks.text: In Galaxy, the camera is not only presenting the environment; it is helping the player understand which surface currently matters. A nearby wall can become the next floor, a jump can curve toward another surface, and the visual horizon can change quickly as Mario crosses a planet. The result is platforming that asks the player to read orientation as part of the challenge.
contentBlocks.heading: Gravity Turns Perspective Into a Platforming Tool

contentBlocks.text: Because individual planets can be small, Nintendo can introduce an idea, explore it briefly and move on before it becomes repetitive. A launch star can send Mario from one miniature concept to another without a loading break or long transition. The developers explicitly highlighted this continuity between planets, which gives levels a rapid rhythm of discovery.
contentBlocks.heading: Planetoids Create Fast, Memorable Ideas

contentBlocks.text: The cleverness of Galaxy is not that gravity behaves unpredictably. It is that a consistent rule produces many different situations: running around spheres, shifting between surfaces, navigating rotating structures, judging curved jumps and understanding where “down” has moved. The game keeps finding new applications without making the core mechanic arbitrary.
contentBlocks.heading: One Rule Produces Many Different Kinds of Challenge

contentBlocks.text: Gravity gives the game dramatic visual moments without separating spectacle from play. Mario can be launched between distant worlds, run across strange surfaces or move around a boss arena that bends in every direction, yet those scenes still depend on player control. The cinematic feeling comes from the same system that powers the ordinary platforming.
contentBlocks.heading: The Mechanic Also Supports Spectacle

contentBlocks.text: Many memorable game mechanics support one or two standout sequences. Galaxy’s gravity system is stronger because it behaves like a design engine. Nintendo could keep asking what a spherical field, a new orientation or a gravity shift might allow, and each answer could become another stage idea. That generative quality is why the concept supported an entire sequel and still feels distinctive.
contentBlocks.heading: Galaxy Still Feels Fresh Because the Idea Is Generative

quickRead: Gravity is the organizing idea behind Super Mario Galaxy’s level design, not just a visual effect.
Spherical fields let Nintendo make compact spaces feel larger because routes can wrap around planets and continue out of sight.
Gravity shifts create new platforming problems while preserving Mario’s familiar movement, which keeps experimentation readable.
The system remains memorable because it generates many different level ideas from one consistent physical rule.
conclusion:
Super Mario Galaxy’s gravity succeeds because it changes the player’s understanding of space while keeping Mario himself easy to control. Spherical fields hide routes, gravity shifts turn walls into floors, compact planets create rapid changes of idea, and launch stars connect those ideas into a seamless journey.

Nintendo found a mechanic that was visually surprising, mechanically useful and flexible enough to generate an entire game’s worth of design. Years later, that combination still makes Galaxy feel less like a platformer with a space theme and more like a platformer built around a genuinely different way of thinking about 3D space.
conclusionHeading: A great mechanic changes how you see the level

title: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe 200cc Guide: Braking, Drifting and Kart Setup
description: A practical Mario Kart 8 Deluxe 200cc guide covering braking, brake drifting, earlier turn-in, kart setup and the habits that make the fastest engine class manageable.
body:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe changes character at 200cc. The tracks are the same, but the extra speed means habits that work at 150cc can send you straight past a corner. The biggest adjustment is simple: 200cc expects you to slow down sometimes.

Nintendo’s own beginner guidance specifically recommends braking on tight corners at higher engine classes, and that is the foundation of good 200cc driving. Learn to start drifts earlier, use the brake while preserving your line, and choose a kart setup that gives you enough handling and acceleration to recover when a corner goes wrong.

For setup fundamentals, read our [Mario Kart 8 Deluxe kart-build guide](/stories/mario-kart-8-deluxe-best-kart-builds/) and [Mario Kart 8 Deluxe review](/stories/mario-kart-8-deluxe-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario drives a red kart beside the Mario Kart 8 Deluxe logo against a purple and pink gradient background.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Mario Kart 8 Deluxe promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart teaches players for years that releasing the accelerator feels wrong, which is why 200cc initially seems chaotic. At this speed, some corners simply cannot be taken cleanly by holding full acceleration and steering harder.

Nintendo’s own Mario Kart 8 Deluxe basics advise pressing the B Button to brake on tight curves, especially in 150cc and 200cc. Treat braking as part of the racing line rather than a failure to maintain speed.
contentBlocks.heading: The First 200cc Lesson Is to Brake

contentBlocks.text:
The faster the kart is moving, the sooner you need to prepare for a corner. A drift that begins at the normal 150cc point may already be too late in 200cc.

Look further ahead and initiate the turn before the corner feels urgent. Early setup gives you room to correct the angle instead of reacting after the kart is already headed toward the outside edge.
contentBlocks.heading: Start Your Drift Earlier

contentBlocks.text:
When a drift is carrying too much speed, a short brake input can slow the kart without forcing you to abandon the turn completely. This is commonly called brake drifting and is one of the most useful habits in 200cc.

The goal is not to hold the brake for the entire corner. Use brief inputs to keep the kart from running wide, then return to full acceleration once the line is under control.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Brake Drifting to Tighten the Line

contentBlocks.text:
A high top-speed stat looks attractive, but 200cc already supplies enormous pace. While learning, a setup with stronger handling and acceleration can make difficult corners easier to read and mistakes less punishing.

There is no single mandatory kart combination for every track. Use a character and vehicle setup that feels predictable, then change one component at a time if you want more speed or a different handling balance.
contentBlocks.heading: Choose Control Before Maximum Speed

contentBlocks.text:
Long drifts build stronger Mini-Turbo boosts, but the longest possible charge is not always worth it in 200cc. Holding a drift too long can push you off the ideal line or create more speed than the next corner can comfortably absorb.

Release boosts when the track gives you room to use them. A smaller boost on a clean line is often faster than a larger one followed by a collision or off-road slowdown.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Force Every Mini-Turbo

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe includes Smart Steering to help keep less experienced racers on the track. It can be genuinely useful while learning unfamiliar 200cc courses or practicing sections with narrow edges.

The tradeoff is that Smart Steering restricts the highest level of Mini-Turbo, so players who become comfortable with the tracks will eventually want to practice without it. There is no problem using the assist first and removing it later.
contentBlocks.heading: Smart Steering Is Useful While Learning

contentBlocks.text:
Shortcuts that feel comfortable in slower classes can require different timing at 200cc. Before trying to save a fraction of a second, learn where the course naturally asks you to brake, where a drift should begin and which corners punish excessive speed.

Time Trials are especially useful because they remove the pressure of items and traffic, letting you repeat the same section until the line makes sense.
contentBlocks.heading: Learn the Track Before Chasing Shortcuts

contentBlocks.text:
The shortest route through a corner is not useful if it makes your kart leave the track. In 200cc, giving yourself slightly more room on entry can produce a cleaner exit and better overall speed.

As your braking and drift timing improve, you can tighten those lines gradually. Consistency should come before optimization.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Safer Lines Until Your Timing Improves

contentBlocks.text:
Trying to memorize every 200cc course at once turns the mode into noise. Pick one cup, learn its braking points and repeat it until the speed begins to feel normal.

Once your eyes adjust to how quickly corners arrive, the skills transfer to other tracks. The goal is not faster reactions so much as earlier decisions.
contentBlocks.heading: Practice One Cup at a Time

quickRead: Braking is normal in 200cc. Nintendo explicitly recommends the B Button on tight corners at higher engine classes.
Start drifts earlier than you would in 150cc and use short brake inputs during a drift when the kart is carrying too much speed.
Favor a controllable setup with useful handling and acceleration while learning; maximum top speed is less valuable if you cannot hold the racing line.
Smart Steering can help beginners stay on the course, but it limits some advanced drifting options, so treat it as a learning aid rather than a permanent requirement.
conclusion:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe 200cc becomes manageable once you stop treating braking as lost time. Start turns earlier, use brief brake inputs to control drifts, and favor a setup you can place accurately rather than chasing maximum speed immediately.

From there, practice individual tracks until their rhythm changes from reactive to predictable. Smart Steering can help during that learning phase, but the long-term skill is understanding where the kart needs to slow down before the corner arrives. In 200cc, control is what makes the speed useful.

title: The 10 Best Games You Can Finish in Under 20 Hours
description: The best games you can finish in under 20 hours, using typical main-story time rather than completionist play — from Portal 2 and Astro Bot to Stray and Firewatch.
body:
Not every great game needs to become a month-long project. This list is for players who want a complete single-player experience that can usually be finished in under 20 hours when following the main story rather than pursuing every collectible, optional challenge, or alternate ending.\n\nRuntime varies by player, difficulty, and exploration style, so the threshold here is intentionally practical rather than absolute. Neural Critic favors games whose shorter length feels purposeful instead of incomplete.

For a closer look at one of the list’s larger adventures that still fits the main-story threshold, read our [Super Mario Odyssey review](/stories/super-mario-odyssey-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario poses beside Cappy against a red world-map background in Super Mario Odyssey promotional artwork, one of the games included in Neural Critic’s under-20-hours list.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Odyssey official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text: A Short Hike can be finished very quickly, but rushing misses much of what makes it special. Climbing, gliding, fishing, talking to other hikers, and finding small detours give the island a relaxed density. It proves that an open-ended structure does not require an enormous map or a huge time commitment to feel generous.
contentBlocks.caption: A Short Hike ranks No. 10: A tiny open world where wandering is the point.
contentBlocks.heading: A Short Hike
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Short Hike artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A tiny open world where wandering is the point

contentBlocks.text: What Remains of Edith Finch is short enough to finish in one or two sittings, yet each family story introduces a new visual or mechanical idea. That compression gives the experience unusual momentum. There is no filler between major moments, and the changing forms of interaction make its small runtime feel deliberate rather than limited.
contentBlocks.caption: What Remains of Edith Finch ranks No. 9: A brief narrative experiment with almost no wasted motion.
contentBlocks.heading: What Remains of Edith Finch
contentBlocks.imageAlt: What Remains of Edith Finch artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A brief narrative experiment with almost no wasted motion

contentBlocks.text: Firewatch builds an entire game around one wilderness assignment and the relationship formed over a radio. Exploration is simple, but the setting, performances, and evolving conversations give ordinary walks narrative purpose. Its compact length fits the story: the game leaves before its central dynamic has time to become routine.
contentBlocks.caption: Firewatch ranks No. 8: A focused mystery carried by atmosphere and conversation.
contentBlocks.heading: Firewatch
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Firewatch artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A focused mystery carried by atmosphere and conversation

contentBlocks.text: Inside wastes almost no time explaining itself. Movement, environmental puzzles, sound, and unsettling visual details carry the player through a short sequence of increasingly strange spaces. Because the game rarely stops to provide exposition, its pacing remains exceptionally tight and the experience can be completed without turning into a long-term commitment.
contentBlocks.caption: Inside ranks No. 7: A tightly controlled journey built on visual storytelling.
contentBlocks.heading: Inside
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Inside artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A tightly controlled journey built on visual storytelling

contentBlocks.text: Stray uses its short runtime to keep the focus on movement through a distinctive robot city. Exploration, light puzzles, environmental storytelling, and the simple pleasure of navigating spaces as a cat give the game personality without requiring a sprawling structure. Optional discoveries can extend the journey, but the central path remains refreshingly manageable.
contentBlocks.caption: Stray ranks No. 6: A compact adventure with a strong sense of place.
contentBlocks.heading: Stray
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Stray artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A compact adventure with a strong sense of place

contentBlocks.text: Rift Apart delivers the scale and visual polish of a major action game while keeping its main campaign relatively focused. Weapons evolve quickly, planets introduce new traversal ideas, and dimensional transitions keep the pace moving. It is a useful reminder that a technically ambitious game does not need an oversized campaign to justify itself.
contentBlocks.caption: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart ranks No. 5: A polished blockbuster that does not overstay its welcome.
contentBlocks.heading: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A polished blockbuster that does not overstay its welcome

contentBlocks.text: Super Mario Odyssey contains far more than a short game’s worth of Power Moons, but reaching the main ending is a focused journey that fits comfortably below the enormous runtimes associated with modern open worlds. Players who want more can keep exploring for dozens of additional challenges; players who want closure can reach it without treating the game like a checklist.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Odyssey ranks No. 4: A main story that stays compact even when the world invites much more.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Odyssey
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Super Mario Odyssey artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A main story that stays compact even when the world invites much more

contentBlocks.text: Hi-Fi Rush synchronizes combat, animation, platforming, and environmental movement to music, giving the campaign an energy that rarely dips. Its chapters are substantial enough to develop new mechanics without becoming repetitive, and the main story stays focused. Optional challenges provide extra depth for players who want to keep mastering the rhythm after the credits.
contentBlocks.caption: Hi-Fi Rush ranks No. 3: Rhythm gives an action campaign exceptional pacing.
contentBlocks.heading: Hi-Fi Rush
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Hi-Fi Rush artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Rhythm gives an action campaign exceptional pacing

contentBlocks.text: Astro Bot offers a complete platforming campaign without asking for an enormous time investment. Levels constantly introduce fresh mechanics, transformations, and playful hardware ideas, which makes the game feel larger than its runtime suggests. Completionists can spend longer finding every Bot and secret, but the core journey remains tightly paced.
contentBlocks.caption: Astro Bot ranks No. 2: A dense platformer where almost every level introduces a new idea.
contentBlocks.heading: Astro Bot
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Astro Bot artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A dense platformer where almost every level introduces a new idea

contentBlocks.text: Portal 2 takes the top spot because its length and structure are almost perfectly matched. Each puzzle concept develops far enough to become interesting before the game moves to the next layer, while dialogue and environmental storytelling give the spaces personality between tests. It feels complete, inventive, and memorable without needing dozens of hours to prove its ideas.
contentBlocks.caption: Portal 2 ranks No. 1: A near-perfect example of a game ending exactly when it should.
contentBlocks.heading: Portal 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Portal 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A near-perfect example of a game ending exactly when it should

quickRead: A tiny open world where wandering is the point
A brief narrative experiment with almost no wasted motion
A focused mystery carried by atmosphere and conversation
conclusion: Shorter games are not valuable because they demand less attention. They are valuable when their length gives ideas enough room to develop without forcing them to repeat. Portal 2 remains an exceptional example of that discipline, while Astro Bot and Hi-Fi Rush show that modern games can still deliver spectacle without becoming enormous commitments.\n\nFor this list, finishing the main story is the standard. Optional content can push several of these games well beyond 20 hours, which is a benefit rather than a contradiction: the player gets to decide whether the credits are the ending or the beginning of a longer completionist run.
conclusionHeading: A complete game does not need to be a long game

title: Super Mario Odyssey Power Moons Explained: How Many You Need and What They Unlock
description: A clear Super Mario Odyssey Power Moon guide explaining how moons power the Odyssey, how many are needed for the story, and what 250, 500, 880 and 999 moons unlock.
body:
Power Moons are the main progression currency in Super Mario Odyssey, but the game never expects you to collect every moon before moving on. Each kingdom gives Mario far more moons than he needs for the next destination, which means you can choose between following obvious objectives, exploring for secrets or returning later with new knowledge.

The important thresholds are easy to remember once you separate story progression from post-game completion. At least 124 Power Moons are needed to finish the main story, 250 unlock the Dark Side, 500 unlock the Darker Side, and the much larger totals beyond that are completion goals rather than requirements for seeing the ending.

For our broader take on Nintendo’s 3D platformer, read the [Super Mario Odyssey review](/stories/super-mario-odyssey-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario poses beside Cappy against a red world-map background in Super Mario Odyssey promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Odyssey official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
The Odyssey airship needs Power Moons to reach new kingdoms. After you complete a kingdom’s main objective, the globe beside the ship shows how many additional moons are required before you can depart.

Those requirements are intentionally lower than the number of moons available in the area. You are free to collect the easiest ones, chase secrets that catch your attention or leave difficult moons for a later visit.
contentBlocks.heading: Power Moons Are Fuel for the Odyssey

contentBlocks.text:
The minimum total needed to progress through the required kingdoms and complete the main story is 124 Power Moons. The game contains far more than that before the final confrontation, so a first playthrough does not need to become a completion run.

If you are stuck on a particular moon, look elsewhere. Another challenge in the same kingdom is often much easier, and the game is designed around having multiple routes to the next threshold.
contentBlocks.heading: You Need 124 Moons to Finish the Main Story

contentBlocks.text:
Major kingdom objectives often award a Multi Moon instead of a single Power Moon. A Multi Moon adds three to your total, which is why completing the main objective in a kingdom usually makes a noticeable contribution toward the next travel requirement.

Treat those story rewards as anchors, then fill the remaining gap with ordinary moons found through exploration, races, platforming challenges, puzzles and character interactions.
contentBlocks.heading: Multi Moons Count as Three

contentBlocks.text:
After the main story is complete, your total moon count begins opening additional destinations. Reaching 250 Power Moons unlocks the Dark Side of the Moon, a post-game kingdom built around tougher challenges and rematches.

You do not need 250 unique moon objectives specifically. What matters is the total displayed by the Odyssey.
contentBlocks.heading: 250 Moons Unlock the Dark Side

contentBlocks.text:
Reaching 500 Power Moons unlocks the Darker Side, the game’s final major challenge kingdom. This is a much more demanding platforming test than the normal story path, so there is no reason for a first-time player to rush toward it immediately after the credits.

The 500-moon target works well as a long-term post-game goal because returning to earlier kingdoms reveals many challenges you may have walked past the first time.
contentBlocks.heading: 500 Moons Unlock the Darker Side

contentBlocks.text:
After finishing the story, previously sealed Moon Rocks can be activated in the kingdoms. Doing so reveals additional Power Moons and adds another layer of objectives to areas you already explored.

That is why trying to fully clear every kingdom before the ending is unnecessary. Some of the game’s moon hunt is deliberately reserved for the post-game.
contentBlocks.heading: Moon Rocks Expand the Post-Game Hunt

contentBlocks.text:
Collecting every unique Power Moon brings the total to 880. Reaching that completion milestone changes the Odyssey’s sail and opens an additional challenge connected to the Moon Kingdom.

This is a true completionist target rather than normal progression. It requires revisiting kingdoms, finishing post-game content and solving challenges that are much more demanding than the minimum story route.
contentBlocks.heading: There Are 880 Unique Power Moons

contentBlocks.text:
The Odyssey’s displayed total can rise to 999 because Power Moons can also be purchased. That means the maximum counter is not the same thing as the number of unique collectible objectives in the world.

If your goal is to experience the game’s actual challenges, focus first on the unique moons. Buying extra moons is mainly useful for raising the displayed total after you have already engaged with the content you care about.
contentBlocks.heading: 999 Is a Counter Milestone, Not 999 Unique Challenges

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Odyssey gives you several ways to get nudges when a moon is proving difficult. Talking to characters, paying attention to kingdom clues and using the game’s hint systems can point you in the right direction without revealing the entire solution.

That approach preserves the joy of discovery while preventing one obscure moon from stopping your progress. The structure is deliberately forgiving: when one objective becomes frustrating, another is almost always available.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Hints Instead of Turning Every Moon Into a Search

quickRead: You need at least 124 Power Moons to complete Super Mario Odyssey’s main story; you do not need every moon in each kingdom.
Collecting 250 total moons after completing the story unlocks the Dark Side, while 500 unlocks the Darker Side.
There are 880 unique Power Moons to obtain through the game’s challenges and exploration; collecting them all changes the Odyssey and unlocks an additional challenge.
The counter can reach 999 because additional Power Moons can be purchased, so 999 does not mean there are 999 unique moon challenges.
conclusion:
For a normal Super Mario Odyssey playthrough, the number that matters first is 124: that is enough to complete the main story. Everything after that turns the moon hunt into a post-game progression ladder, with the Dark Side at 250 and the Darker Side at 500.

Completionists can keep going toward all 880 unique moons and eventually a 999 counter, but the game works best when you treat moons as invitations to explore rather than boxes that must be checked in order. Collect what looks fun, return later when new objectives appear, and let the kingdom structure give you options whenever one challenge stops being enjoyable.

title: Breath of the Wild Best Early Armor and Essential Upgrades
description: The best early Breath of the Wild armor to prioritize, including practical defense, cold resistance, stealth and the Great Fairy upgrades that make early gear last longer.
body:
Breath of the Wild gives Link several useful armor options very early, but the smartest approach is not to chase one supposedly perfect set. Early Hyrule asks you to solve different problems: survive stronger hits, travel through cold regions, move quietly and conserve stamina while exploring.

A small collection of practical armor is more useful than one expensive outfit. Start with affordable defense, keep the Warm Doublet or another climate solution available, consider stealth gear if gathering and sneaking matter to you, and unlock a Great Fairy so the equipment you already own can grow with you.

For broader early-game guidance, start with our [Breath of the Wild beginner’s guide](/stories/breath-of-the-wild-beginners-guide/) and see our [Breath of the Wild review](/stories/the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild-review/) for the wider game.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Link stands on a rocky overlook above Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, with the open landscape stretching into the distance.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
The Hylian set is a dependable early foundation because it is accessible in the first major settlements and does not ask you to complete a difficult combat challenge before you can wear it. Its pieces provide straightforward defense and can be enhanced by Great Fairies later.

You do not need to buy all three pieces at once. Replace your weakest clothing first, then keep enough rupees for arrows, ingredients, lodging and other early expenses.
contentBlocks.heading: Start With Affordable General Defense

contentBlocks.text:
Cold resistance is one of the first environmental systems Breath of the Wild teaches, and it remains relevant well beyond the tutorial. The Warm Doublet is therefore worth keeping even after you find armor with higher defense.

A climate piece saves food and lets you stay in colder regions longer. Later armor can provide stronger or more flexible temperature protection, but an early resistance item is still useful enough to keep in your inventory.
contentBlocks.heading: The Warm Doublet Remains Useful After the Great Plateau

contentBlocks.text:
The Stealth set sold in Kakariko Village improves how quietly Link moves. That matters when approaching wildlife, catching insects, gathering certain materials or avoiding unwanted attention while exploring.

For players who spend a lot of time gathering and cooking, stealth gear can be more valuable than a small increase in armor. It changes how you interact with the world rather than simply reducing incoming damage.
contentBlocks.heading: Stealth Armor Can Save More Time Than Defense

contentBlocks.text:
Hateno Village offers heavier Soldier equipment with strong defensive value, but beginners do not need to rush there and buy the entire set immediately. It costs more than basic clothing and offers less utility outside direct survivability.

Treat it as an option when tougher encounters begin exposing a real defense problem. If the Hylian pieces you already own are doing the job, Great Fairy upgrades may be the more efficient next step.
contentBlocks.heading: Soldier Gear Is a Defense Upgrade, Not an Early Requirement

contentBlocks.text:
Great Fairies enhance armor in exchange for materials. Even one unlocked fountain makes basic equipment noticeably more valuable because you can raise its defense instead of replacing it outright.

The first accessible Great Fairy near Kakariko is an important early progression target. You do not need to abandon the main story to hunt every fountain immediately, but unlocking enhancement early gives purpose to many materials you collect during normal exploration.
contentBlocks.heading: Unlock a Great Fairy as Soon as It Is Convenient

contentBlocks.text:
Because each enhancement consumes materials, improving every item at once spreads your resources too thin. Begin with a general-defense set or pieces you wear constantly, then add upgrades to specialized armor once you know which effects matter to your playstyle.

This keeps rare materials available for later sets while still giving you an immediate defensive improvement.
contentBlocks.heading: Upgrade a Small Core Wardrobe First

contentBlocks.text:
Some complete armor sets gain an additional effect once all three matching pieces have been enhanced sufficiently. Nintendo’s own Explorer’s Guide highlights this as one of the reasons upgrading full sets can matter.

That is useful to remember, but it should not control your first few hours. Early on, mixing a stealth piece, cold-resistance item and stronger defensive clothing is often more practical than forcing a matching outfit.
contentBlocks.heading: Set Bonuses Reward Investment Later

contentBlocks.text:
Monster parts, minerals and other materials are easy sources of rupees, but many are also used by Great Fairies. Selling every stack can leave you buying back progress later through more gathering.

Keep a reasonable reserve of common materials until you know which armor you intend to improve. Sell extras when you need money, not simply because the inventory number looks large.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Sell Materials Before Checking Their Upgrade Value

quickRead: The Hylian set is a strong budget starting point because it is easy to buy, upgradeable and useful almost everywhere.
Keep the Warm Doublet or another cold-resistance option available instead of relying only on food every time the temperature drops.
The Stealth set is one of the best utility purchases for gathering, hunting and approaching wildlife, even when it is not your highest-defense outfit.
Great Fairy upgrades matter more than constantly replacing armor; many sets also gain a bonus once the full set has been enhanced to the required level.
conclusion:
Breath of the Wild’s best early armor strategy is about flexibility. Use affordable Hylian gear for dependable defense, keep the Warm Doublet or another climate option ready, and add stealth equipment if gathering and exploration are a major part of how you play.

Most importantly, unlock Great Fairy enhancement before assuming you need completely new armor. Upgraded early gear can remain useful for a long time, and a small wardrobe that covers defense, weather and utility will carry you farther than one expensive set worn everywhere.
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

title: The 12 Best 3D Platformers
description: The best 3D platformers, ranked for movement, level design, exploration and inventive traversal — from Mario Galaxy and Odyssey to Astro Bot and Psychonauts 2.
body:
The best 3D platformers make movement enjoyable before collectibles, upgrades, or spectacle enter the picture. A jump, dive, spin, roll, or wall-run should feel expressive enough that simply crossing a space becomes part of the reward.\n\nNeural Critic’s ranking favors games with precise movement, inventive level design, strong use of three-dimensional space, and enough mechanical variety to keep traversal interesting from the opening stage to the final challenge.

For more on the top of the list, read our [Super Mario Galaxy 2 review](/stories/super-mario-galaxy-2-review-platforming-ideas-at-full-speed/), [Super Mario Galaxy review](/stories/super-mario-galaxy-review-platforming-masterpiece-among-the-stars/) and [Super Mario Odyssey review](/stories/super-mario-odyssey-review/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario rides Yoshi through a colorful cosmic scene in Super Mario Galaxy 2 promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Nintendo / official game imagery

contentBlocks.text: A Hat in Time embraces the playful structure of older collectathon platformers without feeling trapped by nostalgia. Hats create light ability changes, levels shift between exploration and more directed challenges, and the movement is flexible enough to make revisiting spaces enjoyable. It is uneven in places, but its personality and mechanical confidence earn it a place here.
contentBlocks.caption: A Hat in Time ranks No. 12: A cheerful collectathon with movement that invites experimentation.
contentBlocks.heading: A Hat in Time
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Hat in Time artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A cheerful collectathon with movement that invites experimentation

contentBlocks.text: Crash Bandicoot 4 is far more linear than most games on this list, but that focus lets it build unusually dense platforming challenges. Perspective, timing, masks, wall-running, rails, and moving hazards are layered aggressively. Completionist demands can become excessive, yet the core stages show how strong a tightly authored 3D obstacle course can be.
contentBlocks.caption: Crash Bandicoot 4: It’s About Time ranks No. 11: Precise 3D platforming built around demanding obstacle courses.
contentBlocks.heading: Crash Bandicoot 4: It’s About Time
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Crash Bandicoot 4: It’s About Time artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Precise 3D platforming built around demanding obstacle courses

contentBlocks.text: Sonic X Shadow Generations combines remastered Sonic Generations material with a Shadow campaign that gives high-speed 3D movement more room to evolve. Boosting, rails, homing attacks, alternate routes, and spectacle constantly compete for attention, but at its best the game makes speed feel like something the player earns through route knowledge rather than something happening automatically.
contentBlocks.caption: Sonic X Shadow Generations ranks No. 10: Speed-focused 3D platforming with two distinct rhythms.
contentBlocks.heading: Sonic X Shadow Generations
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Sonic X Shadow Generations artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Speed-focused 3D platforming with two distinct rhythms

contentBlocks.text: The Spyro trilogy remains appealing because its spaces are easy to understand and satisfying to clear. Gliding, charging, collecting, and searching for hidden routes create a relaxed rhythm that contrasts with more demanding platformers. The Reignited presentation modernizes the trilogy without changing the simple movement-and-exploration foundation that made it enduring.
contentBlocks.caption: Spyro Reignited Trilogy ranks No. 9: Exploration-first platforming built around readable spaces.
contentBlocks.heading: Spyro Reignited Trilogy
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Spyro Reignited Trilogy artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Exploration-first platforming built around readable spaces

contentBlocks.text: It Takes Two is broader than a pure platformer, but movement and spatial problem-solving remain central throughout its constantly changing co-op adventure. Each area introduces tools that alter how two players navigate and cooperate, then moves on before the idea becomes repetitive. Its greatest strength is mechanical generosity: almost every chapter wants to teach the pair a new way to move together.
contentBlocks.caption: It Takes Two ranks No. 8: Co-op platforming that keeps replacing its own mechanics.
contentBlocks.heading: It Takes Two
contentBlocks.imageAlt: It Takes Two artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Co-op platforming that keeps replacing its own mechanics

contentBlocks.text: Rift Apart blends shooting with platforming, but its dimensional transitions, rails, wall movement, aerial traversal, and tightly directed environments give movement a major role. The game is more guided than Mario or Psychonauts, yet its technical spectacle is strongest when it changes how the player crosses a level rather than simply decorating it.
contentBlocks.caption: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart ranks No. 7: Platforming and action connected by unusually fast spatial transitions.
contentBlocks.heading: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Platforming and action connected by unusually fast spatial transitions

contentBlocks.text: Psychonauts 2 uses psychic worlds to make level design reflect the personalities and problems of the characters Raz encounters. Platforming, powers, visual metaphors, and storytelling continually reinforce one another. The movement is not the most demanding on this list, but few 3D platformers use the genre’s freedom to make environments this conceptually inventive.
contentBlocks.caption: Psychonauts 2 ranks No. 6: Imaginative worlds turn platforming into character design.
contentBlocks.heading: Psychonauts 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Psychonauts 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Imaginative worlds turn platforming into character design

contentBlocks.text: Kirby and the Forgotten Land succeeds by making 3D movement approachable without making levels empty. Copy abilities, Mouthful Mode, hidden objectives, and compact stages give every area several layers of interaction. It is easier than many platformers here, but the clarity of its design makes exploration consistently rewarding rather than merely simple.
contentBlocks.caption: Kirby and the Forgotten Land ranks No. 5: Nintendo’s pink hero adapts naturally to full 3D spaces.
contentBlocks.heading: Kirby and the Forgotten Land
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Kirby and the Forgotten Land artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Nintendo’s pink hero adapts naturally to full 3D spaces

contentBlocks.text: Astro Bot understands that a platforming level does not need to preserve every idea for later. New mechanics arrive constantly, often supporting one stage or sequence before the game happily replaces them with something else. That confidence creates exceptional pacing, while responsive movement and playful use of hardware make even straightforward jumps feel satisfying.
contentBlocks.caption: Astro Bot ranks No. 4: A modern showcase for tactile, idea-dense platforming.
contentBlocks.heading: Astro Bot
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Astro Bot artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A modern showcase for tactile, idea-dense platforming

contentBlocks.text: Super Mario Galaxy changed the shape of a platforming level by letting gravity point in almost any direction. Small planets, curved surfaces, launch stars, and shifting perspectives repeatedly challenge the player’s sense of orientation without sacrificing readable controls. Its best ideas still feel elegant because gravity is not a gimmick added to Mario’s movement; it changes the spaces that movement can inhabit.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Galaxy ranks No. 3: Gravity turns three-dimensional space into a toy.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Super Mario Galaxy artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Gravity turns three-dimensional space into a toy

contentBlocks.text: Super Mario Odyssey gives the player an enormous vocabulary of movement and then builds kingdoms open enough to reward mastering it. Cappy extends jumps, creates improvised routes, and turns enemies into temporary movement systems through captures. The sheer number of Power Moons means quality varies, but the freedom of traversal makes simply moving through a kingdom unusually satisfying.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Odyssey ranks No. 2: Mario’s most expressive movement sandbox.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Odyssey
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Super Mario Odyssey artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Mario’s most expressive movement sandbox

contentBlocks.text: Super Mario Galaxy 2 takes the gravity-driven foundation of the first game and pushes it toward denser, more focused level design. Yoshi abilities, shifting gravity, disappearing platforms, drills, clouds, and countless one-off ideas are introduced with remarkable efficiency. It has less narrative atmosphere than Galaxy, but as a pure sequence of three-dimensional platforming challenges, it remains Neural Critic’s benchmark.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Galaxy 2 ranks No. 1: Platforming ideas refined into an almost relentless sequence.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Super Mario Galaxy 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Platforming ideas refined into an almost relentless sequence

quickRead: A cheerful collectathon with movement that invites experimentation
Precise 3D platforming built around demanding obstacle courses
Speed-focused 3D platforming with two distinct rhythms
conclusion: Great 3D platformers make space itself interesting. The player should want to move because movement feels good, then discover that the level is constantly finding new ways to test or reward that movement.\n\nGalaxy 2 remains Neural Critic’s top pick because almost every stage introduces a strong idea and develops it without overstaying its welcome. Odyssey offers more freedom, Astro Bot more modern spectacle, and Psychonauts 2 more conceptual storytelling, which shows how many directions the genre can still take.

title: Tears of the Kingdom Best Early Armor and Upgrades
description: The best early Tears of the Kingdom armor to prioritize, plus how Great Fairy upgrades work and which pieces are worth improving first.
body:
Tears of the Kingdom gives Link access to a huge wardrobe, but the early game does not require you to chase rare armor sets across the entire map. A few accessible pieces can cover the problems that matter most at the start: basic defense, cold protection, stealth and movement utility.

The bigger lesson is that armor becomes much more valuable once you unlock Great Fairy upgrades. Instead of constantly replacing what you wear, build a small practical collection, upgrade the pieces you use most, and keep enough monster parts and materials on hand to improve them later.

For broader early-game guidance, start with our [Tears of the Kingdom beginner’s guide](/stories/tears-of-the-kingdom-beginners-guide/) and see our [Tears of the Kingdom review](/stories/the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom-review/) for the wider game.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Link overlooks Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, with floating sky islands visible above the landscape.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
For a new file, the Hylian set is the easiest armor recommendation to make because it solves a basic problem without sending you into a dangerous region or a long side quest. Pieces of the set are sold at Lookout Landing, the settlement the main story naturally introduces near the start of the surface journey.

The set does not provide a flashy special effect, but that is part of its value. It gives you dependable defense, works in almost every situation and can be enhanced later. If you are still wearing low-defense tutorial clothing, replacing it with one or two Hylian pieces is an immediate quality-of-life improvement.
contentBlocks.heading: Start With the Hylian Set at Lookout Landing

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom lets you mix head, body and leg pieces freely. Early on, there is no need to spend all your rupees completing a matching set when one useful piece already solves the problem in front of you.

Buy for function first. A stronger chest piece, a cold-resistance item or a stealth piece can be combined with whatever else you own. Full sets become more important later when you are chasing set bonuses, specialized builds or a particular look.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Buy a Full Set Just Because It Matches

contentBlocks.text:
The opening Sky Island already teaches that temperature matters, and the surface expands that idea across several regions. One piece of cold-resistant armor can reduce how often you need to rely on temporary food effects when traveling through colder areas.

The Archaic Warm Greaves are a useful early example if you picked them up during the opening, while the Snowquill set in Rito Village becomes a stronger long-term option for players spending time in Hebra. You do not need the full Snowquill set immediately; buying only the protection you currently need keeps early spending under control.
contentBlocks.heading: Keep Cold Protection Available Early

contentBlocks.text:
Stealth-focused armor is valuable because it changes how easily you can approach wildlife, gather insects and avoid drawing attention while exploring. That makes it useful even when its raw defense is not your highest available option.

If your playstyle involves collecting materials, approaching animals or moving carefully through enemy-controlled spaces, carrying a stealth piece can save time in ways a slightly stronger defensive item cannot.
contentBlocks.heading: Stealth Armor Is Utility, Not Just Defense

contentBlocks.text:
Armor enhancement is one of the biggest early progression upgrades available. Nintendo’s own beginner guidance points players to the Lucky Clover Gazette in Hebra to begin Potential Princess Sightings, then to Woodland Stable for Serenade to a Great Fairy. Completing that chain opens your first Great Fairy upgrade access.

Once enhancement is available, ordinary armor can become much stronger. That makes improving a useful piece you already own a better investment than repeatedly buying replacements with similar base defense.
contentBlocks.heading: Unlock a Great Fairy Before Chasing Expensive Armor

contentBlocks.text:
Great Fairy upgrades cost rupees and materials, so spreading resources across every armor piece is inefficient early on. Start with the items that appear in your normal exploration loadout: a general-defense piece, a climate item you use often and any utility armor that supports your preferred playstyle.

This approach keeps your materials concentrated where they have an immediate effect while leaving room to build specialized sets later.
contentBlocks.heading: Upgrade the Pieces You Actually Wear

contentBlocks.text:
It is tempting to sell large stacks of horns, fangs and other monster parts whenever you need rupees. Some of those same materials are used in armor enhancement, which means selling everything can create a second grind later.

You do not need to hoard every item forever, but keep a reserve of common drops until you know which armor you intend to upgrade. Rare materials are especially worth checking before you cash them in.
contentBlocks.heading: Save Common Monster Parts for Enhancement

contentBlocks.text:
The armor screen encourages direct comparison through defense numbers, but defense is only one reason to wear a piece. Temperature resistance, stealth, climbing support, skydiving mobility and other effects can be more important than a few extra points of protection depending on where you are going.

A good early wardrobe therefore looks less like one permanent best set and more like a small toolkit. Carry a dependable defensive option, then swap individual pieces when the environment demands something different.
contentBlocks.heading: Defense and Utility Solve Different Problems

quickRead: The Hylian set is the best simple early purchase because it is available at Lookout Landing, inexpensive compared with specialty sets and easy to keep useful through upgrades.
Unlock Great Fairy enhancement early by starting Potential Princess Sightings at the Lucky Clover Gazette and completing Serenade to a Great Fairy near Woodland Stable.
Keep at least one climate-focused piece such as cold-resistance armor available; utility is often more valuable than a small defense increase.
Do not sell every monster part for rupees. Armor upgrades consume materials, and common drops become useful again as soon as Great Fairy enhancement opens up.
conclusion:
The best early armor strategy in Tears of the Kingdom is simple: buy dependable protection at Lookout Landing, keep one or two useful specialty pieces, and unlock Great Fairy enhancement before spending heavily on replacements.

The Hylian set is a strong foundation because it is accessible and upgradeable, but do not confuse a matching outfit with an optimal loadout. Mix pieces freely, save useful materials, and improve the armor that solves the problems you actually encounter. That approach stays useful much longer than chasing every set as soon as you hear about it.
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

title: The 12 Best Turn-Based RPGs
description: The best turn-based RPGs, ranked for tactical combat, party building, progression and storytelling — from Baldur’s Gate 3 to Clair Obscur and Persona 5 Royal.
body:
Turn-based RPGs are in unusually strong shape because the format no longer points to one style of game. A modern turn-based RPG can be a reactive computer RPG, a character-driven JRPG, a tactical party game, or a compact indie adventure. What connects the best of them is that choosing an action feels more important than choosing it quickly.\n\nNeural Critic’s ranking favors battle systems that stay interesting across a full campaign, meaningful party or build decisions, and stories that benefit from the slower pace rather than merely tolerating it.

Our top pick also anchors a growing RPG cluster: see the [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) and [beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The main Baldur’s Gate 3 companions stand together beneath a stormy fantasy sky; Baldur’s Gate 3 ranks first in Neural Critic’s turn-based RPG list.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text: Chained Echoes borrows the visual language of classic 16-bit RPGs without copying their pacing. Its Overdrive system asks the party to balance aggression with control, while character progression avoids some of the grinding associated with older genre traditions. It is a strong choice for players who want a traditional-feeling adventure with modern structural discipline.
contentBlocks.caption: Chained Echoes ranks No. 12: A compact throwback that keeps its systems moving.
contentBlocks.heading: Chained Echoes
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Chained Echoes artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A compact throwback that keeps its systems moving

contentBlocks.text: Sea of Stars makes turn-based combat easy to understand without making every encounter automatic. Timed inputs, combo attacks, and enemy spell locks keep the player engaged between commands, while its bright world and straightforward party structure make it one of the easiest games here to recommend to someone returning to the genre.
contentBlocks.caption: Sea of Stars ranks No. 11: Accessible turn-based combat wrapped in a polished adventure.
contentBlocks.heading: Sea of Stars
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Sea of Stars artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Accessible turn-based combat wrapped in a polished adventure

contentBlocks.text: Rogue Trader is demanding, but its density is the point. Positioning, action economy, character archetypes, and an unusually reactive role-playing structure give the campaign real strategic weight. It is less welcoming than the games above it, but players who enjoy learning a complicated ruleset are rewarded with a party RPG where mechanical and narrative choices regularly intersect.
contentBlocks.caption: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader ranks No. 10: Dense CRPG tactics for players who want consequences and systems.
contentBlocks.heading: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Dense CRPG tactics for players who want consequences and systems

contentBlocks.text: Three Houses works because its tactical maps are inseparable from the characters the player develops between battles. Teaching, relationships, class progression, and recruitment make the roster feel personal, while the campaign structure encourages replay from different perspectives. The strategy is approachable, but the long-term decisions give it staying power.
contentBlocks.caption: Fire Emblem: Three Houses ranks No. 9: Tactical battles made stronger by the people fighting them.
contentBlocks.heading: Fire Emblem: Three Houses
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Fire Emblem: Three Houses artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Tactical battles made stronger by the people fighting them

contentBlocks.text: Octopath Traveler II combines separate character stories with a battle system built around breaking enemy defenses and banking boost points for decisive turns. The structure can feel segmented compared with a fully unified party narrative, but the combat is consistently readable and expressive. It is particularly good at making small tactical decisions matter without burying the player in rules.
contentBlocks.caption: Octopath Traveler II ranks No. 8: Eight journeys supported by one of the genre’s sharpest battle systems.
contentBlocks.heading: Octopath Traveler II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Octopath Traveler II artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Eight journeys supported by one of the genre’s sharpest battle systems

contentBlocks.text: Dragon Quest XI S does not try to reinvent the foundations of the genre. Instead, it demonstrates how effective those foundations can be when the pacing, party roles, exploration, and progression are carefully tuned. Its combat remains approachable for newcomers while still giving experienced players enough control over party composition and difficulty to stay engaged.
contentBlocks.caption: Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age ranks No. 7: Traditional turn-based design polished to an exceptional standard.
contentBlocks.heading: Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Traditional turn-based design polished to an exceptional standard

contentBlocks.text: Infinite Wealth makes positioning part of a command-based battle system. Characters move around the battlefield, attacks can bounce enemies into allies or environmental objects, and job systems create room for experimentation. The result feels distinctly physical for a turn-based RPG, while the cast and side stories give the enormous campaign its personality.
contentBlocks.caption: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth ranks No. 6: Turn-based combat with the energy of a street fight.
contentBlocks.heading: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based combat with the energy of a street fight

contentBlocks.text: Before Baldur’s Gate 3, Divinity: Original Sin 2 established many of the ideas that would define Larian’s modern identity. Surfaces, status effects, vertical spaces, teleportation, and environmental interactions turn battles into small systemic puzzles. Its armor rules can be restrictive, but few turn-based RPGs give the player this much freedom to improvise.
contentBlocks.caption: Divinity: Original Sin 2 ranks No. 5: Larian’s elemental sandbox still rewards experimentation.
contentBlocks.heading: Divinity: Original Sin 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Divinity: Original Sin 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Larian’s elemental sandbox still rewards experimentation

contentBlocks.text: Metaphor adapts Atlus’s press-turn philosophy to an Archetype system that encourages the party to change roles as new challenges appear. Exploiting weaknesses creates extra opportunities, but careless choices can hand momentum back to the enemy. That tension combines with calendar management and strong party relationships to make progression feel strategic inside and outside combat.
contentBlocks.caption: Metaphor: ReFantazio ranks No. 4: A class-driven JRPG where every turn has purpose.
contentBlocks.heading: Metaphor: ReFantazio
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Metaphor: ReFantazio artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A class-driven JRPG where every turn has purpose

contentBlocks.text: Persona 5 Royal remains one of the clearest examples of combat and character progression reinforcing each other. Exploiting weaknesses keeps battles fast, while relationships developed during the calendar feed new abilities back into dungeon exploration. Its campaign is extremely long, but the systems give everyday choices enough meaning to justify the commitment.
contentBlocks.caption: Persona 5 Royal ranks No. 3: Turn-based combat, social life, and time management working together.
contentBlocks.heading: Persona 5 Royal
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Persona 5 Royal artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based combat, social life, and time management working together

contentBlocks.text: Clair Obscur adds real-time dodges and parries to a turn-based framework without letting reflexes replace planning. Party builds, status effects, turn order, and skill choices still matter, but the player remains physically engaged when enemies attack. It is a convincing example of how the genre can modernize its rhythm without abandoning strategic decision-making.
contentBlocks.caption: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 ranks No. 2: Turn-based planning with active defense and dramatic momentum.
contentBlocks.heading: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based planning with active defense and dramatic momentum

contentBlocks.text: Baldur’s Gate 3 takes the top spot because its turn-based combat is only one part of a larger system of player choice. Positioning, spells, environmental interactions, party composition, dialogue, and exploration continually overlap. A good plan can involve damage, deception, gravity, terrain, or avoiding the fight entirely. Few RPGs make tactical decisions feel this connected to role-playing.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur’s Gate 3 ranks No. 1: The most reactive modern turn-based RPG.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur’s Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Baldur’s Gate 3 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most reactive modern turn-based RPG

quickRead: A compact throwback that keeps its systems moving
Accessible turn-based combat wrapped in a polished adventure
Dense CRPG tactics for players who want consequences and systems
conclusion: Turn-based combat works best when the pause between actions creates better decisions rather than simply slower ones. Baldur’s Gate 3 offers the widest systemic freedom, Clair Obscur adds an unusually active rhythm, and Atlus continues to show how strongly party combat can connect to character progression.\n\nThe genre is broad enough that no single ruleset defines it anymore. That variety is exactly why turn-based RPGs feel so healthy: the best games keep finding new reasons for the player to stop, think, and commit to a choice.
conclusionHeading: Turn-based RPGs are defined by decisions, not speed

title: The 10 Best Games Like Baldur’s Gate 3
description: The 10 best games like Baldur’s Gate 3, from reactive CRPGs and party-based tactical adventures to RPGs built around companions, choices and unusual solutions.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 is difficult to replace because its strongest qualities overlap: tactical combat, companions with their own priorities, dialogue that reacts to the player, class-driven problem solving, exploration, and a campaign that is willing to let unexpected decisions stand.

The best follow-up therefore depends on which part mattered most to you. Some of these games are closer to Baldur’s Gate 3 mechanically, while others match its reactive role-playing, party relationships, or willingness to let choices reshape a playthrough. The ranking favors games that preserve that feeling of authorship rather than simply sharing a fantasy setting.

For the reference point behind these recommendations, read our [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) and [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The main Baldur’s Gate 3 companions stand together beneath a stormy fantasy sky in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text: Solasta is one of the clearest choices for players whose favorite part of Baldur’s Gate 3 is translating tabletop-style abilities into turn-based battles. Positioning, spell use, party composition, vertical spaces, and the action economy all matter.
