Its characters and cinematic presentation are much less elaborate than Larian’s, but the combat rules are readable and the game is unusually good at showing how a party’s abilities fit together.
contentBlocks.caption: Solasta: Crown of the Magister ranks No. 10: For players who want more D&D-style tactical combat.
contentBlocks.heading: Solasta: Crown of the Magister
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Solasta: Crown of the Magister artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For players who want more D&D-style tactical combat

contentBlocks.text: Wasteland 3 replaces fantasy with a post-apocalyptic world, but the role-playing structure should feel familiar. A customizable party moves through turn-based combat, dialogue can redirect quests, factions remember decisions, and seemingly small choices can create consequences later. The tone is harsher and more satirical than Baldur’s Gate 3, yet both games are strongest when a mission becomes a problem with several imperfect solutions.
contentBlocks.caption: Wasteland 3 ranks No. 9: Party tactics and consequential choices in a very different setting.
contentBlocks.heading: Wasteland 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Wasteland 3 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Party tactics and consequential choices in a very different setting

contentBlocks.text: Tyranny begins from an unusual premise: the conquering empire has effectively won, and your character helps determine what that victory means on the ground. Dialogue, reputation, allegiance, and earlier decisions continually reshape later situations. Combat is real-time with pause rather than turn-based, but players who loved Baldur’s Gate 3 because it allowed uncomfortable choices and divergent outcomes may find Tyranny’s reactivity unusually satisfying.
contentBlocks.caption: Tyranny ranks No. 8: A shorter CRPG built around consequences from the opening minutes.
contentBlocks.heading: Tyranny
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Tyranny artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A shorter CRPG built around consequences from the opening minutes

contentBlocks.text: Disco Elysium removes almost everything that looks like Baldur’s Gate 3 combat and concentrates on another part of the appeal: inhabiting a character through decisions. Skills interrupt conversations, failed checks can create new scenes instead of simple dead ends, and the protagonist’s personality emerges from what the player repeatedly chooses to value. It is a very different game mechanically, but one of the closest matches for reactive role-playing.
contentBlocks.caption: Disco Elysium ranks No. 7: For players who want skill checks, dialogue, and failure to matter.
contentBlocks.heading: Disco Elysium
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Disco Elysium artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For players who want skill checks, dialogue, and failure to matter

contentBlocks.text: Rogue Trader combines a large party, turn-based encounters, character builds, companion quests, and decisions that can shift relationships across a long campaign. Its Warhammer setting is denser and more rules-heavy than Baldur’s Gate 3, and the game can overwhelm newcomers with terminology. Players willing to learn it, however, get a CRPG that repeatedly asks how power should be used rather than merely whether the next battle can be won.
contentBlocks.caption: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader ranks No. 6: A huge party-based CRPG with turn-based combat and moral pressure.
contentBlocks.heading: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A huge party-based CRPG with turn-based combat and moral pressure

contentBlocks.text: Deadfire offers a dense class system, recruitable companions, faction conflicts, exploration by ship, and quests that rarely fit into simple good-versus-evil categories. Combat is less immediately approachable than Baldur’s Gate 3 and the presentation is more traditional, but the underlying role-playing is extremely flexible. It is especially strong for players who enjoy understanding what every party member can contribute both in battle and conversation.
contentBlocks.caption: Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire ranks No. 5: For deep party building and a world that reacts to competing loyalties.
contentBlocks.heading: Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For deep party building and a world that reacts to competing loyalties

contentBlocks.text: Wrath of the Righteous is much more complicated than Baldur’s Gate 3, but that complexity creates extraordinary build freedom. Classes, archetypes, feats, spells, party composition, and Mythic progression can shape a character in dramatically different directions, while major campaign choices alter how the story develops. It is not the first recommendation for a CRPG newcomer, but it is one of the strongest next steps for someone ready for a denser ruleset.
contentBlocks.caption: Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous ranks No. 4: For players who want far deeper character building and enormous campaign choices.
contentBlocks.heading: Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For players who want far deeper character building and enormous campaign choices

contentBlocks.text: Dragon Age: Origins is older and its real-time-with-pause combat feels very different, but the companion structure remains remarkably easy to connect with after Baldur’s Gate 3. Party members have opinions, relationships can change, dialogue matters, and the protagonist’s origin affects how parts of the world respond. Players who came to BG3 for camp conversations and the feeling of traveling with distinct personalities should still find a great deal to appreciate.
contentBlocks.caption: Dragon Age: Origins ranks No. 3: The classic choice for companion-driven fantasy role-playing.
contentBlocks.heading: Dragon Age: Origins
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dragon Age: Origins artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The classic choice for companion-driven fantasy role-playing

contentBlocks.text: The first Original Sin already contains many of the ideas Larian would later refine. Surfaces interact, positioning can transform a battle, spells combine in unexpected ways, and quests are often designed around several possible solutions. Its writing and companion work are less sophisticated than Baldur’s Gate 3, but playing it reveals how Larian learned to turn a CRPG battlefield into a sandbox rather than a fixed sequence of attacks.
contentBlocks.caption: Divinity: Original Sin ranks No. 2: The earlier version of Larian’s systemic combat philosophy.
contentBlocks.heading: Divinity: Original Sin
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Divinity: Original Sin artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The earlier version of Larian’s systemic combat philosophy

contentBlocks.text: Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the natural next game because so much of Baldur’s Gate 3’s design philosophy is already fully formed. Environmental interactions can rewrite combat, party members bring personal stories and conflicts, quests support multiple approaches, and character builds give the player room to experiment. It lacks the D&D license and the cinematic presentation of BG3, but few RPGs are as willing to let the player test an unusual idea and then continue when it works.
contentBlocks.caption: Divinity: Original Sin 2 ranks No. 1: The closest overall match for Larian-style freedom, tactics, and improvisation.
contentBlocks.heading: Divinity: Original Sin 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Divinity: Original Sin 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The closest overall match for Larian-style freedom, tactics, and improvisation

quickRead: For players who want more D&D-style tactical combat
Party tactics and consequential choices in a very different setting
A shorter CRPG built around consequences from the opening minutes
conclusion:
If what you want is the closest overall substitute, start with Divinity: Original Sin 2. If companions and dialogue mattered most, Dragon Age: Origins remains an excellent bridge. Players who want a much denser ruleset can move toward Pathfinder or Rogue Trader, while Disco Elysium is the best reminder that reactive role-playing does not require tactical combat at all.

What these games share with Baldur’s Gate 3 is not one ruleset or camera angle. It is the feeling that a role-playing game should notice what the player decides to do.
conclusionHeading: The best BG3 alternatives respond to the player

title: Baldur’s Gate 3 Difficulty Modes Explained: Which Should You Choose?
description: Baldur’s Gate 3 difficulty modes explained, including Explorer, Balanced, Tactician, Honour and Custom, plus which setting makes the most sense for a first playthrough.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 has several difficulty options because “difficulty” in this RPG means more than enemy health. The setting can change how demanding combat feels, how forgiving the game is when you make mistakes, and in Honour Mode, even how freely you can reload after a bad outcome.

For most first-time players, Balanced is the best place to start. It preserves the game’s tactical combat without expecting deep knowledge of Dungeons & Dragons rules. Explorer is there if story and experimentation matter more than combat pressure, while Tactician and Honour are better suited to players who already understand the systems.

If you are choosing a first setup, pair this with our [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/) and [best classes for beginners guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-best-classes-beginners/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The central Baldur’s Gate 3 cast stands together against a dramatic fantasy backdrop in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Balanced is the standard experience and the easiest recommendation for a first playthrough. Enemies can still punish poor positioning or careless resource use, but the mode gives you enough room to learn what your spells, actions and companions actually do.

Start here if you enjoy tactical RPGs but do not already know Baldur’s Gate 3 or tabletop D&D well. You can learn initiative, concentration, saving throws, rests and party composition as they become relevant instead of solving the whole ruleset before the first major encounter.

If Balanced starts feeling too easy or too demanding, the game gives you ways to adjust rather than forcing you to restart the campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: Balanced — The Best Starting Point for Most Players

contentBlocks.text:
Explorer is the more forgiving preset. It is designed for players who want to focus on story, companions, exploration and choice without every combat encounter becoming a test of party optimization.

Choosing Explorer does not remove the systems that make Baldur’s Gate 3 interesting. You still make dice rolls, manage a party, explore alternate routes and decide how to approach quests. The difference is that combat gives you more breathing room while you learn.

There is no reason to avoid Explorer because you think it is the “wrong” way to play. If lower combat pressure makes you more willing to experiment with the game’s role-playing systems, the mode is doing its job.
contentBlocks.heading: Explorer — Best If You Want Less Combat Pressure

contentBlocks.text:
Tactician raises the demand on your party and on the decisions you make inside combat. Encounters are less forgiving of weak positioning, wasted actions and parties that do not cover one another’s weaknesses.

This is a better fit once you understand how to create Advantage, protect concentration, control dangerous enemies and use short- and long-rest resources intentionally. It also rewards players who pay attention to equipment and who are comfortable changing tactics when an encounter is not working.

A newcomer can absolutely start on Tactician, but expect a steeper learning curve and more time spent reading tooltips, adjusting the party and reconsidering approaches.
contentBlocks.heading: Tactician — For Players Who Want the Systems to Push Back

contentBlocks.text:
Honour Mode builds on Tactician and adds additional challenge rules, including Legendary Actions for major bosses and a save structure designed to prevent repeatedly reloading old saves to erase mistakes. Larian introduced the mode specifically as a step beyond its previous hardest preset.

That changes the character of the campaign. A failed plan can have consequences you must continue with, which makes knowledge of encounters, character builds and resource management much more valuable.

For that reason, Honour is not the difficulty we recommend for a first blind playthrough. It is much better as a later challenge once you already understand how Baldur’s Gate 3 communicates danger and how its major systems interact.
contentBlocks.heading: Honour Mode — The High-Stakes Challenge Run

contentBlocks.text:
Custom Mode is useful when none of the presets match the experience you want. Instead of accepting one package of rules, you can adjust individual difficulty settings and create something between the standard presets.

That can be useful for players who enjoy tougher combat but still want more forgiving exploration rules, or for groups where different players have very different levels of experience.

Larian also expanded the ability to move an existing campaign into Custom Mode, although Honour campaigns remain a special case. Custom is therefore a practical answer when you know exactly which part of the game you want to make easier or harder.
contentBlocks.heading: Custom Mode — Build the Difficulty You Actually Want

contentBlocks.text:
For the standard presets, difficulty is not a permanent character-creation decision. You can adjust the experience later, and patches have expanded the ability to move set-difficulty campaigns into Custom Mode.

That means beginners do not need to agonize over the choice before they understand the game. Start on Balanced if you are unsure. If fights are interrupting your enjoyment, move toward Explorer or a more forgiving Custom setup. If you are winning without needing most of your party’s tools, move upward.

Honour Mode is intentionally more restrictive, so treat it as a challenge commitment rather than a casual difficulty toggle.
contentBlocks.heading: Can You Change Difficulty After You Start?

contentBlocks.text:
Before lowering or raising the difficulty, check whether the problem is actually your party. A group with no durable frontline presence, no reliable way to recover, or several characters competing for the same role can make ordinary encounters feel much harder than they need to be.

Likewise, a well-built party can make Balanced feel dramatically easier once you understand actions, bonus actions, concentration and positioning. Difficulty and party composition are connected, but they are not the same thing.

If one encounter feels impossible, try changing companions, preparing different spells or approaching from another direction before assuming the entire campaign is set too high.
contentBlocks.heading: Difficulty Does Not Fix a Party That Is Missing Basic Roles

contentBlocks.text:
Choose Balanced if you want the game’s tactical systems to matter but still want room to learn. Choose Explorer if combat friction is getting between you and the role-playing experience. Move to Tactician only if you actively want the rules to demand more from your builds and decisions.

Honour is best saved for a later run, and Custom is ideal once you know which parts of the game you want to tune independently.

The best setting is the one that keeps you making interesting decisions. A difficulty mode that turns every encounter into frustration is not automatically more authentic, and a lower setting that lets you explore more of the game is not a lesser experience.
contentBlocks.heading: Which Difficulty Should a Beginner Choose?

quickRead: Balanced is the best default recommendation for most first-time players.
Explorer reduces combat pressure for players who want to focus more heavily on story and exploration.
Tactician and Honour increase the consequences of mistakes and are better suited to players comfortable with the rules.
Custom Mode is the most flexible choice if you want to tune individual difficulty settings rather than accept one preset.
conclusion:
For most first-time Baldur’s Gate 3 players, start on Balanced. It gives combat enough weight to teach you the systems without requiring the kind of encounter knowledge that Tactician and Honour reward. Explorer is the better choice when you mainly want story and experimentation, while Custom gives you finer control once you know what you want to change.

Do not treat the opening difficulty screen as a permanent test of skill. Baldur’s Gate 3 is a long RPG, and the right setting is the one that keeps its choices, companions and combat interesting across the whole campaign.

For the wider fundamentals, read Neural Critic’s [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/). Our [class guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-best-classes-beginners/) and [companions guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-companions-guide/) can help you build a party that fits the difficulty you choose, while our [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) covers the game as a whole.

title: Baldur’s Gate 3 Best Classes for Beginners: Which Class Should You Pick?
description: The best Baldur’s Gate 3 classes for beginners, with approachable picks for melee combat, spellcasting, dialogue and exploration in the current Patch 8 version.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you 12 base classes before subclasses and multiclassing enter the picture, which can make character creation feel more complicated than it needs to be. For a first playthrough, the best class is not the one with the highest theoretical damage ceiling. It is the one that teaches the game clearly while still giving you useful options when plans go wrong.

In the current Patch 8 version, every base class has more subclass variety than it did at launch, but the fundamentals have not changed: Fighters and Barbarians remain easy to understand in combat, Warlocks offer a relatively compact introduction to spellcasting, and Charisma-focused classes such as Paladin and Bard can make a main character especially flexible in conversations. Your first choice is also not permanent, because Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you access to class respeccing early in the adventure.

If you are still learning the wider ruleset, our [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/) and [difficulty modes guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-difficulty-modes-explained/) are useful next reads.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The central Baldur’s Gate 3 cast stands together against a dramatic fantasy backdrop in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Fighter is the easiest class to recommend to someone learning Baldur’s Gate 3 for the first time because its turn-to-turn decisions are clear. You have strong equipment options, a large health pool, a Fighting Style at Level 1, Second Wind for emergency recovery, and Action Surge from Level 2 for an extra action when a fight suddenly becomes dangerous.

That simplicity does not make Fighter weak or boring. At Level 3 you choose a subclass, and the class can stay straightforward or become more tactical depending on what you pick. Champion keeps the basic weapon-focused rhythm simple, Battle Master adds manoeuvres and resource decisions, Eldritch Knight introduces spellcasting, and Patch 8 added Arcane Archer for players who want a more specialised ranged style.

For a beginner who wants to spend more time learning positioning, actions, equipment and the rest of the party instead of studying a spell list, Fighter is the cleanest starting point.
contentBlocks.heading: Best Overall Beginner Class: Fighter

contentBlocks.text:
Barbarian is the best alternative if you want a direct, aggressive frontline character. Rage is the class’s defining system: while active it increases physical damage output, grants resistance to physical damage, and improves Strength checks and saving throws. That extra durability gives new players more room to make positioning mistakes without immediately losing control of a fight.

Reckless Attack also gives the class an easy way to improve its chance to hit, although enemies gain an advantage when attacking you in return. That trade-off is simple to understand and teaches an important Baldur’s Gate 3 lesson: powerful actions usually come with a cost or condition.

Berserker is an especially easy subclass concept to read, while Wildheart, Wild Magic and Patch 8’s Giant option add more choices. If your ideal first character is someone who gets into the middle of combat and keeps going, Barbarian is one of the most forgiving starts.
contentBlocks.heading: Best Simple Melee Class: Barbarian

contentBlocks.text:
Warlock is a useful first spellcaster because its magic is built around a smaller, more repeatable toolkit than classes such as Wizard, Cleric or Druid. Warlock uses Charisma for spellcasting, learns Eldritch Blast at Level 1, and restores its Warlock spell slots on a short rest rather than waiting for a long rest.

That creates a readable combat rhythm: Eldritch Blast gives you a dependable ranged option, a limited number of stronger spells solve specific problems, and Eldritch Invocations let you customise the class as you level. You still learn spell ranges, concentration, saving throws and positioning, but you are not managing a huge prepared-spell catalogue from the start.

Patch 8 added Hexblade alongside The Fiend, The Great Old One and The Archfey, giving the class another way to lean toward weapon combat. For a first playthrough, though, the main reason to choose Warlock is that it introduces spellcasting without asking you to learn every part of the magic system at once.
contentBlocks.heading: Best Beginner Spellcaster: Warlock

contentBlocks.text:
Paladin is one of the strongest choices for players who want their main character to feel useful both in combat and conversation. The class combines martial equipment, healing, Divine Smite and support abilities with Charisma, which also contributes to important dialogue skills such as Persuasion, Deception and Intimidation.

The trade-off is additional complexity. Paladins manage spell slots and prepared spells while also following the tenets of an oath. Choices that violate that oath can change the class through Baldur’s Gate 3’s Oathbreaker system, so role-playing decisions have a mechanical consequence that Fighters and Barbarians do not need to track.

That makes Paladin slightly less beginner-friendly than Fighter, but potentially more satisfying if you want your custom protagonist to handle important conversations without giving up a powerful frontline role.
contentBlocks.heading: Best for Combat and Dialogue: Paladin

contentBlocks.text:
Bard is the strongest beginner recommendation for someone who cares more about conversations, skills and flexibility than having the simplest combat turn. Charisma powers Bard spellcasting and helps with dialogue, while the class also gains broad skill utility and Bardic Inspiration to support other characters.

The cost of that flexibility is that Bards have more decisions to make. You choose spells, decide when to spend Bardic Inspiration, and eventually specialise through College of Lore, College of Swords, College of Valour or Patch 8’s College of Glamour.

A Bard can be an excellent first main character because so many non-combat situations give you something useful to do. It is not as immediately simple as Fighter or Barbarian, but it rewards players who want the protagonist to be the party’s conversational and problem-solving centre.
contentBlocks.heading: Best for Skills and Dialogue: Bard

contentBlocks.text:
Rogue is easy to understand conceptually but asks you to learn the conditions behind Sneak Attack. You deal extra damage when you have Advantage or when an eligible target is threatened by an adjacent ally, provided you are not attacking with Disadvantage. Once that clicks, Rogue becomes a clear mix of mobility, skills, stealth and burst damage.

Ranger is also approachable, especially for players who want ranged combat, exploration utility and a small amount of spellcasting, but its character-creation choices can make the class look more complicated than its actual early combat rhythm.

Monk is fast and direct but introduces Ki resources and a greater emphasis on positioning, unarmed attacks and bonus actions. None of these classes is a bad first choice. They simply ask you to understand one or two additional systems before they feel as natural as Fighter or Barbarian.
contentBlocks.heading: Rogue, Ranger and Monk Are Accessible With a Little More Context

contentBlocks.text:
The four most spell-focused recommendations require more reading, but they are absolutely playable on a first run if their fantasy appeals to you.

Cleric combines armour, healing, support and a prepared spell list. Druid adds spellcasting, Wild Shape and several different ways to approach combat. Sorcerer has a smaller known-spell list but introduces Metamagic and Sorcery Points. Wizard offers one of the broadest spell toolkits in the game and rewards players who enjoy learning what a large number of spells can do.

These classes can feel more demanding because spell slots, concentration, spell preparation or spell selection matter from the beginning. The upside is that learning one of them teaches a large part of Baldur’s Gate 3’s combat system very quickly. If you already know you want to play a dedicated spellcaster, do not avoid them just because Fighter is simpler.
contentBlocks.heading: Cleric, Druid, Sorcerer and Wizard Are Better If You Want to Learn Magic Deeply

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 still has the same 12 base classes: Barbarian, Bard, Cleric, Druid, Fighter, Monk, Paladin, Ranger, Rogue, Sorcerer, Warlock and Wizard. Patch 8, released in April 2025 as Larian’s final major content patch, added one new subclass to each of those classes rather than adding a thirteenth base class.

Those additions include Giant Barbarian, College of Glamour Bard, Death Domain Cleric, Circle of Stars Druid, Arcane Archer Fighter, Way of the Drunken Master Monk, Oath of the Crown Paladin, Swarmkeeper Ranger, Swashbuckler Rogue, Shadow Magic Sorcerer, Hexblade Warlock and Bladesinging Wizard.

For beginners, that extra variety is useful but not something you need to optimise around during character creation. Start with the base class whose basic turn makes sense to you, then treat subclass selection as a way to refine that playstyle once you have seen the game in motion.
contentBlocks.heading: Patch 8 Added Subclasses, Not New Base Classes

contentBlocks.text:
Multiclassing lets you spend character levels across more than one class, creating combinations that can be extremely powerful or highly specialised. It can also delay important class features and make progression harder to read if you do not already understand what each class is giving up.

Larian itself recommends previous Dungeons & Dragons experience for players who want to take full advantage of multiclassing. That is good advice for a first Baldur’s Gate 3 character too. A single-class build reaches its core features naturally and makes it much easier to understand why your character is improving.

Once you understand actions, spell slots, short rests, feats and the strengths of your party, multiclassing becomes a much more interesting experiment rather than another system to solve during your first hour.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Multiclass Just Because the Option Exists

contentBlocks.text:
The most important reason not to overthink character creation is that Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you a way to rebuild classes early in the adventure. After meeting the relevant camp NPC in Act 1, you can restart a character’s class progression from Level 1 and make new choices for attributes, proficiencies, spells and other class features.

That option applies to your protagonist and can also be used on playable companions. It means a first character is an experiment rather than a permanent contract. If Fighter starts to feel too simple, you can try a caster. If a large spell list becomes overwhelming, you can move toward a martial class without restarting the campaign.

For that reason, the best beginner class is ultimately the one that gets you into the game with the least anxiety about building incorrectly.
contentBlocks.heading: Your First Class Choice Is Not Permanent

quickRead: Fighter is the easiest overall class to recommend to a new Baldur’s Gate 3 player because its core turns are simple and durable.
Barbarian is a forgiving aggressive frontline choice, while Warlock is a manageable introduction to spellcasting.
Paladin and Bard are strong alternatives if dialogue and character interaction matter as much as combat.
Patch 8 added one new subclass to each of the 12 base classes, but beginners are better served by learning one class before multiclassing.
conclusion:
For most new players, Fighter is the safest recommendation because it teaches Baldur’s Gate 3’s combat fundamentals without surrounding every turn with extra resource management. Barbarian is nearly as approachable for aggressive melee play, while Warlock is the cleanest starting point for someone who specifically wants to learn magic.

Paladin and Bard are stronger choices if you want your main character to carry more of the conversation system, and the remaining classes are all viable if their fantasy is what excites you. The important thing is not to build around an endgame spreadsheet before you understand the first few levels. Pick a class whose basic role makes sense, learn how the party supports it, and remember that respeccing gives you room to change your mind.

For a broader introduction to the game, start with Neural Critic’s [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/). Once your class is chosen, our [companions guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-companions-guide/) and [difficulty guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-difficulty-modes-explained/) can help shape the rest of your first playthrough. You can also read our [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) for the wider editorial view.

title: Baldur’s Gate 3 Companions Guide: Who to Recruit and What They Do
description: A spoiler-light Baldur’s Gate 3 companions guide covering all 10 recruitable companions, their default classes, party roles and what each brings to a beginner party.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you more companions than you can take into the field at once, and that is deliberate. Your active party is limited, but the wider camp lets you swap characters in as different quests, conversations and combat situations call for different strengths.

For a first playthrough, the easiest way to think about companions is not as a list of characters you must optimize. Think of them as ready-made specialists. Some are naturally suited to frontline combat, some cover healing or spellcasting, and others excel at stealth, dialogue or exploration. Their default classes are useful starting points, but Baldur’s Gate 3 also gives you room to respec characters later if you want to experiment.

For more help building a first party, see our [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/) and [beginner class guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-best-classes-beginners/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The main Baldur’s Gate 3 companions stand together beneath a stormy fantasy sky in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Your active adventuring party contains your character plus up to three companions. The rest can wait at camp, where you can talk to them, follow their personal stories and swap them into the group when you want a different mix of abilities.

Baldur’s Gate 3 has six recruitable Origin companions — Shadowheart, Lae’zel, Astarion, Gale, Wyll and Karlach — plus four additional companions who can join later: Halsin, Minthara, Jaheira and Minsc. Patch 8 was the final major content patch, and Larian said it would not make significant new changes to companion storylines, so that roster remains the useful current reference point.

For beginners, start by learning what each character does in their default class. You can worry about advanced respecs or unusual party compositions later.
contentBlocks.heading: How Companions Work in Baldur’s Gate 3

contentBlocks.text:
Shadowheart begins as a Cleric, making her one of the easiest companions to understand as the party’s support character. Clerics can heal, protect allies, apply useful buffs and still contribute meaningful damage or control when healing is not needed.

She is especially valuable in a first playthrough because support magic gives you more room to recover from mistakes. Do not reduce her to a dedicated healer, though. A Cleric turn is often better spent preventing damage, controlling an enemy or finishing a threat than restoring a small amount of health after the fact.

If your main character is already a Cleric or another support-heavy caster, you can still use Shadowheart, but she becomes less essential to a balanced beginner lineup.
contentBlocks.heading: Shadowheart — Cleric: Support, Healing and Utility

contentBlocks.text:
Lae’zel is a Fighter, which makes her one of the cleanest companions for new players. Fighters are durable, work well with weapons and armor, and gain strong actions without forcing you to manage a long spell list.

Her job is easy to read: get into a useful position, pressure dangerous enemies and absorb attention that would otherwise fall on more fragile party members. That straightforward role is a major advantage while you are still learning initiative, movement and the action economy.

If your own character is a caster, rogue or support class, Lae’zel is an easy way to add a dependable frontline presence without complicating the party.
contentBlocks.heading: Lae’zel — Fighter: The Straightforward Frontline Choice

contentBlocks.text:
Astarion starts as a Rogue, giving the party excellent Dexterity-based utility. He is naturally useful for tasks such as lockpicking, trap handling and stealth, and his combat strength comes from creating the conditions for Sneak Attack rather than simply trading hits on the front line.

For beginners, his biggest value may be outside combat. Baldur’s Gate 3 constantly presents locked doors, containers and alternate routes, so having a character who handles those interactions reliably makes exploration smoother.

In battle, keep an eye on positioning and Advantage rather than treating him like a Fighter. Astarion rewards players who look for favorable angles and vulnerable targets.
contentBlocks.heading: Astarion — Rogue: Locks, Traps, Stealth and Precision

contentBlocks.text:
Gale is a Wizard, which means he brings a wide range of arcane spells and can adapt to many situations as his spellbook grows. Wizards can deal damage, control groups, protect allies and solve exploration problems with magic.

That flexibility comes with more reading and resource management than a Fighter or Barbarian. New players should resist the urge to memorize every spell immediately. Give Gale a small set of spells whose purposes you understand, then expand as you become comfortable with concentration, spell slots and saving throws.

He is an excellent companion for a party that otherwise leans heavily toward physical combat.
contentBlocks.heading: Gale — Wizard: The Broadest Spell Toolkit

contentBlocks.text:
Wyll begins as a Warlock. Compared with a Wizard, the class works with a smaller spell selection and spell slots that return on a short rest, which can make its rhythm easier to learn.

Warlocks also have reliable repeatable options, so Wyll rarely feels useless when you do not want to spend a limited spell slot. His Charisma is useful for his own class abilities and fits a character whose story frequently intersects with conversation and role-playing choices.

If you want magical damage in the party without managing Gale’s larger spellbook, Wyll is a good alternative.
contentBlocks.heading: Wyll — Warlock: A Simpler Route Into Spellcasting

contentBlocks.text:
Karlach is a Barbarian, built around an aggressive frontline role. Rage improves her ability to stay in a fight, and the class is easy to understand because its strongest decisions are usually about positioning, target priority and when to commit to an attack.

For players who find Lae’zel’s Fighter appealing but want something even more direct and forceful, Karlach fills a similar party slot with a different rhythm. You usually do not need both in a standard four-person beginner party unless your main character and fourth slot are covering enough support and utility.

Choose between them based on whose playstyle and personality you enjoy rather than assuming one is universally better.
contentBlocks.heading: Karlach — Barbarian: Simple, Aggressive Frontline Power

contentBlocks.text:
Halsin and Minthara can become companions later depending on how your playthrough develops. Halsin is a Druid, bringing spellcasting, support and Wild Shape flexibility. Minthara is a Paladin, combining frontline durability with Charisma-based magic and burst damage.

Their recruitment is more dependent on story progression than the six early Origin companions, so a spoiler-light beginner guide should not treat either one as a character you need to build around from the opening hours.

If they join you, evaluate them by role: Halsin can cover a flexible caster/support slot, while Minthara is comfortable as a durable frontline character with magical tools.
contentBlocks.heading: Halsin and Minthara — Later Alternatives With Very Different Roles

contentBlocks.text:
Jaheira and Minsc are returning Baldur’s Gate characters who can join later in the adventure. Jaheira’s default Druid class gives her broad spell and Wild Shape utility, while Minsc arrives as a Ranger with a more martial, exploration-oriented toolkit.

Because both come later, they are better understood as options for reshaping a party you already know rather than solutions to early-game weaknesses. By the time they become relevant, you should have enough experience with combat and party roles to decide whether they replace someone in your established group.

Their value is as much about story and character perspective as mechanical coverage.
contentBlocks.heading: Jaheira and Minsc — Experienced Reinforcements for Later in the Adventure

contentBlocks.text:
There is no single best four-character party because your custom character already occupies one of those slots. A Fighter protagonist does not need the same support as a Wizard protagonist.

A useful beginner template is one frontline character such as Lae’zel or Karlach, one support or control caster such as Shadowheart or Gale, and one flexible utility slot such as Astarion, Wyll or whichever companion covers a weakness in your own class. That gives you durability, magic and exploration tools without demanding advanced multiclass planning.

Swap companions when you want their story perspective, when a quest clearly involves them, or when your current party keeps struggling with the same kind of problem. Baldur’s Gate 3 is designed around changing the group, not locking yourself into one mathematically perfect lineup.
contentBlocks.heading: The Best Beginner Party Is the One That Covers Your Main Character’s Weaknesses

quickRead: Your active group is your character plus up to three companions, while the rest can wait at camp and be swapped in later.
The six recruitable Origin companions are Shadowheart, Lae’zel, Astarion, Gale, Wyll and Karlach.
Halsin, Minthara, Jaheira and Minsc are additional recruitable companions who join under different conditions.
For a first playthrough, learn what companions do in their default classes before worrying about advanced respecs or unusual party compositions.
conclusion:
Baldur’s Gate 3’s companions work best when you stop asking which three are “the best” and start asking what your current party is missing. Shadowheart covers support, Lae’zel and Karlach provide straightforward frontline strength, Astarion handles Dexterity-heavy utility, Gale brings the broadest arcane toolkit, and Wyll offers a simpler style of spellcasting. The later companions give you even more ways to reshape the group as the campaign develops.

For a first playthrough, keep the default classes long enough to understand their identities, then experiment when you know what problem you are trying to solve. The strongest party is usually not the one copied from an optimized build list — it is the one whose abilities you understand and whose characters you actually want beside you.

If you are still deciding how your own character fits into the party, our [Baldur’s Gate 3 class guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-best-classes-beginners/) and [beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/) cover the fundamentals. Our [difficulty guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-difficulty-modes-explained/) explains which preset best matches the kind of campaign you want, while the [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) looks at the game’s broader strengths and trade-offs.

title: Why Baldur’s Gate 3’s Companions Make Player Choice Feel Personal
description: An analysis of how Baldur’s Gate 3 uses companion relationships, approval, conflict and reactivity to make player decisions feel personal.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 makes companion relationships feel personal because party members are not treated as passive quest dispensers. They watch what the player does, respond to values and decisions, argue with one another, reveal information at different times and can push back when the player’s choices conflict with their own priorities.

The result is not perfect simulation, but it is convincing reactivity. Choice matters because it changes how the people travelling with you understand the character you are choosing to become.

For more on the RPG around those relationships, read our [Baldur’s Gate 3 review](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-review/) and [Baldur’s Gate 3 beginner’s guide](/stories/baldurs-gate-3-beginners-guide/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The main Baldur’s Gate 3 companions stand together beneath a stormy fantasy sky in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official promotional artwork.

contentBlocks.text: A dialogue option can be mechanically small and still feel important when a companion reacts to it. Baldur’s Gate 3 repeatedly places party members close enough to the player’s decisions that moral, practical and impulsive choices acquire a social audience. That turns “what outcome do I want?” into a second question: “what does this tell the people travelling with me?”
contentBlocks.heading: Companions Turn Abstract Choices Into Social Consequences

contentBlocks.text: The approval system gives the game a way to track accumulated impressions, but the strongest moments are usually more specific. A companion may challenge an action, remember a decision, open a new conversation or change how warmly they respond later. Larian has continued fixing these contextual reactions across patches, which shows how much the illusion depends on the right response appearing at the right time.
contentBlocks.heading: Approval Is Useful, but It Is Not the Whole Relationship

contentBlocks.text: A party where everyone supports every decision would make choice easier but less meaningful. Baldur’s Gate 3 allows companions to have incompatible values, histories and priorities. Helping one person can frustrate another. A compassionate response may impress one companion and irritate someone more pragmatic. Those tensions create the sense that the party exists independently of the player’s need for validation.
contentBlocks.heading: Disagreement Makes Companions Feel Like People

contentBlocks.text: Camp is where many immediate decisions gain a second life. A choice made during exploration can return later as a conversation, confession, argument or change in tone. Because these scenes are separated from the original event, the game creates the feeling that companions have been thinking about what happened rather than simply firing a scripted response and forgetting it.
contentBlocks.heading: Camp Gives Reactions Time to Become Relationships

contentBlocks.text: Companions often arrive with an obvious surface identity: the guarded cleric, the proud warrior, the charming rogue, the heroic warlock. Their personal stories gradually complicate those first impressions. Player choice feels more personal because later decisions are made with knowledge that did not exist at the beginning, forcing the player to reconsider assumptions as relationships deepen.
contentBlocks.heading: Personal Quests Reframe Earlier Impressions

contentBlocks.text: Only a limited number of companions travel with the player at once. That practical party limit also becomes a narrative filter. Different combinations produce different comments, banter, skill coverage and reactions, so two players can pass through the same location while receiving a different social texture. The party is therefore part of how the game edits its own story around the player.
contentBlocks.heading: Party Composition Changes the Story You Notice

contentBlocks.text: Baldur’s Gate 3 cannot react uniquely to every possible action. Its strength is choosing enough high-value moments to maintain the impression that the world is listening. When a companion recalls an earlier decision or responds to a specific piece of information, that precision can make the surrounding, more conventional RPG structure feel more reactive than it technically is.
contentBlocks.heading: Reactivity Works Because It Is Selective

contentBlocks.text: The game’s largest branching decisions matter, but companion design gives smaller decisions emotional weight. A choice can affect who trusts the player, who challenges them, what conversation appears at camp or how a relationship develops. The consequence is not always a new quest branch. Sometimes it is simply a person looking at the player differently, which can be more immediate.
contentBlocks.heading: Choice Feels Personal When Someone Else Cares

quickRead: Baldur’s Gate 3 makes companion reactions part of the consequence system rather than treating party members as passive followers.
Approval matters because relationships develop through repeated decisions, disagreements and personal quest choices.
Camp conversations give major decisions room to echo after the immediate quest is over.
conclusion:
Baldur’s Gate 3 makes player choice memorable by attaching it to characters with their own opinions. Approval provides structure, but disagreement, camp conversations, personal quests and contextual reactions are what make that structure feel human.

That is why the companion system strengthens the game’s larger promise of RPG freedom. The player is not only choosing what happens next. They are choosing what kind of person their party believes they are — and discovering which relationships can survive that version of the story.
conclusionHeading: Reactivity becomes meaningful when it has a face

title: The 12 Best Soulslike Games
description: The 12 best Soulslike games, ranked across combat, exploration, progression, boss design and the different ways developers have built on FromSoftware’s formula.
body:
“Soulslike” is useful shorthand, but it has never had a perfectly clean boundary. Some players use it only for games made outside FromSoftware; others use it for the entire design lineage that grew out of Demon’s Souls and Dark Souls. This ranking uses the broader reader-facing definition: the Soulsborne games themselves and the strongest games that build on their ideas.

Neural Critic is ranking them by combat quality, level and encounter design, progression, exploration, boss design, and how successfully each game turns difficulty into learning rather than simple punishment. The result is not a list of the hardest games. It is a list of the games that make the Soulslike loop most rewarding.

For more FromSoftware coverage, read our [Elden Ring review](/stories/elden-ring-review-monumental-open-world/) and our feature on [Dark Souls Remastered’s interconnected world design](/stories/dark-souls-remastered-interconnected-world-design/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished stands beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring, the top-ranked game in Neural Critic’s Soulslike list.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / Elden Ring gameplay screenshot.

contentBlocks.text: Aggro Crab turns the genre’s familiar structure into something lighter without removing the need to learn. Its underwater world is playful, shells function as temporary defenses with different abilities, and the combat still rewards patience, positioning, and understanding enemy patterns. It is especially valuable as an entry point because its personality makes failure feel less intimidating without reducing the satisfaction of overcoming a difficult encounter.
contentBlocks.caption: Another Crab’s Treasure ranks No. 12: A welcoming Soulslike that proves accessibility and challenge can coexist.
contentBlocks.heading: Another Crab’s Treasure
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Another Crab’s Treasure artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A welcoming Soulslike that proves accessibility and challenge can coexist

contentBlocks.text: Remnant II changes the genre’s usual rhythm by making firearms and ranged positioning central to the combat loop, but its structure remains recognizably Soulslike: dangerous spaces, checkpoint resets, build experimentation, difficult bosses, and repeated runs that become easier as the player understands them. Procedural elements make its worlds less tightly authored than FromSoftware’s best areas, but co-op and class-style Archetypes give it a distinct identity.
contentBlocks.caption: Remnant II ranks No. 11: Soulslike pressure rebuilt around ranged combat and co-op.
contentBlocks.heading: Remnant II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Remnant II artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Soulslike pressure rebuilt around ranged combat and co-op

contentBlocks.text: Blasphemous 2 translates Soulslike tension into a 2D action-platformer without simply copying Dark Souls from the side. Its interconnected world, deliberate combat, strange religious imagery, bosses, and weapon-based traversal create a strong sense of place. It is more approachable than some 3D entries because the rules are visually clear, but precision still matters and careless play is punished quickly.
contentBlocks.caption: Blasphemous 2 ranks No. 10: A 2D Soulslike where movement and religious horror carry equal weight.
contentBlocks.heading: Blasphemous 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Blasphemous 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A 2D Soulslike where movement and religious horror carry equal weight

contentBlocks.text: Lords of the Fallen is at its best when its Umbral mechanic changes how exploration works. Moving between the living world and its darker counterpart can reveal routes, alter encounters, and turn death into another layer of navigation. Combat and enemy density are less consistently refined than the games above it, but the world design is ambitious and the game understands that discovery is as important to the genre as difficult bosses.
contentBlocks.caption: Lords of the Fallen ranks No. 9: A large dark-fantasy Soulslike built around two overlapping worlds.
contentBlocks.heading: Lords of the Fallen
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Lords of the Fallen artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A large dark-fantasy Soulslike built around two overlapping worlds

contentBlocks.text: Nioh 2 is less interested in imitating Dark Souls’ world structure than in pushing action-RPG systems much further. Multiple weapon types, stances, Yokai abilities, equipment, statistics, and skill trees create enormous build depth, while Ki management gives every fight a distinctive rhythm. The mission structure is more segmented than a FromSoftware world, but few Soulslikes reward mechanical mastery and character experimentation this strongly.
contentBlocks.caption: Nioh 2 ranks No. 8: The deepest combat and build sandbox in the genre.
contentBlocks.heading: Nioh 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Nioh 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The deepest combat and build sandbox in the genre

contentBlocks.text: Demon’s Souls is where many of the genre’s defining ideas first came together: dangerous levels, limited knowledge, recoverable currency, opaque systems, shortcuts, and bosses that often test understanding more than raw character power. The remake makes Boletaria visually spectacular, but the underlying structure remains intentionally old-fashioned. Some encounters reveal the series’ age; the atmosphere and level identity still feel singular.
contentBlocks.caption: Demon’s Souls ranks No. 7: The foundation still feels strange, severe, and remarkably influential.
contentBlocks.heading: Demon’s Souls
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Demon’s Souls artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The foundation still feels strange, severe, and remarkably influential

contentBlocks.text: Lies of P succeeds because it does more than borrow bonfires and difficult bosses. Its weapon assembly system encourages experimentation, guarding and perfect timing create an aggressive defensive rhythm, and Krat has a strong visual identity of its own. The level structure is more directed than Dark Souls or Elden Ring, but that focus lets the game maintain a remarkably consistent difficulty curve and sense of forward momentum.
contentBlocks.caption: Lies of P ranks No. 6: The most convincing non-FromSoftware refinement of the formula.
contentBlocks.heading: Lies of P
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Lies of P artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most convincing non-FromSoftware refinement of the formula

contentBlocks.text: Dark Souls remains essential because Lordran is not just a sequence of difficult rooms. Shortcuts fold distant areas together, elevators recontextualize spaces you thought you understood, and exploration constantly changes the mental map in your head. Combat is slower and less flexible than later FromSoftware games, but the world’s structure gives every step unusual weight. Few games have made geography itself such an important part of progression.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls Remastered ranks No. 5: The interconnected world that turned a design philosophy into a genre.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls Remastered
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dark Souls Remastered artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The interconnected world that turned a design philosophy into a genre

contentBlocks.text: Dark Souls III trades much of the first game’s maze-like world for faster combat, clearer forward momentum, and an exceptional sequence of bosses. Weapons and builds remain varied, but the game feels most confident when it asks the player to read movement, control spacing, and adapt to increasingly elaborate attack patterns. It is one of the easiest FromSoftware games to recommend after Elden Ring because the combat language feels immediately familiar.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls III ranks No. 4: A focused collection of some of FromSoftware’s best boss fights.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls III
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dark Souls III artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A focused collection of some of FromSoftware’s best boss fights

contentBlocks.text: Sekiro strips away much of the genre’s build flexibility and replaces it with a sharper question: can you learn the fight? Deflection, posture, aggression, and movement make combat feel closer to a duel than a traditional action RPG. That narrower design means there are fewer ways to overpower a difficult encounter, but it also produces some of FromSoftware’s clearest lessons and most satisfying victories.
contentBlocks.caption: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice ranks No. 3: FromSoftware’s most demanding and precise combat system.
contentBlocks.heading: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: FromSoftware’s most demanding and precise combat system

contentBlocks.text: Bloodborne changes player behavior through a few decisive ideas. Shields largely disappear, the regain system rewards immediate retaliation, transforming weapons encourage flexible attacks, and Yharnam’s dense streets create a constant sense of danger. The result is faster than Dark Souls without becoming careless. Its Gothic and cosmic-horror identity also remains one of the strongest worlds FromSoftware has created.
contentBlocks.caption: Bloodborne ranks No. 2: Aggression transforms the Souls formula into something faster and stranger.
contentBlocks.heading: Bloodborne
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Bloodborne artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Aggression transforms the Souls formula into something faster and stranger

contentBlocks.text: Elden Ring earns the top position because its open world changes the relationship between difficulty and progression. A boss can block one road without blocking the entire adventure. Exploration can produce levels, weapons, spells, summons, upgrade materials, or simply a better understanding of the world before you return. That freedom sits on top of FromSoftware’s deepest build variety and some of its most memorable legacy dungeons and bosses. It is both the genre’s broadest invitation and its most complete expression.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring ranks No. 1: The fullest expression of Souls combat, exploration, and player freedom.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Elden Ring artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The fullest expression of Souls combat, exploration, and player freedom

quickRead: A welcoming Soulslike that proves accessibility and challenge can coexist
Soulslike pressure rebuilt around ranged combat and co-op
A 2D Soulslike where movement and religious horror carry equal weight
conclusion:
The Soulslike genre works because difficulty is only the surface. The best games create a cycle in which exploration produces knowledge, failure produces information, and character growth gradually turns something intimidating into something understandable.

Elden Ring is the strongest overall expression of that idea, but the rankings beneath it show how flexible the formula has become. Bloodborne rewards aggression, Sekiro demands precision, Nioh 2 celebrates systems mastery, and games such as Lies of P prove that the genre now has an identity beyond the studio that created it.
conclusionHeading: The best Soulslikes make learning feel like progression

title: Elden Ring Early Game Progression Guide: What to Upgrade First
description: A practical Elden Ring early-game progression guide covering Vigor, flask upgrades, equipment strengthening, Spirit Ashes, exploration and the systems worth prioritizing first.
body:
Elden Ring becomes much easier to read once you stop treating every new level as a damage upgrade. The early game is really about building a reliable foundation: enough health to survive mistakes, stronger recovery, a combat setup you understand, and access to the systems that make exploration more productive.

That matters even more in 2026, because Elden Ring now has additional starting-class options through the Tarnished Pack and Tarnished Edition. Those classes change your opening statistics and equipment, but they do not replace the basic progression priorities that help almost every new character.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished stands beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring, with ruined stone structures and the Lands Between below.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / Elden Ring gameplay screenshot.

contentBlocks.text:
For most new characters, Vigor is the most useful early stat because it increases maximum HP. More health gives you room to survive an unfamiliar attack, heal, and learn what the game was trying to teach you.

That does not mean every level should go into Vigor. Raise the attributes you actually need for the equipment, spells, or playstyle you want to use, but avoid scattering points across several damage stats before you know what your character is becoming. Elden Ring rewards focused investment far more clearly than a little bit of everything.

For the broader first-playthrough basics, see Neural Critic’s [Elden Ring beginner’s guide](/stories/elden-ring-beginners-guide/).
contentBlocks.heading: 1. Build survivability before chasing damage

contentBlocks.text:
Character levels are only one part of progression. The game also expects you to strengthen the equipment you are already using with upgrade materials found throughout the Lands Between.

The safest early approach is to commit resources to one main setup that already feels comfortable rather than trying to improve every new item you pick up. A familiar, upgraded setup usually does more for early consistency than constantly changing direction in search of something supposedly perfect.
contentBlocks.heading: 2. Strengthen a setup you already understand

contentBlocks.text:
Flask upgrades are among the most valuable permanent improvements in the early game. Increasing the number of charges gives you more recovery between checkpoints, while improving the amount restored makes each use more effective.

Because those upgrades help almost every build, they are worth prioritizing whenever exploration gives you the required resources. They also make difficult areas easier without forcing you to change the identity of your character.
contentBlocks.heading: 3. Improve your flasks as soon as you can

contentBlocks.text:
Runes pay for levels and purchases, but carrying a large amount into an unfamiliar dungeon or boss encounter creates pressure that can make experimentation harder.

If you are close to a level or a planned purchase, spend the runes first. If you lose some anyway, remember that discovered Sites of Grace, collected equipment, map progress, upgrades, and everything you learned remain with you. Losing currency is frustrating; it is not the same as losing your character.
contentBlocks.heading: 4. Spend runes before taking unnecessary risks

contentBlocks.text:
The main path is not the only place progression happens. Mines and caves in the opening regions contain upgrade materials and other useful rewards, while churches, ruins, merchants, and optional encounters expand the tools available to you.

This is why walking away from an overwhelming boss is often the correct decision. Exploring somewhere else can improve your character in several different ways before you return, and the game is built around that freedom.
contentBlocks.heading: 5. Let mines, caves, and side areas fund your progression

contentBlocks.text:
Spirit Ashes are a built-in support system that can create breathing room in encounters where the game allows them. If you use a particular summon regularly, its own upgrade path is worth treating as part of your character progression rather than as an afterthought.

You do not have to use summons, but you also do not gain anything by ignoring a system that makes the game more readable or enjoyable for you. Elden Ring supports several different ways of approaching difficult encounters.
contentBlocks.heading: 6. Upgrade Spirit Ashes if they are part of your playstyle

contentBlocks.text:
Sites of Grace are more than checkpoints. They support fast travel and several core progression functions, while Guidance of Grace points toward important routes without forcing you to follow them.

Map fragments make new regions easier to understand, and custom markers help you remember caves, merchants, locked paths, or difficult encounters you want to revisit. The goal is not to clear every icon. It is to turn the open world into a record of useful opportunities.
contentBlocks.heading: 7. Use Sites of Grace and the map to open the world

contentBlocks.text:
Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence, Faith, Arcane, Mind, and Endurance all matter in the right build, but their value depends on what your character is actually doing.

Meet the requirements for the gear or magic you want to use, then invest with a purpose. If stamina, FP, or equipment load is creating a real limitation, address it. If it is not, do not spend levels there just because the stat exists. Our [Elden Ring stats and soft-caps guide](/stories/elden-ring-stats-soft-caps-explained/) goes deeper into how those attributes scale.
contentBlocks.heading: 8. Do not over-invest in stats you are not using

contentBlocks.text:
Patch 1.17 added Heavy Knight and Idus Knight as starting-class options through the Tarnished Pack, with both included in Tarnished Edition on Nintendo Switch 2. They give new characters additional opening choices, but they do not create a mandatory new progression route.

Whatever class you begin with, the same principles still apply: survive long enough to learn, strengthen the setup you actually use, improve recovery, explore for permanent upgrades, and spend levels where they solve a real problem.

If you are comparing the available openings first, our [Elden Ring starting-class guide](/stories/elden-ring-best-starting-classes-beginners/) covers all 12 current classes.
contentBlocks.heading: 9. The 2026 starting classes do not change the basic priority order

quickRead: Prioritize Vigor early so mistakes are less punishing before you start chasing small damage gains.
Improve your flasks and strengthen one reliable combat setup instead of spreading resources across everything you find.
Treat exploration as progression: Sites of Grace, map fragments, mines, caves and Spirit Ashes all expand your options before the next major boss.
conclusion:
The best early Elden Ring progression is deliberately boring in the right places. Build enough survivability to learn from mistakes, keep your recovery improving, strengthen one dependable setup, and let exploration supply the materials and systems that make the next challenge easier.

You do not need a perfectly optimized character before Stormveil. You need a character whose strengths you understand. Once that foundation is in place, the Lands Between give you plenty of room to specialize later.

title: The 10 Best Games Like Elden Ring
description: The 10 best games like Elden Ring, from FromSoftware action RPGs and modern Soulslikes to open worlds that recreate its freedom, discovery and build experimentation.
body:
There is no single replacement for Elden Ring because its appeal comes from several games working together at once: demanding action combat, flexible character builds, enormous freedom to explore, mysterious storytelling, memorable bosses, and the ability to walk away from one problem and discover something else.

This list therefore does not rank games by how closely they copy the Lands Between. Each recommendation matches a different part of the experience. Some are the closest mechanical relatives; others recreate the same feeling of curiosity, dangerous exploration, or character growth through a very different design.

Start with our [Elden Ring review](/stories/elden-ring-review-monumental-open-world/) and [Elden Ring beginner’s guide](/stories/elden-ring-beginners-guide/) if you want to compare these recommendations with the game that inspired the list.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished stands beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring, the reference point for Neural Critic’s games-like-Elden-Ring recommendations.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / Elden Ring gameplay screenshot.

contentBlocks.text: Jedi: Survivor borrows enough from Souls design to feel familiar without demanding the same level of punishment. Rest points reset parts of the world, exploration loops back through shortcuts, combat rewards timing and positioning, and new movement abilities keep opening routes through earlier spaces. Its cinematic storytelling is much more direct than Elden Ring’s, but players who enjoyed moving carefully through hostile areas may appreciate the structure.
contentBlocks.caption: Star Wars Jedi: Survivor ranks No. 10: For exploration, checkpoints, traversal, and readable melee combat.
contentBlocks.heading: Star Wars Jedi: Survivor
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Star Wars Jedi: Survivor artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For exploration, checkpoints, traversal, and readable melee combat

contentBlocks.text: Remnant II replaces swords-first combat with ranged weapons, Archetypes, and co-op, but the larger loop remains familiar. Checkpoints, dangerous encounters, build choices, boss learning, and repeated exploration all matter. Its procedural world generation creates a different kind of discovery than Elden Ring’s handcrafted map, yet it also means separate runs can reveal encounters and routes you did not see the first time.
contentBlocks.caption: Remnant II ranks No. 9: For co-op players who want bosses, builds, and repeated discovery.
contentBlocks.heading: Remnant II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Remnant II artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For co-op players who want bosses, builds, and repeated discovery

contentBlocks.text: Dragon’s Dogma 2 is not a Soulslike, but it shares Elden Ring’s willingness to let exploration become the story. Long journeys can turn into improvised battles, night travel changes the level of risk, large monsters disrupt otherwise ordinary routes, and the Pawn system gives the player a flexible party without removing uncertainty. Combat is more class-driven and chaotic, but the world has a similar ability to surprise you between planned destinations.
contentBlocks.caption: Dragon’s Dogma 2 ranks No. 8: For the feeling that an open-world journey can go wrong in interesting ways.
contentBlocks.heading: Dragon’s Dogma 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dragon’s Dogma 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For the feeling that an open-world journey can go wrong in interesting ways

contentBlocks.text: Nioh 2 gives up Elden Ring’s seamless open world in exchange for a much denser combat and progression system. Weapon stances, Ki management, equipment, Yokai abilities, statistics, and skills create an enormous number of ways to shape a character. Players who spent hours experimenting with Elden Ring builds may find the same satisfaction here, provided they are comfortable with mission-based levels and a steeper systems-learning curve.
contentBlocks.caption: Nioh 2 ranks No. 7: For players who want far more build depth and mechanical complexity.
contentBlocks.heading: Nioh 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Nioh 2 artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For players who want far more build depth and mechanical complexity

contentBlocks.text: Black Myth: Wukong is more linear and more action-focused than Elden Ring, but it understands the appeal of arriving somewhere new and realizing a major boss is waiting. Its combat centers on a defined protagonist rather than open-ended character creation, so the build freedom is narrower. In exchange, the game offers a fast, visually elaborate succession of encounters that suits players who loved Elden Ring most when it became a test of reading and surviving a boss.
contentBlocks.caption: Black Myth: Wukong ranks No. 6: For spectacular bosses and a more directed action-RPG journey.
contentBlocks.heading: Black Myth: Wukong
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Black Myth: Wukong artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For spectacular bosses and a more directed action-RPG journey

contentBlocks.text: Tears of the Kingdom is the least Soulslike game in the ranking and one of the closest to Elden Ring’s spirit of discovery. Hyrule rarely insists on one route or one correct solution. The player sees something unusual, travels toward it, experiments with the systems available, and often creates an answer the game never explicitly taught. Combat is more forgiving, but the pleasure of following curiosity across a world that trusts the player is remarkably similar.
contentBlocks.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom ranks No. 5: For open-world curiosity and the freedom to invent a solution.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For open-world curiosity and the freedom to invent a solution

contentBlocks.text: Bloodborne compresses the sense of mystery that fills the Lands Between into the streets and hidden spaces of Yharnam. Character builds remain important, but the combat pushes players toward aggression through faster weapons and the regain mechanic. It is a more focused journey with fewer ways to escape a difficult road, yet its environmental storytelling, shortcuts, strange discoveries, and boss design make the connection to Elden Ring unmistakable.
contentBlocks.caption: Bloodborne ranks No. 4: For FromSoftware atmosphere and combat that rewards aggression.
contentBlocks.heading: Bloodborne
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Bloodborne artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For FromSoftware atmosphere and combat that rewards aggression

contentBlocks.text: Sekiro removes much of the build freedom that defines Elden Ring, which is exactly why it belongs here. Instead of letting equipment or leveling solve every problem, it asks the player to learn deflection, posture, movement, and aggression. If Elden Ring’s best moments were the fights where a boss slowly went from impossible to readable, Sekiro builds almost the entire game around that feeling.
contentBlocks.caption: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice ranks No. 3: For players who want FromSoftware combat distilled into pure execution.
contentBlocks.heading: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: For players who want FromSoftware combat distilled into pure execution

contentBlocks.text: Lies of P is the easiest recommendation for players who want Elden Ring’s combat discipline without another enormous open world. Its guarding system, weapon assembly, upgrade choices, shortcuts, and boss progression all feel familiar, while the city of Krat gives the game a strong visual and narrative identity. It is more linear and less flexible than Elden Ring, but that tighter structure makes its pacing unusually consistent.
contentBlocks.caption: Lies of P ranks No. 2: The strongest modern Soulslike outside FromSoftware.
contentBlocks.heading: Lies of P
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Lies of P artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The strongest modern Soulslike outside FromSoftware

contentBlocks.text: Dark Souls III is the most direct answer to “what should I play after Elden Ring?” because so much of Elden Ring’s combat language is already here. Weapons, scaling, dodging, stamina, spellcasting, checkpoints, cryptic quests, and demanding bosses all feel immediately recognizable. The world is far more directed, but that smaller scale also means less downtime between major areas and some of FromSoftware’s strongest boss encounters.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls III ranks No. 1: The closest compact version of Elden Ring’s combat and build philosophy.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls III
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Dark Souls III artwork or gameplay imagery illustrating the game’s visual style.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The closest compact version of Elden Ring’s combat and build philosophy

quickRead: For exploration, checkpoints, traversal, and readable melee combat
For co-op players who want bosses, builds, and repeated discovery
For the feeling that an open-world journey can go wrong in interesting ways
conclusion:
The right Elden Ring follow-up depends on what you miss most. Dark Souls III and Lies of P are the safest choices for familiar combat. Sekiro and Bloodborne take FromSoftware’s ideas in sharper directions. Nioh 2 is the systems-heavy option, while Tears of the Kingdom and Dragon’s Dogma 2 are better matches for players who mainly miss wandering into the unknown.

That variety is part of Elden Ring’s legacy: no other game reproduces all of it, but many excellent games can reproduce one of the reasons the Lands Between stayed memorable.
conclusionHeading: Choose the part of Elden Ring you want more of

title: What Makes FromSoftware Boss Fights So Memorable?
description: An analysis of how FromSoftware combines combat, presentation, learning, pacing and encounter design to create memorable boss fights.
body:
FromSoftware boss fights are remembered for more than difficulty. The studio’s strongest encounters combine readable mechanics, character identity, music, arena design and a learning process that turns repeated attempts into a growing understanding of the fight.

That combination matters because difficulty by itself is easy to imitate. What is harder to reproduce is the feeling that an encounter is teaching, expressing character and building tension at the same time. The best FromSoftware bosses make those layers feel inseparable.

For more on FromSoftware’s wider design language, read our [Elden Ring review](/stories/elden-ring-review-monumental-open-world/) and [Dark Souls Remastered world-design feature](/stories/dark-souls-remastered-interconnected-world-design/).
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished stands beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring, one of FromSoftware’s best-known modern action RPGs.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / Elden Ring gameplay screenshot.

contentBlocks.text: FromSoftware is often reduced to difficulty, but the fights that endure are usually the ones where challenge supports a larger idea.
