contentBlocks.heading: Weight Helps in Collisions but Comes With Tradeoffs
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Two racers make contact during a Mario Kart 8 Deluxe race, illustrating the effect of vehicle and character weight.

contentBlocks.text:
Drivers are grouped into different statistical profiles, so changing character can alter speed, acceleration, weight, handling, traction, Mini-Turbo, and invincibility even when the kart parts stay the same.

Yoshi, Peach, Daisy, Birdo, and Peachette share the same Mario Kart 8 Deluxe stat profile, which is one reason they are popular starting points for balanced builds. They offer a useful blend of speed and Mini-Turbo without pushing too far toward either extreme.

If you prefer another character, keep using them. The game is balanced enough that driving quality matters far more than copying a popular driver purely for a small statistical gain.
contentBlocks.caption: Changing drivers alters the final stat profile even when the kart body, tires, and glider stay the same.
contentBlocks.heading: Character Choice Changes the Build More Than It Appears
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Mario Kart 8 Deluxe character selection screen displays racers from different weight classes.

contentBlocks.text:
Tires make a noticeable difference because their stat tradeoffs can move a setup toward speed, acceleration, handling, or Mini-Turbo. They should not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought.

Roller and Azure Roller are especially strong general-purpose choices because their advantages complement the way Mario Kart 8 Deluxe rewards drifting and recovery. The smaller visible speed bar can look like a disadvantage until you feel how quickly the kart responds through corners and after interruptions.

If you change only one component while testing a build, tires are one of the best places to start because the difference is easy to feel.
contentBlocks.caption: Tires can meaningfully shift speed, acceleration, handling, and Mini-Turbo, making them one of the most important parts to test.
contentBlocks.heading: Tires Can Change a Build More Than the Body
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Mario Kart 8 Deluxe vehicle customization screen shows the tire selection, including Roller-style wheels.

contentBlocks.text:
Gliders still contribute statistics, but their differences are generally smaller than the choices made through your driver, body, and tires. That makes them the easiest component to adjust around preference once the rest of the build is settled.

Paper Glider, Cloud Glider, Parachute, and Flower Glider sit in a useful lightweight stat group and fit comfortably into many balanced setups.

Do not spend too much time chasing a perfect glider if the rest of the combination already feels good. The bigger gains usually come from choosing the right driver, body, tires, and then driving the course well.
contentBlocks.caption: Gliders still affect statistics, but their differences are usually smaller than the choices made through the driver, body, and tires.
contentBlocks.heading: Gliders Usually Make the Smallest Difference
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Mario Kart 8 Deluxe vehicle customization screen shows the available glider options.

contentBlocks.text:
For a strong general-purpose setup, start with Yoshi, the Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and the Paper Glider. Peach, Daisy, Birdo, or Peachette can replace Yoshi without changing the driver statistics, while Azure Roller can replace Roller.

The appeal of this combination is balance. It keeps enough ground speed to remain competitive while preserving strong acceleration, handling, and Mini-Turbo. The Teddy Buggy also avoids the extreme weaknesses that make some high-speed bodies difficult to recover with.

This is the build to try first if you want one setup that works comfortably across a wide range of tracks and race conditions.
contentBlocks.caption: Yoshi with Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and Paper Glider is a strong all-around setup with useful speed, acceleration, handling, and Mini-Turbo.
contentBlocks.heading: Best All-Around Build: Yoshi, Teddy Buggy, Roller, Paper Glider
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Yoshi is paired with the Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and Paper Glider in Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.

contentBlocks.text:
If you value responsive steering, quick recovery, and frequent drift boosts, try Yoshi with Mr. Scooty, Roller tires, and the Cloud Glider. The Biddybuggy is another body worth testing in the same general direction.

This setup gives up some top speed compared with more speed-focused combinations, but it feels agile and rewards tracks where you can chain drifts and repeatedly build Mini-Turbo. It is also forgiving after item hits because its acceleration is strong.

Players who are still learning optimal lines may find this easier to drive consistently than a heavier, faster build.
contentBlocks.caption: The Yoshi and Mr. Scooty combination favors responsive handling, strong recovery, and frequent Mini-Turbo boosts.
contentBlocks.heading: Best Mini-Turbo and Forgiving Build: Yoshi, Mr. Scooty, Roller, Cloud Glider
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Yoshi is paired with Mr. Scooty, Roller tires, and the Cloud Glider in Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.

contentBlocks.text:
If the standard Yoshi-style setup feels a little too light, moving to a heavier driver such as Rosalina while keeping Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and Paper Glider creates a more speed-biased version of the same idea.

You gain more speed and weight while keeping the forgiving qualities of the body and tires. The tradeoff is weaker acceleration and Mini-Turbo than the lighter balanced setup, so mistakes cost slightly more.

This is a useful option for players who already drive cleanly and want more straight-line pace without jumping all the way to an extreme heavyweight configuration.
contentBlocks.caption: Rosalina adds more speed and weight to the balanced Teddy Buggy setup while giving up some acceleration and Mini-Turbo.
contentBlocks.heading: Best Speed-Biased Balanced Build: Rosalina, Teddy Buggy, Roller, Paper Glider
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Rosalina is paired with the Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and Paper Glider in Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.

contentBlocks.text:
Heavy characters paired with speed-focused bodies and tires can produce impressive top-speed bars, but those combinations often sacrifice the acceleration, handling, and Mini-Turbo that make a build dependable in normal races.

They can still be fun, and certain Time Trial routes may reward specialized statistics, but they are not automatically better simply because the speed bar is larger. Online races in particular create too many interruptions for raw top speed to tell the entire story.

If you want to experiment, compare an extreme speed setup against your balanced build on the same course. The difference in recovery and cornering will make the stat tradeoff much easier to understand.
contentBlocks.caption: Extreme speed builds make the tradeoff easy to see: a larger speed bar can come at the expense of acceleration, handling, and Mini-Turbo.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Extreme Speed Builds to Understand the Tradeoff, Not as a Default
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A speed-focused Mario Kart 8 Deluxe build is shown on the vehicle selection screen with a high speed stat and lower supporting stats.

contentBlocks.text:
The easiest way to choose a kart build is to remove as many variables as possible. Pick one familiar track, run several laps with one setup, then change only one component at a time.

Notice where the difference appears. Does the kart recover faster after a mistake? Can you hold a tighter drift? Are you reaching higher Mini-Turbo stages more often? Does extra speed actually improve your lap, or does worse handling cancel it out?

A stat sheet can identify strong combinations, but the best build for your races is the one that turns those numbers into repeatable clean driving.
contentBlocks.caption: Testing different builds on the same track makes it easier to feel which stat changes actually improve your driving.
contentBlocks.heading: Test Builds on the Same Track Before You Decide
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Time Trial or solo test run is shown on track for comparing kart setups under the same conditions.

conclusion:
The best Mario Kart 8 Deluxe build is not simply the one with the highest speed bar. The game combines visible and hidden statistics, and real races constantly reward recovery, cornering, and Mini-Turbo alongside top speed.

For most players, Yoshi with Teddy Buggy, Roller tires, and Paper Glider is an excellent place to start because it offers a strong balance without a major weakness. Mr. Scooty pushes farther toward acceleration and Mini-Turbo, while a heavier driver such as Rosalina can add speed without completely abandoning that balanced structure.

Once you understand what each stat changes, stop chasing a universal answer and test the setup yourself. A kart that lets you hit cleaner lines, drift more consistently, and recover quickly will usually win more races than a theoretically faster combination you struggle to control.

title: Baldur’s Gate 3 Beginner’s Guide: Classes, Combat and Exploration Explained
description: A clear introduction to classes, ability checks, turn-based combat, companions, rests, exploration, and the choices new Baldur’s Gate 3 players face early on.
body:
Baldur’s Gate 3 can feel dense at first because it asks you to learn several systems at once: character classes, dice rolls, dialogue checks, turn-based combat, companions, spells, rests, exploration, and a world that often reacts to what you say or do. The important thing is that you do not need to understand every rule before you begin.

Your first hours are better spent learning how the game responds to choices. Try things, read tooltips, use your companions, and accept that some rolls will fail. Baldur’s Gate 3 is built around adaptation rather than perfect play, and many of its best moments come from plans that do not go exactly as expected.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The central Baldur’s Gate 3 cast is shown together against a dramatic fantasy backdrop in official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Your class shapes your abilities, combat role, and some dialogue options, but beginners do not need to solve the entire character-building system before starting.

Pick the class fantasy that sounds interesting. Fighters are straightforward in combat, Rogues reward positioning and skills, Clerics combine support with strong utility, Wizards offer a wide range of spells, and the other classes each create their own rhythm. What matters most is choosing something you are curious enough to learn.

Do not worry about creating a flawless build on the character-creation screen. Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you time to understand your abilities, and your companions also cover many roles your main character does not.
contentBlocks.caption: Class choice shapes your early abilities and combat role, but the best starting point is a class you genuinely want to learn.
contentBlocks.heading: Choose a Class You Want to Play, Not the “Best” One
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Baldur’s Gate 3 character creation screen displays class options for a new character.

contentBlocks.text:
A large part of Baldur’s Gate 3 runs on ability checks. Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma influence different actions, while proficiencies improve checks tied to skills your character knows well.

You do not need to memorize the whole ruleset. Start by noticing which checks your character is naturally good at. A high-Charisma character may excel in Persuasion or Deception, while a Dexterity-focused character may be better suited to Stealth or Sleight of Hand.

When a dialogue or exploration check appears, pay attention to the bonuses shown on screen. The game is constantly teaching you which characters are suited to which problems.
contentBlocks.caption: Ability scores and proficiencies explain what a character is naturally good at, making them more useful to understand than chasing an optimized build immediately.
contentBlocks.heading: Read Your Ability Scores and Proficiencies Before Chasing Builds
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Baldur’s Gate 3 character screen shows ability scores, skills and proficiencies.

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 uses visible dice rolls for many conversations and interactions. It is tempting to treat every failed roll as something that must be corrected, but failure often creates a different route rather than ending your progress.

A failed Persuasion check might lead to a fight, another conversation, or a completely different solution. A missed Perception check may simply mean you discover something later from another angle.

Save often because the game rewards experimentation, but try not to turn every roll into a demand for the perfect result. Learning to continue after an imperfect outcome is one of the easiest ways to enjoy the game’s reactive structure.
contentBlocks.caption: Failed checks often create different consequences rather than ending progress, which is part of Baldur’s Gate 3’s reactive storytelling.
contentBlocks.heading: Let Failed Dice Rolls Become Part of the Story
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A dice-roll ability check appears during a conversation in Baldur’s Gate 3.

contentBlocks.text:
Your companions are not just extra damage in combat. Each character brings different proficiencies, abilities, spells, and dialogue strengths, so switching who handles a task can make a major difference.

If your main character struggles to pick a lock, another party member may be better equipped. If a conversation involves knowledge of religion, magic, or nature, a companion with the right background may have stronger options. In combat, one character can control enemies while another attacks, heals, or takes a better position.

Think of the party as a shared toolbox. You do not need one character who can do everything when four characters can solve problems together.
contentBlocks.caption: Companions bring different skills, spells and combat roles, so the party works best when treated as a shared toolbox.
contentBlocks.heading: Use the Whole Party, Not Just Your Main Character
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A four-character adventuring party travels together in Baldur’s Gate 3.

contentBlocks.text:
Combat pauses the action and gives every participant a place in the initiative order, so there is rarely a reason to rush your turn.

Before committing to an attack, look at the battlefield. Check elevation, movement range, nearby hazards, enemy positions, and which party members still have actions available. Moving to higher ground, taking cover, spreading the party out, or focusing several characters on one dangerous enemy can matter as much as raw damage.

The strongest beginner habit is simple: use the time the game gives you. Read what your actions do and make a plan for the full party instead of treating each character as a separate turn.
contentBlocks.caption: Elevation, movement and enemy positioning can matter as much as raw damage, so taking time to read the battlefield is usually rewarded.
contentBlocks.heading: Turn-Based Combat Rewards Positioning More Than Speed
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A turn-based battle in Baldur’s Gate 3 shows party members and enemies positioned across the battlefield.

contentBlocks.text:
Most turns are built around a few basic resources. Characters usually have movement, an action, and sometimes a useful bonus action, with specific abilities explaining what they consume.

An attack or spell may use your action, while jumping, shoving, drinking a potion, hiding, or certain class abilities may use a bonus action depending on the situation. Learning which resource an ability spends makes turns much easier to plan.

Before ending a turn, glance at what is still available. Beginners often leave useful movement or a bonus action unused simply because the interface contains more options than expected.
contentBlocks.caption: Learning how actions, bonus actions and movement fit together makes each combat turn easier to plan efficiently.
contentBlocks.heading: Understand Actions, Bonus Actions, and Movement
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Baldur’s Gate 3 combat interface shows available actions and abilities during a character’s turn.

contentBlocks.text:
Powerful abilities are limited for a reason, but saving every spell slot or class feature for a hypothetical future battle can make ordinary encounters harder than they need to be.

Use strong tools when they solve a real problem. A control spell that stops several enemies from acting, a healing ability that keeps a party member standing, or a class feature that turns a difficult round in your favor is doing exactly what it is meant to do.

The important part is learning which resources return on a short rest and which come back after a long rest. Once you understand that rhythm, using abilities feels much less risky.
contentBlocks.caption: Spells and class abilities are resources meant to solve real problems, not items that need to be saved indefinitely.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Hoard Spells and Abilities Forever
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Baldur’s Gate 3 interface displays several spells and class abilities available to a character.

contentBlocks.text:
Short rests and long rests are part of the game’s normal progression. They restore health and class resources in different ways, and camp is also where many companion conversations and story moments take place.

Do not treat resting as a sign that you played badly. If your party is low on health, spell slots, or important abilities, continuing into another difficult encounter may create a much harder problem than simply taking a break.

Long rests use camp supplies, so gathering food and supply packs while exploring is useful. Resting regularly also helps you see camp scenes that can deepen your understanding of the companions travelling with you.
contentBlocks.caption: Resting restores important resources and also creates space for companion conversations and other camp story moments.
contentBlocks.heading: Rest Before the Party Is Completely Exhausted
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The adventuring party gathers at camp in Baldur’s Gate 3.

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 hides useful routes above, below, behind, and around the obvious path. Ladders, rooftops, caves, ledges, doors, destructible objects, and small side paths can completely change how you approach an area.

The environment also matters during combat. Height can improve your position, narrow doorways can control movement, and interactive objects may give you options that are not obvious from the ability bar.

If an encounter or location seems impossible from the front, stop and look around. The game often rewards players who treat the map like a space to investigate rather than a corridor to clear.
contentBlocks.caption: Ladders, ledges, rooftops and environmental objects can open routes that are easy to miss when following only the obvious path.
contentBlocks.heading: Explore Vertically and Interact With the Environment
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Baldur’s Gate 3 party explores an elevated or alternate route through the environment.

contentBlocks.text:
Many situations that look dangerous can be approached through conversation, stealth, exploration, or a different route. Dialogue is not just story between battles; it is one of the game’s main systems.

Speak to characters, ask questions, and pay attention to what your class, background, race, skills, and companions add to conversations. Different dialogue options can reveal information, change relationships, or open paths that are not available through direct confrontation.

You will not see every outcome in one playthrough, and that is part of the design. Follow the version of events your character creates instead of trying to uncover every branch at once.
contentBlocks.caption: Dialogue is one of the game’s main systems, and many encounters can change through conversation before combat ever begins.
contentBlocks.heading: Talk to People Before Assuming Combat Is the Only Answer
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Baldur’s Gate 3 dialogue scene presents multiple conversation choices during an encounter.

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 gives you enormous freedom, which also means mistakes happen. You may start a fight earlier than expected, spend a resource badly, misunderstand a spell, or choose a dialogue option with consequences you did not predict.

Frequent saves make experimentation easier, especially before entering a dangerous area or testing an unfamiliar idea. But constant reloading can also make the game feel like a puzzle with one correct answer when it usually is not.

Use saves as a safety net, not as a demand for perfection. The game is at its best when choices have enough room to surprise you.
contentBlocks.caption: Frequent saves support experimentation, but imperfect outcomes are often part of what makes a playthrough feel personal.
contentBlocks.heading: Save Often, but Do Not Try to Perfect Every Decision
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Baldur’s Gate 3 adventuring party moves through an uncertain exploration scene.

conclusion:
Baldur’s Gate 3 becomes much easier once you stop trying to master every rule at the same time. Learn your own class first, use the rest of the party as a shared set of tools, and take combat one turn at a time. Read what abilities cost, pay attention to positioning, and rest when your resources are running low.

Outside combat, explore patiently and treat dialogue, dice rolls, and failed plans as part of the game rather than interruptions to it. You are not expected to find every secret or produce the perfect outcome on your first run. The real beginner skill is learning how many different solutions Baldur’s Gate 3 is willing to accept — and becoming comfortable choosing one of them.

title: Tears of the Kingdom Beginner’s Guide: Essential Tips for Exploring Hyrule
description: A spoiler-light introduction to Ultrahand, Fuse, Ascend, Recall, exploration, resources, and the systems that define Tears of the Kingdom.
body:
Tears of the Kingdom can feel even more overwhelming than Breath of the Wild because it gives you several new abilities almost immediately and then opens Hyrule in multiple directions. The key is not to master every system at once. Learn what each ability is good at, keep useful materials on hand, and treat experimentation as part of the game rather than something you need to optimize.

This beginner’s guide stays spoiler-light and focuses on the systems that matter most during the opening hours: Ultrahand, Fuse, Ascend, Recall, Zonai devices, shrines, stamina, resources, and how to move between the sky and the surface without turning exploration into a checklist.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
imageAlt: Link overlooks the vast landscape of Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, with floating sky islands visible above the open world.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
Great Sky Island is designed to introduce Tears of the Kingdom’s core abilities before the wider world fully opens. Take your time there. Each early shrine teaches one of Link’s major new powers, and the routes between them make you use those abilities in practical situations.

The most important goal is not speed. It is understanding what each power changes about how you move through the world. Ultrahand solves construction problems, Fuse improves equipment, Ascend creates vertical shortcuts, and Recall lets you manipulate movement and timing.

Once those ideas start to feel natural, the rest of Hyrule becomes much easier to read because many later puzzles are simply more complicated versions of the same principles.
contentBlocks.caption: Great Sky Island introduces the abilities and traversal ideas that shape the rest of Tears of the Kingdom.
contentBlocks.heading: Use Great Sky Island as a Systems Tutorial
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link explores Great Sky Island in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, with floating islands and the open sky visible around him.

contentBlocks.text:
Ultrahand lets Link pick up, rotate, move, and attach objects. You can build elaborate vehicles with it, but beginners should start much simpler.

Ask what the immediate problem is. Do you need a bridge, a raft, a platform, or a way to move something heavy? Build only enough to solve that problem. Two or three correctly placed pieces are often more useful than a complicated machine that takes several minutes to assemble.

The game rewards creativity, but creativity does not mean complexity. If a crude solution works, it is a successful solution.
contentBlocks.caption: Ultrahand is most useful when you build only what the immediate problem requires.
contentBlocks.heading: Treat Ultrahand as a Problem-Solving Tool, Not a Building Contest
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link uses Ultrahand to move and attach objects while building a simple structure in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Fuse is one of the most important systems to understand because it changes how weapons, shields, and arrows work. Fusing materials can increase damage, improve durability, extend reach, or add useful effects depending on the combination.

Do not save every monster horn or useful material for later. If your current weapon is weak, attaching a suitable material can immediately make it more useful. Common monster parts are especially good early choices because you will keep finding more of them.

Arrows also become much more flexible when fused with materials. Experiment with items you already carry instead of assuming every combat problem needs a different weapon.
contentBlocks.caption: Fuse turns ordinary weapons and materials into more useful tools, making experimentation more valuable than hoarding early gear.
contentBlocks.heading: Fuse Early and Often
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link uses Fuse to attach a material to a weapon in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Ascend allows Link to pass through many solid surfaces above him. It is easy to forget because climbing already feels familiar, but Ascend can save stamina and turn awkward vertical routes into simple shortcuts.

Whenever you are inside a cave, beneath a platform, under a bridge, or at the bottom of a structure, look upward before committing to a long climb. If the ceiling is valid, Ascend may take you directly to the next level.

This habit matters throughout the game. Tears of the Kingdom often hides an easy vertical solution in a place that initially looks like a climbing problem.
contentBlocks.caption: Ascend can turn awkward vertical routes into quick shortcuts and save valuable stamina.
contentBlocks.heading: Look Up Before You Start Climbing — Ascend May Be Faster
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link uses Ascend beneath a solid surface in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Recall reverses an object’s recent movement. The early game teaches obvious uses, such as sending moving platforms backward, but the ability becomes much more useful once you start watching the environment for motion.

Falling rocks, moving machinery, rolling objects, and things that have just been thrown or displaced can all become opportunities. If something moved in a useful direction a moment ago, Recall may let you reuse that movement in reverse.

When a puzzle seems to depend on timing, pause and ask whether you can manipulate the movement instead of trying to react faster.
contentBlocks.caption: Recall becomes much more flexible once you start treating recent movement itself as a resource.
contentBlocks.heading: Recall Is More Useful Than It First Appears
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link activates Recall on a moving object in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Fans, wheels, rockets, wings, and other Zonai devices can power vehicles and solve environmental problems, but beginners do not need to memorize every combination.

First learn what each device does on its own. A fan creates thrust, a wheel creates rotation, and a rocket produces a strong burst of movement. Once you understand the basic behavior, combining devices with Ultrahand becomes much easier.

Also remember that powered devices consume energy. Early builds should be simple enough that your available battery can support them for the time you actually need.
contentBlocks.caption: Understanding individual Zonai devices makes simple, reliable builds easier than memorizing complicated machines.
contentBlocks.heading: Learn What Zonai Devices Do Before Building Around Them
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A simple Zonai device build uses basic components in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Shrines remain one of the clearest forms of progression. Discovering them expands your fast-travel network, while completing them earns Light of Blessing that can eventually be exchanged for additional hearts or stamina.

That makes a visible shrine useful even if you are not ready to solve it immediately. Activating the entrance gives you a travel point you can return to later.

If the world begins to feel too open, heading toward a shrine is usually productive because it gives you a short puzzle, a permanent travel anchor, and progress toward stronger base stats.
contentBlocks.caption: Shrines provide Light of Blessing, fast-travel anchors, and a steady way to improve Link’s base stats.
contentBlocks.heading: Shrines Still Matter for Progression and Fast Travel
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link approaches a shrine in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Stamina affects climbing, swimming, sprinting, and gliding, so it continues to shape how freely you can explore. Hearts improve survivability, but stamina often determines whether you can reach the place you are trying to investigate.

When spending Light of Blessing, choose based on what is actually stopping you. If combat mistakes are the main problem, more hearts may help. If you constantly run out of stamina while climbing or gliding, another stamina segment may open more routes immediately.

There is no single correct early order. Build around the limitations you notice in your own play.
contentBlocks.caption: Stamina directly affects climbing, gliding, swimming, and how freely you can explore Hyrule’s vertical world.
contentBlocks.heading: Stamina Is Still an Exploration Stat
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link moves through Hyrule while the green stamina wheel is visible in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

contentBlocks.text:
Materials are more versatile in Tears of the Kingdom because the same item may be useful for cooking, selling, upgrading, throwing, or fusing to equipment.

That makes gathering especially valuable. Pick up monster parts, plants, ores, Zonai materials, and useful environmental items as you explore. You do not need to hoard everything forever, but a broad inventory gives you more options when a puzzle or fight suddenly asks for a specific effect.

The game is built around improvisation, and improvisation is much easier when you have a healthy supply of ordinary materials.
contentBlocks.caption: A broad stock of materials gives you more options for Fuse, cooking, upgrades, selling, and improvised solutions.
contentBlocks.heading: Pick Up More Materials Than You Think You Need
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The materials inventory in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom shows a range of collected resources and monster parts.

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom expands exploration vertically. The sky, surface, caves, and wells are not separate activities so much as different layers of the same world.

A sky island may reveal a destination below. A cave may contain an Ascend route back to the surface. A fallen object may provide a Recall route upward. Once you start thinking vertically, travel becomes less about following roads and more about finding connections between layers.

When you feel stuck in one direction, changing elevation can be as useful as changing region.
contentBlocks.caption: The sky, surface, caves, and wells work best when you treat them as connected layers rather than separate activities.
contentBlocks.heading: Use the Sky, Surface, Caves, and Wells as Connected Layers
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link explores one of Hyrule’s vertical layers in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, with terrain extending above and below.

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom is full of impressive player-made machines, but you do not need advanced engineering to play well. The game is designed to accept many kinds of solutions, including awkward ones.

If a bridge reaches the other side, it worked. If a fused weapon gets you through a fight, it worked. If a simple fan-powered platform crosses a gap, there is no bonus for making it ten times more complicated.

The best beginner habit is to try an idea quickly, learn from what happens, and adjust. The game becomes much more approachable once experimentation feels disposable instead of precious.
contentBlocks.caption: A simple solution that works is usually better than spending extra time building something unnecessarily complicated.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Overengineer Your First Solutions
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link uses a simple improvised construction to solve a traversal problem in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

conclusion:
Tears of the Kingdom becomes easier to understand once you stop treating its new systems as separate mechanics you need to master one by one. Ultrahand, Fuse, Ascend, and Recall are all different ways of changing the problem in front of you. Use them together, keep ordinary materials available, and let simple solutions teach you what works.

Most importantly, do not compare your early creations or routes to elaborate builds you may have seen elsewhere. Hyrule is designed around experimentation. A rough bridge, an improvised weapon, or an unexpected Ascend shortcut is exactly the kind of success the game encourages. Learn the tools, stay curious, and let the world give you reasons to use them.
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

title: Breath of the Wild Beginner’s Guide: What to Do First in Hyrule
description: The essential things new players should understand about exploration, shrines, weapons, cooking, stamina, and surviving Hyrule’s opening hours.
body:
Breath of the Wild can feel unusually open during its first few hours. After a short introduction, Hyrule starts presenting towers, shrines, enemy camps, mountains, weather, ingredients, breakable equipment, and distant landmarks without giving you a strict order for handling them.

The important thing to understand is that the game is built around experimentation. You are not expected to clear every nearby challenge immediately or follow one perfect route. The Great Plateau teaches you the basic tools, then the rest of Hyrule rewards curiosity, preparation, and the willingness to change plans when the environment pushes back.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
imageAlt: Link stands on a rocky overlook above Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, with the open landscape stretching into the distance.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild official artwork.

contentBlocks.text:
The Great Plateau is more than an opening area. It is a compact version of the systems Breath of the Wild expects you to use everywhere else.

Take time to visit its shrines, experiment with the Sheikah Slate runes, climb to high points, gather ingredients, and test how temperature and terrain affect Link. The Plateau is small enough to make mistakes without feeling lost, but varied enough to teach the habits that matter later.

Do not rush toward the edge simply because the larger map is waiting. Leaving with a basic understanding of movement, runes, cooking, and environmental problem-solving will make the rest of Hyrule much easier to read.
contentBlocks.caption: The Great Plateau is a compact introduction to Breath of the Wild’s core systems before Hyrule fully opens up.
contentBlocks.heading: Use the Great Plateau as Your Tutorial
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link stands on the Great Plateau overlooking the open landscape of Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
Shrines are one of the most useful landmarks in the game. Completing them earns Spirit Orbs, while discovering them also gives you convenient fast-travel points.

That means a shrine can be valuable even before you are ready to finish its challenge. If you spot one from a tower, mountain, or ridge, reaching it can expand your travel network and give you another anchor point on the map.

Spirit Orbs eventually let you increase Link’s health or stamina, so shrine hunting naturally supports both exploration and progression. You do not need to complete every shrine as soon as you find it; marking difficult ones for later is perfectly reasonable.
contentBlocks.caption: Shrines provide Spirit Orbs, fast-travel points, and a steady way to build Link’s health or stamina.
contentBlocks.heading: Shrines Are More Than Puzzle Rooms
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link approaches a glowing Sheikah shrine in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
Towers reveal large sections of the map and give you excellent vantage points for spotting shrines, roads, villages, stables, and unusual landmarks.

They are useful early objectives, but the map is intentionally not covered in traditional quest markers. Use towers to understand the landscape, then decide what actually interests you. A glowing shrine in the distance, a strange ruin, a stable, or a mountain that looks climbable can all become a worthwhile destination.

Breath of the Wild works best when the map helps you choose a direction rather than telling you exactly what to clear next.
contentBlocks.caption: Climbing towers reveals regional map data and gives you a useful vantage point for choosing where to explore next.
contentBlocks.heading: Climb Towers Early, but Do Not Treat Them as Checklists
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Sheikah Tower rises above the surrounding landscape in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
One of the biggest adjustments for new players is weapon durability. Most equipment wears out through normal use, so losing a favorite early weapon is part of the game’s rhythm rather than a mistake.

The useful habit is to think of your inventory as a rotating set of tools. Pick up replacements when you find them, keep a few different options available, and avoid becoming attached to one early piece of gear.

This system encourages improvisation. A weapon breaking during a fight is inconvenient, but it also pushes you to pay attention to what the environment and defeated enemies are giving you instead of relying on one permanent loadout.
contentBlocks.caption: Weapons are temporary tools in Breath of the Wild, so a healthy inventory is more useful than relying on one favorite weapon.
contentBlocks.heading: Expect Weapons to Break
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Breath of the Wild inventory screen displays Link’s collection of weapons and equipment.

contentBlocks.text:
Cooking is one of Breath of the Wild’s most important survival systems. Ingredients found across Hyrule can restore health, and many dishes can also provide temporary bonuses such as resistance to harsh temperatures or improvements to other abilities.

A simple beginner habit is to cook whenever you reach a safe pot instead of waiting until your inventory is nearly empty. Keeping a small range of healing meals and situational dishes makes exploration much more forgiving.

You do not need to memorize an enormous recipe list. Pay attention to ingredient descriptions, combine items with similar effects, and learn through experimentation. The game gives you enough ingredients that early mistakes are rarely costly.
contentBlocks.caption: Cooking before a difficult journey gives Link healing meals and useful temporary effects for exploration.
contentBlocks.heading: Cook Before You Need the Food
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link cooks ingredients in a cooking pot in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
Stamina controls climbing, sprinting, swimming, and several other actions, which makes it one of the most important exploration resources in the game.

When climbing, watch the stamina wheel and look for ledges or flat surfaces where Link can recover. Rain can make climbing much harder, so sometimes the right choice is to find another route or wait for better conditions.

When it comes time to spend Spirit Orbs, both hearts and stamina are useful. Hearts provide more room for mistakes in combat, while stamina expands what you can reach and how freely you can move through the world. There is no single correct early balance; choose based on what is limiting you most.
contentBlocks.caption: Stamina determines how far Link can climb, swim, sprint, and glide, making it one of the game’s most important exploration resources.
contentBlocks.heading: Stamina Changes How Much of Hyrule You Can Reach
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link climbs a steep surface in Breath of the Wild while the green stamina wheel is visible.

contentBlocks.text:
Hyrule’s climate can be just as important as its enemies. Cold, heat, storms, and other environmental conditions can turn a simple route into a problem that needs preparation.

Clothing, food effects, fire, and alternate paths can all help depending on the situation. If Link starts taking environmental damage or a climb becomes unreliable in the rain, treat that as information rather than punishment.

Breath of the Wild frequently asks you to solve travel problems with the same mindset you would use in a shrine: observe what is happening, check the tools you have, and change your approach.
contentBlocks.caption: Temperature and weather can turn travel into a puzzle, so clothing, food effects, and route choices all matter.
contentBlocks.heading: Weather and Clothing Are Part of the Puzzle
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link travels through a cold region of Hyrule while dressed for the freezing environment in Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
If the open world ever feels too directionless, roads and stables provide a useful rhythm. Stables can act as safe stopping points, and the roads around them naturally connect different parts of Hyrule.

They are also good places to reset after a long stretch of exploration. You can organize your inventory, prepare food, register or retrieve horses, and decide which nearby landmark to investigate next.

You do not have to stay on the road, but following one for a while can help you learn how regions connect before you disappear back into the wilderness.
contentBlocks.caption: Stables and roads provide useful structure when Hyrule’s open world starts to feel overwhelming.
contentBlocks.heading: Explore Stables and Roads When You Need Structure
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link rides a horse near a stable in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
Early rupees can feel scarce because shops quickly introduce armor, arrows, ingredients, and other useful purchases.

You do not need to buy everything you see. Prioritize items that solve an immediate problem, especially clothing or supplies that open up areas you are currently struggling to explore. Selling excess materials can help, but keep some common ingredients and monster parts because they remain useful for cooking, elixirs, upgrades, and quests.

A small reserve of rupees gives you flexibility when you reach a new village or discover a piece of gear that genuinely changes what you can do.
contentBlocks.caption: Keeping some rupees in reserve gives you flexibility when a village or shop offers something that solves an immediate problem.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Spend Every Rupee Immediately
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Breath of the Wild interface shows Link’s current rupee total during gameplay.

contentBlocks.text:
After collecting enough Spirit Orbs, you can increase either Link’s hearts or stamina. New players often worry that there is a perfect order, but the better question is what currently prevents you from progressing comfortably.

If ordinary fights are ending too quickly, more health can make the learning process less punishing. If you constantly fall just short of a climb, swim, or glide, more stamina may improve exploration immediately.

You can continue earning both over the course of the game, so an early choice is not a commitment to one style forever.
contentBlocks.caption: Spend Spirit Orbs on hearts or stamina according to what is limiting you most rather than following a fixed upgrade order.
contentBlocks.heading: Choose Hearts or Stamina Based on What Is Stopping You
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link stands before a Goddess Statue in Breath of the Wild where Spirit Orbs can be exchanged for a Heart Container or Stamina Vessel.

contentBlocks.text:
Once you have the Paraglider and leave the Great Plateau, Hyrule becomes dramatically larger. The main quest gives you useful direction, but you do not need to turn that direction into a strict itinerary.

Pick one visible goal and let the journey change along the way. A tower may reveal a shrine. A shrine may lead you toward a stable. A stable may point you toward a village or road you had not planned to visit. That chain of discoveries is the structure of Breath of the Wild.

The most important beginner skill is learning to trust your curiosity. You will miss things, take inefficient routes, and occasionally reach places before you are ready. That is not playing incorrectly; it is how the game creates a personal version of Hyrule.
contentBlocks.caption: Once the Paraglider opens Hyrule, following your curiosity becomes more important than following a strict route.
contentBlocks.heading: Leave the Great Plateau With a Direction, Not a Schedule
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link glides over Hyrule with the Paraglider after leaving the Great Plateau in Breath of the Wild.

conclusion:
Breath of the Wild becomes much easier to understand once you stop looking for the one correct route. Use the Great Plateau to learn the core systems, seek out shrines and towers when they are useful, cook before difficult journeys, and treat stamina, weather, clothing, and equipment as parts of the same exploration toolkit.

Most importantly, let the world interrupt your plans. A distant shrine, a mountain, a road, or an unfamiliar ruin can become the next objective simply because it caught your attention. Hyrule is designed around that freedom, and a first playthrough is strongest when discovery still feels like your own.
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

title: Elden Ring Beginner’s Guide: What to Know Before Entering the Lands Between
description: A practical starting guide to exploration, combat, leveling, equipment, Sites of Grace, and the early decisions that make Elden Ring easier to understand.
body:
Elden Ring is intimidating because it gives you very little pressure to follow a single route. Within the first hour, the Lands Between can put a difficult field boss in front of you, point you toward a castle, scatter caves and ruins in every direction, and hand you a character sheet full of statistics that are not immediately obvious.

The useful thing to understand is that Elden Ring is designed around that uncertainty. You are not expected to defeat every enemy the moment you meet it, build a perfect character from the start, or follow the Guidance of Grace as if it were a mandatory quest marker. A strong first playthrough comes from learning how the world communicates, strengthening the parts of your character that keep you alive, and treating exploration as part of progression rather than a distraction from it.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished stands beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring, framed by golden branches, ruined stone structures and the Lands Between below.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / Elden Ring gameplay screenshot.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring asks you to choose a starting class before you have enough context to know exactly how you want to play. Do not let that choice paralyze you.

A class mainly determines your opening statistics and equipment. It does not lock your character into a permanent role, and the game gives you room to develop in another direction as you gain levels and discover new gear, spells, and systems. The Idus Knight and Heavy Knight starting classes added with the Tarnished Pack follow the same basic idea: your class shapes your first steps, not your entire journey.

For a first character, choose something that makes immediate sense to you rather than trying to predict an endgame setup. The more important decision is what you learn about your own preferences during the opening hours.
contentBlocks.caption: Starting class determines your opening stats and equipment, but it does not lock you into a permanent build.
contentBlocks.heading: Your Starting Class Is a Beginning, Not a Build
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring starting-class screen shows Samurai, Prisoner and Confessor with their starting stats and equipment.

contentBlocks.text:
Shortly after the opening, Elden Ring gives you access to the Cave of Knowledge. It is worth doing even if you have played other FromSoftware games.

The tutorial introduces several systems the wider game expects you to understand but rarely stops to explain again. It also gives you a safe place to learn how movement, stamina, targeting, skills, and other basic interactions fit together before the open world starts introducing more complicated situations.

You can revisit tutorial information later through the Info section of your inventory, so there is no need to memorize every prompt. The goal is simply to recognize the game’s basic language before you start exploring Limgrave.
contentBlocks.caption: The Cave of Knowledge is easy to miss, but it introduces combat and movement systems the wider game expects you to understand.
contentBlocks.heading: Do the Cave of Knowledge Tutorial
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The player character stands inside the dimly lit Cave of Knowledge tutorial area in Elden Ring.

contentBlocks.text:
Sites of Grace are checkpoints, fast-travel points, and places where several progression systems become available. Some of them also point in a suggested direction through the Guidance of Grace.

Treat that guidance as a recommendation, not an instruction. Following it early helps you reach the encounters that unlock core systems, including leveling and your spectral steed, Torrent. Once those pieces are in place, exploring away from the main route becomes one of the best ways to make progress.

If a castle gate, field boss, or difficult area feels far beyond you, mark it mentally or on the map and leave. Elden Ring repeatedly rewards players who return later with more health, better-upgraded gear, additional flask charges, stronger summons, and a better understanding of the game.
contentBlocks.caption: Sites of Grace point toward important early objectives, but their guidance is a direction to consider rather than a route you must follow.
contentBlocks.heading: Follow Grace Until the Game Opens Up — Then Wander
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring map shows Sites of Grace and Guidance of Grace routes across Limgrave and nearby early-game areas.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring’s stat screen can encourage new players to spread points everywhere. That usually makes the opening harder to read because every level feels small and your character remains fragile.

For most beginners, Vigor is the most useful early safety stat because it increases maximum HP. More health gives you room to survive mistakes long enough to understand what happened, which is often more valuable than chasing a small increase in damage.

After that, invest with a purpose. Raise the attributes required by the gear or magic you actually want to use, and avoid trying to support every possible playstyle on one early character. A focused character is easier to understand, and Elden Ring eventually provides ways to reconsider parts of your build later in the game.
contentBlocks.caption: Vigor increases maximum HP, giving new players more room to survive mistakes while learning enemy attacks.
contentBlocks.heading: Make Vigor Your Early Safety Net
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring status screen shows a high Vigor value alongside the character’s other attributes and defensive statistics.

contentBlocks.text:
One of the easiest systems to overlook is equipment load. Your equipped gear contributes to a weight total, and that weight affects how your character moves.

You do not need to chase the lightest possible setup, but you should pay attention to the load category shown on the status screen. If your character suddenly feels much less responsive after equipping heavier gear, check that value before assuming the controls changed.

This is a good example of how Elden Ring communicates through systems rather than tutorials. When something about your character feels different, the status screen often explains why.
contentBlocks.caption: Equip Load affects how your character moves and rolls, so heavier equipment is not automatically the safer choice.
contentBlocks.heading: Equipment Load Matters More Than It First Appears
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring equipment screen highlights the character’s Equip Load and Medium Load status.

contentBlocks.text:
Character levels are only one part of progression. Elden Ring also expects you to improve the gear and supporting tools you are already using.

Smithing Stones are used to strengthen many pieces of equipment, while Spirit Ashes have their own upgrade path later. Flask upgrades increase how much recovery you can carry or how effective each use becomes. These improvements can make a larger practical difference than several unfocused character levels.

Beginners often save every resource because they are worried something better may appear later. It is usually more useful to strengthen a setup that already works for you. Elden Ring contains many upgrade materials across its world, and early investment helps you reach the places where more become available.
contentBlocks.caption: Upgrading a weapon you already use can make a larger early-game difference than waiting for a supposedly perfect replacement.
contentBlocks.heading: Upgrade What You Use Instead of Waiting for Perfect Gear
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring blacksmith menu shows a weapon upgrade and the Smithing Stone materials required to strengthen it.

contentBlocks.text:
The world map starts deliberately incomplete. New regions become much easier to read once you find their map fragments, which are often indicated by small monument symbols on the unexplored map.

From there, use markers for your own memory. A cave you skipped, a merchant you want to revisit, a sealed path, an unusually difficult enemy, or an unexplored ruin can all be worth marking.

This keeps exploration from becoming a list of chores. You are building your own record of the Lands Between instead of trying to clear every icon before moving on. That matters because Elden Ring often expects you to notice something interesting, investigate it, and decide for yourself whether it is worth pursuing now.
contentBlocks.caption: Custom markers are useful for remembering caves, merchants, difficult encounters and other places worth revisiting.
contentBlocks.heading: Use the Map as a Memory Tool, Not a Checklist
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring world map is open with the custom marker menu displayed over Limgrave, Liurnia and Caelid.

contentBlocks.text:
Dying in Elden Ring causes you to drop the runes you were carrying. If you reach that location again before dying a second time, you can recover them.

That can make every loss feel more serious than it really is. Runes are valuable because they pay for levels and purchases, but losing a pile of them is not the same as losing your character’s progress. You keep discovered Sites of Grace, collected equipment, map knowledge, upgrade progress, and—most importantly—what you learned.

A useful habit is to spend a large amount of runes when you are close to a level or planned purchase before entering an area that looks especially difficult. Beyond that, accept that some runes will disappear. Treating every lost currency drop as a disaster makes experimentation much harder than the game intends.
contentBlocks.caption: Losing runes can sting, but discovered locations, equipment, upgrades and everything you learned remain with you.
contentBlocks.heading: Death Costs Runes, Not Progress
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Elden Ring map is centered on an early-game area with the player’s location and nearby landmarks visible.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring gives you several forms of assistance, including Spirit Ashes in eligible encounters, summonable NPCs in some situations, and cooperative multiplayer.

Using them is not a lesser way to play. They are systems deliberately built into the game, and they can make difficult encounters easier to understand by giving you more room to observe what is happening.

Spirit Ashes can also be upgraded, so a summon that feels useful early can remain relevant for longer if you invest in it. If you prefer playing alone, you can still use many of these single-player support systems without turning the game into a multiplayer experience.
contentBlocks.caption: Spirit Ashes and other summons are built into Elden Ring as tools that can create breathing room during difficult encounters.
contentBlocks.heading: Spirit Ashes, NPC Help, and Co-op Are Part of the Game
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A spectral Spirit Ash ally materializes beside the player character on a stone path in Elden Ring.

contentBlocks.text:
The main route quickly points toward Stormveil Castle, but there is no prize for arriving there underprepared.

Limgrave contains caves, tunnels, ruins, churches, merchants, flask upgrades, equipment, and optional encounters that teach the game at a gentler pace. The Weeping Peninsula to the south is also a useful early region for players who want more room to explore before pushing deeper into the main path.

This is one of Elden Ring’s most important lessons: when a major obstacle feels impossible, the answer is often somewhere else on the map. Exploring is not procrastination. It is how the game lets you build strength, gather options, and return with a better chance of understanding the challenge.
contentBlocks.caption: Limgrave gives new players plenty of room to explore, upgrade and learn before committing to the path through Stormveil.
contentBlocks.heading: Explore Limgrave Before Forcing Your Way Through Stormveil
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished rides Torrent through the grassy landscape of Limgrave with a large castle visible ahead.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring has enough hidden quests, rare items, branching character stories, and build possibilities to make a perfect first playthrough unrealistic.

Trying to follow an exact checklist can also undermine the reason the open world works so well. The strongest moments often come from seeing something strange in the distance, finding a path you were not looking for, or realizing that an area you once avoided is now manageable.

Use guides when a system is genuinely confusing or when you are stuck, but give yourself permission to miss things. You can return to large parts of the world later, and a first journey through the Lands Between is more memorable when discovery still belongs to you.
contentBlocks.heading: Do Not Turn Your First Playthrough Into an Optimization Project

conclusion:
Elden Ring becomes much easier to understand once you stop treating every obstacle as a test you must pass immediately. Follow Grace far enough to unlock the core systems, invest in survivability, keep the gear and summons you use upgraded, and let exploration do much of the work of progression.

Most importantly, do not measure a first playthrough by how efficiently you reach the next major boss. The Lands Between are built around curiosity. Mark places you want to revisit, walk away from challenges that are not working yet, and let your character develop around the discoveries that actually interest you. That rhythm is not a workaround for Elden Ring’s difficulty — it is one of the ways the game is designed to be played.

title: Which Game Has Won the Most GOTY Awards? The Most-Awarded Games Explained
description: Which games have won the most Game of the Year awards? Neural Critic breaks down the modern GOTY record, why award totals vary by tracker, and the games that dominate the all-time conversation.
body: There is no single official worldwide Game of the Year count. For this ranking, Neural Critic uses Meta Awards' current documented totals, which count both media-outlet GOTY picks and readers' choice awards. The database can change as historical records are added or reclassified, so these figures should be read as a tracker snapshot rather than one universal official total.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Last of Us Part II
imageAlt: The Game Awards logo displayed over the event’s stylized orange winged trophy artwork.
imageCredit: The Game Awards

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 544 Game of the Year wins for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, putting it at the top of the tracker’s all-time table. That total includes 390 media-outlet picks and 154 readers’ choice awards. The figure is a tracker snapshot rather than an official industry-wide count, and it can change as the database adds or reclassifies historical records.
contentBlocks.caption: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 became the current leader in Meta Awards’ all-time GOTY tracker after a dominant 2025 awards season.
contentBlocks.heading: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Members of Expedition 33 face a surreal landscape of floating ruins and monumental structures in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The current leader in Meta Awards’ all-time tracker

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 438 GOTY wins for Elden Ring. Its 2022 awards season reset the modern ceiling at the time and remains one of the strongest consensus runs in the tracker’s history.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring combined enormous critical acclaim with a dominant awards run following its 2022 release.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished kneels beneath a glowing Elden Ring symbol in key art for Elden Ring.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The 2022 benchmark that still sits second all time
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 325 GOTY wins for The Last of Us Part II. It was the modern tracker leader before Elden Ring overtook it and remains one of the most decorated releases in the database.
contentBlocks.caption: The Last of Us Part II became one of the most decorated games of its generation during the 2020 awards season.
contentBlocks.heading: The Last of Us Part II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Ellie stands against the flooded ruins of Seattle in key art for The Last of Us Part II.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The previous modern record holder before Elden Ring

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 292 GOTY wins for Baldur's Gate 3. Its 2023 run paired hundreds of publication and reader picks with victories across the highest-profile industry ceremonies, making it one of the broadest consensus seasons of the modern era.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur’s Gate 3 turned its extraordinary critical reception into one of the strongest Game of the Year awards runs of the modern era.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur's Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The main cast of Baldur’s Gate 3 gathers beneath a stormy sky as dragons and other creatures emerge around them.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A 2023 sweep across outlets, readers and major ceremonies

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 281 GOTY wins for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. That total keeps CD Projekt Red’s 2015 RPG firmly inside the tracker’s all-time top five.
contentBlocks.caption: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt became one of the most celebrated RPGs of its generation, collecting major Game of the Year recognition throughout the 2015 awards season.
contentBlocks.heading: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt logo in white and red against a dark background.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A 2015 awards sweep that still holds a top-five place
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 267 GOTY wins for God of War, placing the 2018 release just ahead of Breath of the Wild on the tracker’s all-time table. Its season was especially notable because it shared the year with Red Dead Redemption 2, another major critical favorite.
contentBlocks.caption: God of War emerged from a fiercely competitive 2018 field as one of the year’s most celebrated releases.
contentBlocks.heading: God of War
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Kratos and Atreus confront a massive troll during combat in God of War.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The 2018 winner that currently holds sixth place

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 265 GOTY wins for The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, two fewer than God of War in the tracker’s present all-time table. Its 2017 awards run remains one of Nintendo’s strongest modern consensus seasons.
contentBlocks.caption: Breath of the Wild transformed Nintendo’s open-world design and became one of 2017’s defining award winners.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link overlooks the vast landscape of Hyrule from a grassy cliff in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Nintendo’s 2017 landmark currently sits seventh

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 257 GOTY wins for The Last of Us. Together with its sequel’s 325 wins, that helps make The Last of Us one of the strongest franchises in the tracker’s aggregate awards history.
contentBlocks.caption: Naughty Dog’s The Last of Us dominated year-end recognition in 2013 and became one of the defining games of its era.
contentBlocks.heading: The Last of Us
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Ellie and Joel stand together during a scene from The Last of Us.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A 2013 landmark with 257 tracked GOTY wins

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 230 GOTY wins for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. Because the awards ecosystem was smaller in 2011 than it is today, its raw total also reflects a very different media landscape from more recent record-setters.
contentBlocks.caption: Skyrim became a landmark open-world RPG and one of the most acclaimed releases of 2011.
contentBlocks.heading: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Dragonborn walks through the Nordic village of Riverwood in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A 2011 giant from an era with fewer tracked awards
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox 360, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch

contentBlocks.text: Meta Awards currently records 191 GOTY wins for Uncharted 4: A Thief's End, making Naughty Dog’s 2016 release the tenth game on the tracker’s current all-time leaderboard. Astro Bot sits just outside that top ten with 185 tracked wins in the same database.
contentBlocks.heading: Uncharted 4: A Thief's End
contentBlocks.subtitle: The current cutoff for Meta Awards’ all-time top ten

quickRead: Meta Awards currently lists Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 first with 544 tracked GOTY wins
Elden Ring remains second with 438 tracked GOTY wins
The Last of Us Part II sits third with 325 tracked GOTY wins
conclusion: The safest way to read GOTY records is not as one immutable number but as a measure of awards-season reach. Different trackers will disagree at the margins, yet the historical picture is remarkably consistent: a small group of games — led in the modern era by Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and Elden Ring — collected an extraordinary share of year-end recognition. Neural Critic will keep this page updated as tracking databases revise historical totals and future awards seasons produce new challengers.
conclusionHeading: Why GOTY totals are useful — and why they are never perfectly official

title: GTA 6 Extended Look: Everything Rockstar Revealed About Vice City, Jason and Lucia
description: Rockstar’s first extended look at Grand Theft Auto VI puts the scale and detail of Leonida front and center, while revealing more about Jason and Lucia, missions, nightlife, activities and the systems shaping Vice City.
body: Rockstar Games has finally given Grand Theft Auto VI its most substantial official showcase yet. The roughly 26-minute Extended Look, premiered through Netflix on August 27, offered a much broader view of Leonida than the game’s earlier trailers, moving between story scenes, mission footage, driving, combat, nightlife and quieter environmental moments. The clearest takeaway is scale. Vice City and the wider state of Leonida are presented as unusually dense spaces, packed with interiors, crowds, traffic, businesses, nightlife and incidental detail. Rockstar also used the presentation to put Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos at the center of the game, showing how their relationship and criminal work connect the story to the world around them. Grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled to launch November 19, 2026 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork featuring Jason and Lucia alongside scenes from Leonida, including vehicles, wildlife and supporting characters surrounding the GTA VI logo.
imageCredit: Rockstar Games — Grand Theft Auto VI official media

contentBlocks.text:
More than any individual mission or mechanic, the showcase sells **Leonida as a place**. Rockstar moves rapidly between apartments, streets, beaches, rooftop venues, clubs, stores and the wider cityscape, repeatedly emphasizing how much activity exists around Jason and Lucia.

The environmental density is one of the presentation’s strongest features. Small props fill interiors, crowds occupy nightlife spaces, traffic and pedestrians make streets feel busy, and the skyline stretches far beyond the immediate action. The result is a world that appears designed around observation as much as traversal.

Rockstar’s official material describes Leonida as extending beyond Vice City, and the studio’s media library now contains dozens of screenshots and character/location assets that reinforce the scale shown during the presentation. 

The roughly 26-minute presentation was captured entirely from in-game footage on **PlayStation 5**, giving players Rockstar’s most extensive official look at GTA 6 yet.

Reporting published alongside the showcase says Rockstar describes GTA VI’s playable map as roughly **three times the size of Red Dead Redemption 2’s**. That figure comes from Rockstar-backed press coverage rather than a measurement demonstrated in the video itself.

Nelson has also described a layer of exploration that Rockstar does not necessarily direct players toward with objectives, map icons or blips. He says taking time to explore Leonida will be rewarded substantially, reinforcing the idea that some of the world’s discoveries are intended to emerge naturally rather than appear as checklist markers. That should not be read as confirmation that those encounters are procedurally generated; Rockstar is describing how players discover content, not how every encounter is authored.

Rockstar has also disclosed more about the production work behind that density. The studio says GTA VI contains **more than 600,000 animations**, compared with roughly 300,000 created for Red Dead Redemption 2 and about 55,000 for GTA V. The figure refers to animations — not hundreds of thousands of unique NPCs — and helps illustrate the scale of the behavioral library Rockstar has built for Leonida.

Rockstar North co-studio head **Aaron Garbut** told The New York Times that the company established a dedicated Los Angeles team of writers, directors and producers focused on realizing NPCs. Rather than treating pedestrians as interchangeable population filler, Rockstar says characters are individually art-directed, while interiors are authored around the people who occupy them — including contextual details and photographs tied to those spaces. The result supports the Extended Look’s emphasis on a city whose density comes not only from the number of people and objects on screen, but from the amount of authored context behind them.

Rockstar’s pursuit of authenticity extends beyond technology. In a Dazed feature produced with access to the GTA VI team, Rockstar says it has maintained a **dedicated research team in Miami**, while other development groups have repeatedly visited the city and surrounding areas over the course of production. Game writer Michael Wiafe says the goal is to understand South Florida beyond familiar stereotypes, and senior Rockstar staff say a **majority of the game’s characters grew out of that real-world research**. The team has met people across different parts of local life and cross-referenced those experiences with books and journalism before filtering the material through GTA’s fictional world.

That context helps explain why Leonida’s population is being treated as more than visual background. Rockstar says firsthand research informs the cultural and visual details associated with different communities, while its character, animation and environment teams turn that reference material into fictional people and places rather than direct reproductions of real individuals.
contentBlocks.heading: The Extended Look makes Leonida the star

contentBlocks.text:
The Extended Look spends substantial time establishing **Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as a partnership rather than two disconnected protagonists**. They live, travel and work together, but the presentation also shows tension between them as criminal jobs become more complicated.

Rockstar’s official character profiles describe Jason as a former Army serviceman who fell back into work for drug runners in the Leonida Keys, while Lucia is newly out of prison and determined to change her circumstances. The central setup remains that an apparently easy score goes wrong, pulling them into a conspiracy stretching across Leonida.

Recent reporting based on developer interviews also indicates that players can operate as the pair together or separately, expanding the character-switching concept beyond the three-protagonist structure of GTA V.

Press previews published alongside the Extended Look add an important mechanical detail: players can switch between Jason and Lucia and choose whether to spend time together or explore independently. Reporting also indicates that the state of their relationship can respond to player choices. Those details come from Rockstar-backed developer previews rather than from the Extended Look alone.

Rockstar North co-studio head **Rob Nelson** has since clarified an important limit to that relationship system: Jason and Lucia **remain partners regardless of their romantic state**. Players can influence how close the pair become, and whether the relationship is nurtured can affect how their story plays out, but the two cannot permanently split up as partners. This distinction keeps the player-responsive relationship from being mistaken for a system that can remove either protagonist from the central partnership.
contentBlocks.heading: Jason and Lucia are at the center of everything

contentBlocks.text:
The showcase opens the door on the kind of criminal work Jason and Lucia will undertake. One sequence follows the pair into an apartment building on a job connected to Vice City businessman and nightclub owner Boobie Ike before the situation erupts into violence and an escape. Elsewhere, Rockstar shows robberies, police pursuits and larger confrontations.

The underlying third-person structure remains recognizably Grand Theft Auto, but the environments around those encounters appear more reactive and physically detailed. Office furniture and glass respond during firefights, while interior spaces contain considerably more visual clutter than earlier GTA environments.

The presentation also shows Jason and Lucia communicating through their phones during dangerous situations, reinforcing how central the device appears to both missions and the wider world.

The police system is also more information-driven than GTA V’s. Rockstar North co-studio head **Rob Nelson** told press that a crime has to be witnessed or trigger an alarm before it is reported. During pursuit, police can retain information about Jason and Lucia’s faces, clothing, vehicle and whether they are travelling together. Changing vehicles or splitting up can therefore reduce what officers know about the suspects. The Extended Look also confirms the return of a **six-star wanted level**, restoring the maximum used by earlier GTA games.

Developer interviews add another layer to how those encounters can unfold. Nelson told Famitsu that GTA VI introduces a **suppression-fire** option: rather than directly attacking someone, players can deliberately fire nearby to frighten or confuse them and create an opportunity to escape. Rockstar says the mechanic is intended to give Jason and Lucia ways out of confrontations without automatically escalating every situation into lethal violence, fitting the story of two criminals trying to stay ahead of the authorities.

That choice also connects to the broader **Criminal Profile** system. Nelson describes GTA VI as tracking how players behave during crimes, including whether they escalate situations unnecessarily. The system should not yet be treated as a direct replacement for Red Dead Redemption 2’s Honor meter, but developer comments make clear that the degree of violence used can matter to how the game evaluates criminal behavior. Civilians can also react before a robbery fully begins: if someone notices suspicious behavior during the setup, they may alert police before the player has completed the crime.
contentBlocks.heading: Missions mix familiar GTA chaos with denser spaces

contentBlocks.text:
Rockstar devotes a significant part of the Extended Look to **Vice City after dark**. Jason and Lucia visit rooftop venues and clubs, while music, crowds and neon-lit streets give the city a distinct nighttime identity. A full day-and-night cycle naturally changes the atmosphere as the presentation moves between locations.

Phones appear repeatedly, including a busy social-media-style feed that fits Rockstar’s long-running habit of parodying contemporary culture through in-world media. Television and satirical advertising also return, with the protagonists’ apartment showing that GTA’s fictional entertainment ecosystem remains part of everyday play.
