That matters because GTA VI’s world is being presented as more than scenery for missions. Rockstar appears intent on surrounding the player with fictional culture — music, businesses, personalities, social media and television — that continues whether or not a major story mission is underway.

Rockstar-backed previews also confirm the return of **Snapmatic**. Jason and Lucia can use it, although reporting says the pair avoid publicly posting their own activity because of their criminal circumstances — a small detail that connects GTA VI’s social-media satire to the protagonists themselves.
contentBlocks.heading: Vice City nightlife and social media are everywhere

contentBlocks.text:
A rapid montage broadens the picture beyond scripted missions. The presentation shows a wide range of optional activities and encounters across Leonida.

Rockstar North co-studio head **Rob Nelson** also provided an unusually useful indication of the game’s scale in reporting published alongside the showcase. A playthrough he completed in February reportedly lasted about **80 hours**, covering the main story and some optional objectives with narrative consequences. That is not a promise that every GTA VI playthrough lasts 80 hours — player behavior and optional content can change the total — but it is the clearest developer-backed indication yet of the campaign’s potential scope.

Developer previews also reveal a much deeper character-fitness system than the Extended Look itself explains. Nelson told Famitsu that GTA VI tracks attributes including **health, cardio and fitness**, and that Jason and Lucia can physically change through their habits — including becoming more muscular through training or gaining weight through eating. Gyms are interactive rather than decorative: workouts consume stamina, reward controlled technique and can raise base health and stamina over time. Nelson said most gym equipment can be used, including exercises such as pull-ups.

Food is tied into those systems as well. Nelson said eating and drinking can provide temporary **buffs** to character gauges, while items such as energy drinks can boost stamina. Rockstar experimented with a more detailed refrigerator-restocking system during development before simplifying it, an example of the studio balancing simulation with convenience.

One smaller activity also comes with an important clarification. Tennis courts and rackets exist in Leonida, but reporting from the preview indicates GTA V’s structured tennis minigame does **not** simply return unchanged; players can instead pick up a racket and hit a ball as part of the more freely interactive world.

Rockstar’s official site has introduced characters spread across Vice City and the Leonida Keys. The Extended Look still does not provide a complete activity list, but the combination of the showcase and developer previews points to a substantial amount of optional life outside the central plot.

The physical-state simulation also extends beyond exercise and diet. Rockstar says spending prolonged periods away from Jason or Lucia’s bed — including extended stretches on the run — can leave **visible effects on their faces and bodies**. It is another indication that GTA VI is carrying some of Red Dead Redemption 2’s attention to physical condition into a modern setting, although Rockstar has not yet detailed every gameplay consequence attached to those changes.
contentBlocks.heading: There looks to be plenty to do away from the main story

contentBlocks.text:
For all the footage shown, Rockstar remains relatively guarded about the larger narrative. We know Jason and Lucia are partners, that an easy score goes wrong, and that they become caught in a wider criminal conspiracy across Leonida. The showcase adds context to their day-to-day relationship and the people around them without revealing the full shape of that conspiracy.

That restraint leaves some of GTA VI’s biggest questions unanswered. Rockstar has not used the Extended Look to fully explain the game’s progression structure, the limits of character switching, or the long-term consequences of player decisions. GTA Online also remains outside the focus of this single-player presentation.

For now, the world is arguably making the strongest impression. The presentation gives Rockstar’s version of Florida an extraordinary amount of texture; whether Jason and Lucia’s story can ultimately match that ambition is something the finished game will have to prove.

The unusually long road to GTA VI also helps explain Rockstar’s approach to its story and satire. Nelson told French magazine TROISCOULEURS that development began in **2015**, although the majority of the team did not move onto the project until after **Red Dead Redemption 2** shipped in 2018. That gives the project a more concrete development timeline than the broad “more than a decade” descriptions often attached to the game.

Nelson says those long production cycles also force Rockstar to be selective about contemporary satire. Ideas can become dated during the years required to write, cast, shoot and implement them, so the team tries to focus on situations and behavior that can remain relevant and that serve the story Rockstar is telling. That does not mean GTA VI is avoiding modern culture — the Extended Look is filled with social media, nightlife and contemporary Florida-inspired imagery — but it helps explain why Rockstar is aiming for satire that can survive the game’s unusually long development cycle.
contentBlocks.heading: The story is clearer, but Rockstar is still holding plenty back

contentBlocks.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI remains scheduled for **November 19, 2026** on **PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S**. Rockstar North co-studio head **Rob Nelson** has now directly reaffirmed that schedule in an interview with Famitsu, saying the game will be released as planned. He described the current phase of development as continued refinement, with the team working daily to deliver stable, smooth performance across GTA VI’s many interconnected systems. The comment reinforces Rockstar’s current November target, although it should not be treated as a guarantee that every technical option or performance mode has already been finalized. Rockstar currently lists GTA VI as a single-player experience, and no PC release date has been announced.

The Extended Look significantly expands our understanding of Leonida, Jason and Lucia and the kinds of situations players will encounter, but it is not a complete mechanical breakdown. Details surrounding GTA Online, a PC version and several underlying gameplay systems remain unconfirmed.

That distinction matters after months of leaks surrounding the game: this article focuses on material shown or supported through Rockstar’s official presentation and corroborated reporting, rather than treating unofficial footage as final-game confirmation.

Several deeper systems have now been described through Rockstar-backed press previews rather than Rockstar’s short Newswire announcement. Vehicle theft reportedly varies by vehicle security, with newer or more valuable cars sometimes requiring additional equipment. Preview coverage also describes a **Criminal Profile** system that tracks aspects of the player’s criminal behavior; it should not yet be treated as a direct equivalent of Red Dead Redemption 2’s Honor system.

Rockstar has officially confirmed that the entire Extended Look was captured from **in-game footage on PlayStation 5**. That makes the presentation a particularly useful look at what the game is already achieving on current-generation console hardware rather than an unspecified target render.

Performance reporting still requires an important distinction. Reporting from a Rockstar North preview visit says co-studio head and head of development **Rob Nelson** demonstrated console builds running at **30 frames per second** and described 30fps as the game’s current console performance during development. However, Nelson reportedly stopped short of confirming the complete launch configuration and said the technical team would need to determine whether a **60fps performance option** could be available at launch or later. The safest conclusion, therefore, is that 30fps is the clearest demonstrated current console target — not that Rockstar has formally announced every final performance mode. Final resolution targets and any additional graphics modes remain unannounced. GTA VI is also being designed primarily around **third-person play**. Reporting from the same Rockstar North access says Nelson indicated that a full, switchable first-person mode is **not planned for launch**, as the team is prioritizing its extensive third-person animation work. Limited first-person perspectives can still appear in specific interactions, but Rockstar has not announced a full-game first-person option or any plan to add one later.

Rockstar has also addressed two modern production and business questions during developer access surrounding the showcase. In an exchange reported from Kinda Funny’s Rockstar North visit, **Rob Nelson** said GTA VI does not use **generative AI for its game content**. That distinction matters because the game still relies heavily on conventional game AI for NPCs, traffic and world simulation; the developer statement concerns generative content creation rather than those traditional systems. The answer also fits Rockstar’s broader description of GTA VI as an unusually large-scale, human-authored production.

Nelson also reportedly said there are **no real-money microtransactions in the single-player experience being presented**. That statement should not be extended to GTA VI’s eventual online ecosystem: Rockstar has not yet detailed a GTA Online successor, its launch timing or its business model. It therefore confirms the position of the current single-player game without establishing how any future online component will be monetized.
contentBlocks.heading: What Rockstar confirmed — and what remains unknown

title: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition Hits 91 on Metacritic After Switch 2 Performance Fears
description: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition is now available on Nintendo Switch 2, and final reviews suggest FromSoftware has turned a worrying early port into a surprisingly strong handheld version of the Lands Between.
body:
Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition launched on Nintendo Switch 2 on August 28, 2026, with a far stronger critical reception than its troubled road to release once suggested. Initial review roundups put the new edition at 91 on Metacritic from 31 critic reviews, and the score remained at 91 as more reviews were added. Reviewers repeatedly highlighted how well FromSoftware’s enormous open-world RPG survived the move to Nintendo’s hybrid hardware.

That reception is particularly notable because Tarnished Edition spent much of its pre-release cycle under a cloud of performance concerns. Earlier demonstrations raised questions about whether the Switch 2 version could deliver the consistency Elden Ring demands. After additional development time, however, final-build reviews described a surprisingly accomplished port.

Tarnished Edition includes Elden Ring, the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion, and additional content created for this release.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition key art for Nintendo Switch 2, featuring a Tarnished from FromSoftware’s acclaimed open-world action RPG.
imageCredit: Bandai Namco Entertainment / FromSoftware

contentBlocks.text: Ahead of launch, review roundups reported a **91 Metacritic score from 31 critic reviews**, a striking result for a port whose technical condition had become part of the story.\n\nNow that Tarnished Edition is actually available, full final-build reviews reinforce the broader point behind that early score: critics are largely finding that Elden Ring survives the move to Switch 2 far better than its troubled pre-release demonstrations suggested. The precise Metacritic average and review count can continue to move as additional reviews are added, so the more durable story is the strength of the overall reception rather than a permanently fixed number.
contentBlocks.heading: A 91 Metacritic score changed the conversation

contentBlocks.text:
The path to release was not straightforward. Earlier Switch 2 demonstrations raised serious performance concerns, making the quality of the finished port one of Tarnished Edition’s biggest questions.

Final reviews paint a considerably better picture. Nintendo Wire reports that the game targets **30 FPS in both handheld and docked modes** and says it maintained that target most of the time across more than 20 hours of play, although occasional slowdowns still occurred. UnGeek likewise describes the final build as very playable while noting drops below the 30 FPS target in demanding open-world situations. WorthPlaying calls the finished version generally consistent despite clear visual and frame-rate compromises.

The important distinction is that Tarnished Edition is not suddenly the technically definitive version of Elden Ring. The Switch 2 release still makes compromises, and different reviewers report different levels of slowdown. What has changed is that the final build is being reviewed as a viable, enjoyable port rather than the technical problem many feared.
contentBlocks.heading: From performance fears to a much stronger final port

contentBlocks.text: The Switch 2 version’s strongest argument is portability. Several reviews emphasize how impressive it is to have Elden Ring’s enormous world available as a handheld experience, even when the image and performance cannot match PlayStation 5, Xbox Series consoles or a capable PC.\n\nThat advantage also helps explain why assessments of docked and handheld play vary. Some reviewers report a remarkably consistent experience between the two modes, while others prefer handheld presentation because the smaller display makes visual compromises less noticeable. The consensus is therefore less “Switch 2 is the best version” and more “this is a surprisingly credible portable version of Elden Ring.”
contentBlocks.heading: Handheld play may be Tarnished Edition’s real advantage

contentBlocks.text: **Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition includes the base game and Shadow of the Erdtree expansion** on Switch 2, alongside the new Tarnished Pack content. Bandai Namco’s August 28 launch announcement confirms two additional starting classes — **Heavy Knight and Idus Knight** — four new armor sets and three appearance options for Torrent.\n\nPatch 1.17 adds further detail. The new starting-class equipment can also be obtained elsewhere in the Lands Between, additional weapons have been added, and the update introduces **two new NPC invasion events**, one in Caelid and another in Leyndell, Royal Capital. The Tarnished Pack content is included by default with Tarnished Edition and is also available separately for existing Elden Ring players on supported platforms.
contentBlocks.heading: Tarnished Edition includes more than the original game

contentBlocks.text:
Tarnished Edition launched on **August 28, 2026**, marking Elden Ring’s first appearance on a Nintendo platform. For players who prioritize maximum image quality or higher performance, the existing console and PC versions remain stronger choices.

But that is no longer the most interesting question surrounding this release. After the concern created by its early demonstrations, FromSoftware has delivered a Switch 2 version that reviewers broadly consider capable of preserving the scale, combat and atmosphere that made Elden Ring exceptional.

That makes Tarnished Edition less a story about whether Switch 2 can run Elden Ring at all and more about the compromises players are willing to accept in exchange for taking the Lands Between with them.
contentBlocks.heading: The turnaround is now the real story

conclusion: ==The strongest story surrounding Tarnished Edition may not be that Elden Ring remains an exceptional game four years later. It is that a Switch 2 version once defined by technical concern reached launch with critics talking about how successfully FromSoftware turned it around. For players who wanted to explore the Lands Between on Nintendo hardware, the finished release is a much stronger proposition than the port’s early showings suggested.==

title: Future Games Show at gamescom 2026 Delivers 13 World Premieres and a Packed Slate of Release Updates

title: Crazy Taxi: World Tour Reveals Germany Map, New Crazy Drift Move and September Network Test

body: Crazy Taxi: World Tour is ==playable publicly for the first time at gamescom 2026==, where Sega is showing a newly revealed ==Germany map — one of five international locations planned for the game==. The latest update also details a new Crazy Drift move, a Nitro Boost mechanic, and an upcoming multiplayer closed network test that will give players outside gamescom an early chance to try the game.
author: Rouane Mounssif

contentBlocks.heading: Germany is one of five international maps

contentBlocks.text: Returning Crazy Moves such as Crazy Dash and Crazy Stop are joined by the ==new Crazy Drift==. Players can also use ==Nitro Boost== for extra speed, with missions and challenges designed around linking movement techniques into fast, risky routes.
contentBlocks.heading: Crazy Drift and Nitro expand the driving toolkit

contentBlocks.text: Sega says the Crazy Taxi: World Tour Multiplayer Closed Network Test will run from ==September 11 to September 13==, with ==applications closing August 31==. The game is currently scheduled to arrive on PlayStation 5 in 2027.
contentBlocks.heading: A multiplayer test is coming in September

title: Persona 4 Revival Gamescom Demo Reveals Modernized Dungeons and a New Prime Time Meter
description: Sega and P-Studio have detailed Persona 4 Revival’s first public playable demo at gamescom 2026, including three demo channels, modernized dungeons, and the new Prime Time combat meter.

The remake’s hands-on build is split into three “Channels” covering the opening story, dungeon exploration, and daily life in Inaba. The demo also introduces a ==new Prime Time meter==, giving the first concrete look at one of the remake’s new combat systems ahead of its February 18, 2027 release on PlayStation 5.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The protagonist of Persona 4 Revival poses at the center of colorful promotional artwork surrounded by members of the Investigation Team and their Personas.

Channel 2 shifts toward free exploration inside a ==modernized version of Yukiko’s Castle==, ending with a fight against Shadow Chie.
contentBlocks.heading: Three demo Channels show different sides of the remake

contentBlocks.text: A third section, available to press and creators, focuses more heavily on daily life before returning to the dungeon. Sega says this section introduces the ==new Prime Time meter, which can be used to trigger high-impact combo sequences in battle==.
contentBlocks.heading: Prime Time is one of the newly detailed combat systems

contentBlocks.text: Sega says Persona 4 Revival will launch on PlayStation 5 on ==February 18, 2027==. The gamescom demo is the clearest look yet at how P-Studio is updating the RPG’s dungeon flow and combat while preserving the Inaba setting and social-life structure.
contentBlocks.heading: Persona 4 Revival launches in February 2027

title: Baldur’s Gate 3 Review: A New Standard for RPG Freedom
description: Larian’s role-playing epic turns player choice, flexible problem solving, and memorable companions into one of the most reactive adventures in modern RPGs.
body:
Baldur's Gate 3 begins with a familiar role-playing promise: create a character, gather a party, make choices, and see where the adventure goes. What separates Larian's RPG is how seriously it takes the last part. The game is unusually willing to let plans fail, conversations spiral in unexpected directions, quests resolve through methods the designers never explicitly highlight, and consequences follow decisions far beyond the moment they were made.

That reactivity gives Baldur's Gate 3 a rare sense of ownership. A player can talk their way through an encounter, fight it, sneak past it, manipulate the environment, use magic in an unconventional way, or create a disaster and live with the result. The game constantly invites experimentation because it has been built to respond to experimentation.

It is not frictionless. Inventory management is clumsy, camera and pathfinding issues can disrupt exploration, and the final act is so dense that performance, pacing, and quest clarity become less consistent. Yet those weaknesses sit beside some of the strongest companion writing, tactical combat, and role-playing freedom in the genre. Baldur's Gate 3 does not simply offer many choices. It makes those choices feel like part of a world capable of answering back.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The main companions of Baldur’s Gate 3 stand together beneath a stormy fantasy sky, with the game’s logo and a looming mind flayer threat framing the official promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Larian Studios / Baldur’s Gate 3 official promotional artwork.

cons: Inventory management remains cumbersome across a long campaign
Camera, pathfinding, and vertical navigation can become awkward
Act 3 is less focused and can feel overloaded compared with the earlier acts
The number of systems, spells, and rules can be intimidating for newcomers
pros: Exceptional player freedom and quest reactivity
Companions are memorable, layered, and deeply integrated into the story
Turn-based combat rewards creativity rather than a single optimal solution
Exploration constantly produces meaningful discoveries and alternate paths
Outstanding replayability thanks to classes, origins, choices, and branching outcomes
reviewMeta.verdict: A landmark RPG whose extraordinary reactivity, characters, and tactical freedom outweigh occasional technical friction and an overstuffed final act.

contentBlocks.text:
Many RPGs present choices through dialogue menus. Baldur's Gate 3 expands that idea into nearly every system. A door can be lockpicked, broken, bypassed from another route, opened with magic, or ignored entirely. A hostile encounter might become a negotiation, an ambush, a rescue, or a mistake that changes several quests at once.

The important part is not that every possibility exists. It is that enough possibilities work consistently for players to trust experimentation. Once that trust forms, the game becomes much more than a sequence of authored solutions.

Failure contributes to that freedom. A missed dice roll does not always mean reloading a save. Sometimes failure reveals a different conversation, relationship, or route through a quest. Baldur's Gate 3 is strongest when players allow imperfect outcomes to become part of their version of the story.
contentBlocks.heading: Choice Matters Because the Game Is Prepared to Respond

contentBlocks.text:
Shadowheart, Lae'zel, Astarion, Gale, Wyll, Karlach, and the rest of the cast begin with strong archetypes, but their stories become more complicated as the campaign develops. Beliefs change, loyalties are tested, and personal quests can reshape how entire characters are understood.

The writing benefits from patience. Companions react not only to major story decisions but also to smaller patterns in the player's behavior. Approval systems are still systems, yet they rarely feel completely detached from characterization.

Performance capture and voice acting add enormous weight. A conversation in camp can carry as much emotional importance as a major battle because the characters feel present rather than stored away until their next quest marker appears. The party is not simply a collection of combat abilities; it is the emotional center of the campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Companions Are More Than Party Roles

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur's Gate 3 translates Dungeons & Dragons combat into a system that is tactical without becoming rigid. Positioning, elevation, surfaces, spell interactions, environmental objects, summons, stealth, and improvised weapons create opportunities that extend far beyond choosing the strongest attack each turn.

A difficult fight can change completely after pushing an enemy from a ledge, blocking a doorway, extinguishing fire, creating an electrified surface, or using a spell for a purpose that has nothing to do with direct damage.

The large number of classes and subclasses makes party composition equally flexible. Some combinations are naturally stronger than others, but the game is generous enough that experimentation rarely feels punished on standard difficulty. Combat becomes another language for role-playing: the way a party fights can reflect the characters the player chose to build.
contentBlocks.heading: Turn-Based Combat Rewards Imagination

contentBlocks.text:
The environments are dense rather than enormous. Roads branch, caves hide beneath familiar areas, rooftops reveal alternate entrances, and apparently decorative spaces can contain quests, secrets, or entirely different approaches to an objective.

That density makes exploration meaningful. The game frequently rewards players for reading notes, talking to animals, noticing a suspicious wall, jumping somewhere inconvenient, or revisiting a location after learning new information.

Because quests overlap geographically and narratively, discoveries often connect. A small clue can alter a later conversation, and a side path can reveal context that changes how a major faction is understood. Baldur's Gate 3 rarely needs to place a giant reward at the end of exploration because information itself is often valuable.
contentBlocks.heading: Exploration Constantly Rewards Looking Twice

contentBlocks.text:
The visible dice system makes chance part of the game's identity. Persuasion, deception, investigation, saving throws, attacks, and many other actions depend on probabilities shaped by character abilities and circumstances.

That randomness can create frustration, especially when a carefully planned conversation collapses because of one poor roll. But it also prevents the player from controlling every outcome and gives character builds meaning outside combat.

A persuasive bard and an intimidating barbarian can experience the same scene differently because their strengths change which risks are reasonable. Inspiration, bonuses, spells, and advantage give the player ways to influence chance without eliminating it completely. The result is a campaign that feels authored and unpredictable at the same time.
contentBlocks.heading: Dice Rolls Give Uncertainty a Visible Shape

contentBlocks.text:
For all of its systemic sophistication, Baldur's Gate 3 can be surprisingly awkward to manage. Long campaigns generate enormous inventories, containers multiply, useful items are easy to forget, and shifting equipment between party members can become tedious.

Camera behavior is another persistent weakness. Vertical spaces sometimes make it difficult to understand where party members are standing, and pathfinding can produce strange routes or leave companions behind.

None of these issues destroys the experience, but they accumulate because the game is so long and so dense with objects. Larian built a world where almost everything can matter; the interface is not always equally good at helping the player manage everything they have collected.
contentBlocks.heading: Inventory and Interface Friction Never Fully Disappear

contentBlocks.text:
The city of Baldur's Gate is packed with characters, quests, locations, companion resolutions, faction conflicts, and major story decisions. That density is exciting, but it also changes the rhythm of the campaign.

Earlier acts are easier to read because exploration, narrative momentum, and major objectives are more naturally separated. Act 3 can feel like everything arrives at once. Quest logs grow, important characters compete for attention, and technical performance has historically been less consistent in the busiest areas.

There are extraordinary moments throughout the final act, including some of the game's best character conclusions. The issue is not a lack of quality. It is concentration. Baldur's Gate 3 becomes so full of possibility that its structure struggles to make every possibility feel equally urgent.
contentBlocks.heading: Act 3 Is Ambitious Enough to Become Overwhelming

contentBlocks.text:
Replayability is where Baldur's Gate 3 separates itself most clearly from many story-driven RPGs. Different classes change exploration and conversation. Origin characters provide new perspectives. The Dark Urge creates a substantially different role-playing framework. Companion choices, romances, faction decisions, quest outcomes, and simple dice luck can redirect entire sequences.

More importantly, players learn how much they missed. Finishing one campaign often reveals how many situations could have unfolded differently, which makes a second playthrough feel less like repetition and more like testing another interpretation of the same world.

The game does not require players to see everything. In fact, its confidence comes partly from allowing content to disappear when choices close doors. That willingness gives each campaign more identity.
contentBlocks.heading: Few RPGs Offer This Much Reason to Start Again

conclusion:
==Baldur's Gate 3 is one of the clearest demonstrations of what role-playing games can achieve when systems, writing, exploration, and character choice are allowed to overlap. Its greatest strength is not simply the number of options available, but the confidence that the world will usually recognize what the player tried to do.==

==Inventory friction, awkward navigation, and an overloaded final act keep the experience from feeling perfectly controlled, but perfection would almost work against the game's personality. Baldur's Gate 3 is messy because it is extraordinarily reactive, and that reactivity makes its best moments feel personal in a way few modern RPGs can match.==

title: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom Review: A Brilliant Sequel Built on Possibility
description: Tears of the Kingdom expands Breath of the Wild’s freedom with creative building systems, layered exploration, and a Hyrule designed around player invention.
body:
Tears of the Kingdom begins with an impossible assignment: follow one of the most influential open-world games ever made without simply repeating it. Nintendo’s answer is not to replace Breath of the Wild’s philosophy, but to stretch it in every direction. Hyrule now reaches into the sky and beneath the surface, Link can fuse objects into weapons, assemble vehicles and machines with Ultrahand, reverse motion with Recall, and approach problems with an even broader set of improvised solutions.

The result is one of Nintendo’s most technically astonishing games and one of the most flexible adventure sandboxes ever made. Almost every encounter invites experimentation, and the systems frequently combine in ways that feel authored by the player rather than prescribed by the designer.

Yet Tears of the Kingdom is also a sequel in the truest sense. Its expanded Hyrule is richer and more mechanically expressive, but it cannot fully recreate the shock of discovering Breath of the Wild’s world for the first time. Some inherited frustrations remain, the enormous Depths can become visually repetitive, and the game occasionally asks so much of its building systems that momentum gives way to menu management and construction. It is a phenomenal sequel — just slightly less magical than the revolution that came before it.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
imageAlt: Link crouches on the edge of a floating sky island overlooking the clouds and scattered ruins above Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom official promotional artwork.

cons: Returning to the same Hyrule cannot match Breath of the Wild’s original sense of discovery
Weapon durability remains divisive even with Fuse softening the problem
The Depths become visually and structurally repetitive over long sessions
Building and material selection can interrupt the pace when experimentation turns into menu work
pros: Ultrahand and Fuse create extraordinary freedom for experimentation
Sky islands, caves, and the Depths dramatically expand the scale of exploration
Improved dungeons and stronger quest structure give the adventure more traditional Zelda identity
Systemic interactions reward creativity in combat, traversal, and puzzle solving
An astonishing technical achievement on Nintendo Switch
reviewMeta.verdict: A spectacular sequel that expands Zelda’s systemic freedom into something even more expressive, though a reused Hyrule, familiar durability frustrations, and some repetitive underground exploration keep it just below Breath of the Wild’s first-time magic.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review of the Nintendo Switch release. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild gave players a remarkably permissive set of rules. Tears of the Kingdom goes further by giving them tools that can create entirely new solutions. Ultrahand lets Link connect objects into vehicles, bridges, weapons platforms, flying machines, improvised elevators, and devices that often look nothing like what Nintendo might have expected.

The important part is not that the game contains a building system. It is that the building system operates inside the same physics-driven world as everything else. Wheels provide motion, fans create lift, rockets produce bursts of force, stabilizers correct orientation, and environmental objects can become structural pieces. The player is constantly asking not only “Where can I go?” but “What can I make that gets me there?”

That shift makes problem solving feel deeply personal. Two players can arrive at the same shrine, monster camp, or canyon and solve it in completely different ways without either solution feeling like an exploit.
contentBlocks.heading: Ultrahand Changes the Meaning of Player Freedom

contentBlocks.text:
Weapon durability returns, and anyone who disliked breaking swords in Breath of the Wild will still feel some of that friction. Tears of the Kingdom’s smartest response is Fuse, which turns monster parts, rocks, horns, elemental materials, and countless objects into extensions of Link’s equipment.

Fuse does not remove durability, but it gives disposable weapons more personality. A weak sword can become useful when combined with a powerful monster horn. An arrow can inherit elemental effects, tracking behavior, light, or explosive properties depending on what is attached to it. Shields become platforms for stranger experiments, including mobility tricks and defensive gadgets.

The system transforms loot into potential rather than simple numerical upgrades. Even so, players who prefer building a permanent relationship with a favorite weapon may still find the constant cycle of replacement unsatisfying.
contentBlocks.heading: Fuse Makes Disposable Weapons More Interesting

contentBlocks.text:
The surface map is recognizably the Hyrule from Breath of the Wild, and that familiarity is both a strength and the sequel’s biggest limitation. Returning players understand its geography, landmarks, and major regions immediately, which lets Nintendo create pleasure through change: settlements have evolved, caves open beneath familiar terrain, regional crises reshape old locations, and new routes alter how the player moves through the landscape.

But familiarity inevitably reduces some of the original game’s mystery. In Breath of the Wild, a distant mountain could represent a completely unknown space. In Tears of the Kingdom, the same mountain often comes with memories attached.

Nintendo compensates with density rather than novelty. The world contains more layers, more entrances, more side quests, more caves, more systems, and more reasons to reconsider places you thought you understood. It is an impressive transformation, even if it cannot reproduce the sensation of seeing Hyrule for the first time.
contentBlocks.heading: Hyrule Is Familiar, but It Is No Longer the Same World

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom’s new vertical structure gives exploration a different rhythm. Sky islands provide compact challenges, aerial navigation, and some of the game’s most beautiful vistas. Launching from a tower, gliding between islands, and improvising a machine to reach something that looks impossibly distant creates the kind of spontaneous adventure the series does exceptionally well.

The Depths are a more complicated addition. Descending into darkness and gradually illuminating an enormous underground map is initially one of the game’s most striking ideas. The atmosphere is hostile, resources become more important, and familiar surface geography gains an eerie parallel beneath it.

Over time, however, the Depths reveal less visual variety than the surface. Their enormous scale can become repetitive once the basic environmental language is understood. They remain valuable for exploration and resources, but they do not sustain mystery as consistently as Hyrule above.
contentBlocks.heading: The Sky Adds Wonder; the Depths Add Scale

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom still uses shrines as its primary collection of compact puzzle spaces, but its new abilities give those challenges a wider vocabulary. Ultrahand, Recall, Ascend, and Fuse encourage players to think about construction, motion, verticality, and physical relationships rather than searching for a single intended switch.

The larger regional temples are also a meaningful improvement. They retain the freedom and openness of the modern Zelda formula while providing stronger themes, more distinct identities, and more memorable journeys leading into them.

They are not a complete return to the sprawling traditional dungeons of older Zelda games, but the balance is stronger. Tears of the Kingdom feels more comfortable acknowledging the series’ history without giving up the systemic freedom that defines this era.
contentBlocks.heading: Shrines and Dungeons Feel Closer to Classic Zelda

contentBlocks.text:
The same systems that make Tears of the Kingdom extraordinary can occasionally make it cumbersome. Building a machine is exhilarating when an idea comes together quickly. It is less exciting when the player repeatedly opens menus, searches through materials, rotates components, repairs a misaligned object, or rebuilds something that fell apart before it could function.

Autobuild eventually reduces some of this repetition, but the game still asks players to enjoy the process of experimentation itself. For many people that is the appeal. For others, especially those who prefer Zelda’s faster movement and cleaner action, the construction layer can sometimes feel like work between adventures.

That tension is fundamental to the sequel. Tears of the Kingdom provides more freedom than Breath of the Wild, but additional freedom also means additional complexity.
contentBlocks.heading: Creativity Is Also Where the Friction Lives

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom presents a more direct sense of crisis and a stronger central mystery than Breath of the Wild. Zelda’s role in the story carries emotional weight, Ganondorf gives the conflict a more recognizable villain, and several major characters receive satisfying development across the adventure.

The memory-based structure remains somewhat awkward because players can discover major scenes out of narrative order. Freedom of exploration is one of the game’s core principles, but unrestricted discovery can weaken dramatic pacing when an important revelation appears before the scenes designed to build toward it.

Even with that problem, the story feels more present throughout the journey. Regional arcs, recurring characters, and the final sequence give the adventure stronger momentum than its predecessor.
contentBlocks.heading: The Story Is Stronger, Even When Its Delivery Is Awkward

contentBlocks.text:
On almost every mechanical measure, Tears of the Kingdom is more ambitious than Breath of the Wild. It contains more systems, more spaces, more ways to solve problems, more elaborate quests, stronger dungeons, and one of the most impressive physics sandboxes ever built into a console game.

But greatness is not always a matter of quantity. Breath of the Wild’s defining achievement was making Hyrule feel unknown. Tears of the Kingdom inherits that world and transforms it brilliantly, yet the player arrives with knowledge the first game deliberately denied them.

That is why the sequel can be technically richer while landing slightly lower overall. Tears of the Kingdom is an extraordinary game of invention. Breath of the Wild was an extraordinary game of discovery. The former expands almost everything; the latter changed the feeling of Zelda itself.
contentBlocks.heading: Bigger and More Ingenious — but Not Quite More Magical

conclusion:
==Tears of the Kingdom is a remarkable sequel precisely because it refuses to play things safe. Ultrahand, Fuse, Recall, Ascend, the sky, and the Depths transform a familiar Hyrule into a playground for ideas, while stronger dungeons and a more present story bring some traditional Zelda identity back into Nintendo’s open-air formula.==

==Its weaknesses are mostly the cost of that ambition. The reused world cannot fully restore Breath of the Wild’s original mystery, weapon durability still divides opinion, the Depths eventually repeat themselves, and building can occasionally interrupt the adventure’s momentum. None of those issues seriously diminish what Nintendo accomplished. Tears of the Kingdom is one of the finest open-world adventures of its generation — just a little less singular than the game that made this version of Hyrule feel limitless in the first place.==

==9.4/10 — OUTSTANDING==
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom

title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Review: An Unforgettable Western Epic
description: Rockstar’s vast western pairs extraordinary world detail and character writing with a deliberately paced journey through the final days of an outlaw gang.
body:
Red Dead Redemption 2 opens in retreat. The Van der Linde gang is already running, winter has closed around them, and the dream of a freer life is beginning to crack. From that point forward, Rockstar builds a western less interested in making the player feel unstoppable than in making an entire way of life feel temporary.

That choice defines almost everything about the game. Its open world is enormous, but the strongest moments often arrive at a walking pace: sharing coffee at camp, riding through a storm, helping a stranger on the roadside, or watching Arthur Morgan quietly process what his life has become. Red Dead Redemption 2 is technically an action game, yet its lasting power comes from observation, character, and atmosphere.

It is also deliberately heavy. Movement has weight, animations take time, missions often expect the player to follow Rockstar's exact choreography, and the game's devotion to physical detail can become friction. Those weaknesses are real. They are also part of the same design philosophy that makes this world feel unusually tangible. The result is one of Rockstar's most ambitious games: occasionally cumbersome, frequently extraordinary, and difficult to forget once the credits roll.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Arthur Morgan aims a revolver toward the viewer in stylized red-and-yellow promotional artwork for Red Dead Redemption 2, with members of the Van der Linde gang riding in silhouette across the background.
imageCredit: Rockstar Games / Red Dead Redemption 2 official promotional artwork.

cons: Movement, looting, and repeated animations can feel unnecessarily slow
Main missions are often far more restrictive than the open world surrounding them
The deliberately measured pacing will test players who prefer constant action
Control complexity can make simple interactions feel cumbersome
pros: One of the most detailed and convincing open worlds ever created
Arthur Morgan anchors an exceptional character-driven story
Outstanding performances, music, sound design, and visual direction
Exploration feels organic thanks to memorable encounters and environmental storytelling
Camp life and small interactions give the world unusual emotional texture
reviewMeta.verdict: A remarkable western epic whose character writing, world detail, and atmosphere outweigh its cumbersome controls and unusually rigid mission design.

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 works because Arthur Morgan is more than an avatar for the player. He begins as a loyal enforcer who believes in Dutch van der Linde's vision because that belief gives his life structure. As the gang's plans fail, Arthur is forced to examine the difference between loyalty and denial.

The writing rarely rushes that transformation. Arthur's personality emerges through camp conversations, optional encounters, journal entries, quiet rides, and the way he responds to people outside the gang. His arc feels earned because the game gives him room to be contradictory: intimidating and gentle, cynical and hopeful, selfish in one moment and deeply compassionate in another.

That depth elevates the entire cast. Dutch, Hosea, John, Sadie, Charles, Javier, and the rest of the gang are not simply quest dispensers. They occupy the camp, argue, sing, complain, disappear on errands, and react to the gang's changing fortunes. By the time relationships begin to fracture, the loss feels personal because the game spent so much time making those relationships ordinary first.
contentBlocks.heading: Arthur Morgan Gives the Story Its Soul

contentBlocks.text:
Rockstar's greatest achievement is not the size of the map. It is the density of believable detail inside it. Towns have routines, wildlife behaves according to the environment, weather changes the mood of a journey, and random encounters often feel like stories rather than interruptions.

There are icons and structured activities, but Red Dead Redemption 2 is at its best when the player stops treating the map like a checklist. A ride across several miles can lead to a robbery, an injured traveler, a strange cabin, a hunting opportunity, or nothing more dramatic than a beautiful view. That uncertainty gives travel purpose.

The world also remembers more than most open worlds do. People recognize Arthur, crimes can affect how towns respond to him, camp members notice prolonged absences, and small actions feed into the broader impression that the player is moving through a place rather than a collection of isolated systems. The illusion is not perfect, but it remains unusually convincing.
contentBlocks.heading: The Open World Feels Lived In Rather Than Filled In

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 wants physical actions to feel physical. Arthur opens drawers, skins animals, cleans weapons, searches bodies, mounts horses, eats, drinks, and handles objects with animations that are often more detailed than they need to be.

Early on, that commitment is impressive because it gives the game texture. Hours later, the same commitment can become exhausting. Picking up several items in a room or looting after a large fight can take longer than the decision-making itself. Even basic movement can feel imprecise in tight interiors because Arthur's momentum is designed around weight rather than instant responsiveness.

This is the clearest example of the game's central tradeoff. Rockstar frequently chooses immersion over convenience. For some players that makes the world richer. For others it creates unnecessary distance between intention and action. Both reactions are understandable, and neither can be separated completely from what the game is trying to accomplish.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Slowness Is Both a Strength and a Weakness

contentBlocks.text:
The biggest contradiction in Red Dead Redemption 2 is the gap between its open world and its story missions. Outside missions, the player can improvise constantly. During missions, leaving the expected route, approaching from the wrong angle, or trying an unconventional solution can trigger failure.

That rigidity gives Rockstar control over pacing and presentation. Major missions can feel carefully directed because the game knows where Arthur will be and what he is likely to see. The downside is that a world built around possibility suddenly becomes narrow whenever the story needs to move forward.

The contrast becomes especially noticeable because the simulation is otherwise so flexible. A game that lets the player solve small problems organically often refuses to tolerate creativity during its biggest set pieces. The missions are frequently spectacular, but the design underneath them can feel older and more restrictive than the world they inhabit.
contentBlocks.heading: The Mission Design Is Strangely Rigid

contentBlocks.text:
Gunfights are effective without being the primary reason to play. Weapons have convincing sound and recoil, Dead Eye adds a satisfying layer of control, and the physical reactions of enemies make shootouts feel dramatic. Still, cover shooting becomes repetitive over a long campaign, and the game's heavy controls can make fast movement less elegant than the presentation suggests.

What keeps combat memorable is context. A shootout in a muddy street, a train robbery at night, or a desperate escape through the mountains feels different because the environment, music, weather, and narrative stakes change around the mechanics.

Red Dead Redemption 2 understands spectacle, but it understands anticipation even better. The ride toward danger, the conversation before weapons are drawn, and the silence afterward are often as important as the shooting itself. That sense of rhythm helps otherwise familiar combat carry more emotional weight.
contentBlocks.heading: Combat Is Functional, but Atmosphere Does More of the Work

contentBlocks.text:
The camp system is one of the game's quietest strengths. It gives the gang a physical center and allows relationships to develop outside formal missions. Characters move through routines, tell stories, argue, sing, ask favors, and react to the changing state of the group.

Many of these interactions can be missed, which makes them feel more authentic. The game does not always announce when something meaningful is happening. Sometimes Arthur simply walks past a conversation or sits near the fire long enough to hear a story that changes how a character is understood.

Because the camp begins as a place of relative warmth, its deterioration becomes one of the game's most effective storytelling devices. As trust fades and pressure rises, the same physical space begins to feel different. Few open-world games use a home base this effectively as an emotional barometer.
contentBlocks.heading: Camp Makes the Gang Feel Like a Community

contentBlocks.text:
The visual achievement of Red Dead Redemption 2 is not limited to resolution or texture quality. Its art direction gives regions distinct identities through light, weather, color, architecture, vegetation, and sound. The world can shift from peaceful to threatening without changing maps or loading a new zone.

Animation quality remains equally important. Horses move with extraordinary detail, characters react naturally to terrain, clothing and equipment respond to motion, and facial performances carry subtle emotion during quieter scenes. The soundtrack understands when to swell and when to disappear entirely.

All of that craft supports the same goal: making the western feel physical and temporary. Red Dead Redemption 2 is beautiful, but its beauty often carries melancholy. The world is changing, the gang is running out of places to hide, and the game makes that decline visible in almost every part of its presentation.
contentBlocks.heading: A Technical and Artistic Achievement That Still Holds Up

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 is not built for efficiency. Players who rush between objective markers may find the pacing frustrating and the controls unnecessarily elaborate. Players willing to inhabit the world are more likely to understand why the game has endured.

The best memories are often not the loudest ones. They come from an unexpected conversation, a long ride with a companion, a town remembered because of what happened there, or a quiet moment when Arthur's internal conflict becomes impossible to ignore.

That patience is demanding, but it gives the story unusual weight. By the end, the player has not simply completed missions with the Van der Linde gang. They have spent enough time around these people to understand what is being lost.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Greatest Moments Come From Letting the Game Take Its Time

conclusion:
==Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the most accomplished open-world games ever made, but it earns that status in ways that can also make it difficult to love moment to moment. Rockstar's obsession with detail gives the world extraordinary texture while slowing basic interaction, and its cinematic missions often restrict the freedom that makes exploration so compelling.==

==Those frustrations matter, yet they rarely overshadow Arthur Morgan, the Van der Linde gang, and a version of the American frontier that feels alive, beautiful, and already vanishing. Few games create such a strong sense of place, and fewer still use that place to tell a story with this much patience and emotional weight.==

title: Super Mario Odyssey Review: Nintendo’s 3D Platforming Playground
description: Super Mario Odyssey turns movement, possession, and discovery into a joyful globe-trotting platformer packed with playful ideas.
body:
Super Mario Odyssey arrives with the confidence of a series that has spent decades redefining how movement can feel. Mario's basic controls are already excellent, but Cappy transforms familiar platforming into something more flexible: a traversal tool, a weapon, a temporary platform, and a way to possess dozens of creatures and objects across the world.

The result is one of Nintendo's most generous 3D platformers. Kingdoms constantly introduce new mechanics, Power Moons reward almost every kind of curiosity, and Mario's moveset gives skilled players enormous freedom to improvise routes that beginners may never realize are possible.

That abundance occasionally works against the game. Some Moons are so easy or repetitive that individual discoveries can feel less special, and a handful of captures exist more as amusing ideas than fully developed mechanics. Even so, Odyssey's best moments are Nintendo design at its most playful: movement feels wonderful, surprises arrive constantly, and almost every kingdom contains something worth poking, climbing, throwing Cappy at, or trying to reach the wrong way.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario poses beside Cappy against a red world-map background in official promotional artwork for Super Mario Odyssey.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Odyssey official promotional artwork.

cons: The huge number of Power Moons makes many individual rewards feel less meaningful
Some captures are clever one-off ideas rather than deep mechanics
Motion-control shortcuts are less comfortable for players who prefer standard inputs
A portion of the late-game Moon hunting leans on repetition and filler
pros: Mario has one of the most expressive and satisfying movesets in the series
Cappy and captures constantly reinvent how levels can be explored
Kingdoms are packed with visual variety and playful ideas
Power Moons reward experimentation and curiosity at almost every turn
Excellent presentation, music, animation, and post-game content
reviewMeta.verdict: A joyful, inventive 3D platformer with extraordinary movement and constant surprises, held back only slightly by an overabundance of low-impact collectibles and a few underdeveloped ideas.

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey begins with one of the strongest foundations in 3D platforming: Mario himself. Running, long jumping, rolling, wall jumping, ground pounding, diving, and chaining those moves together feels precise without becoming inaccessible.

Cappy pushes that movement even further. Throwing the hat can extend jumps, alter momentum, activate objects, and create temporary footholds. Skilled players can combine cap throws and dives to reach places that look impossible, while newcomers can still finish the game using a much simpler set of moves.

That layered design is one of Odyssey's greatest strengths. The game rarely demands advanced technique, but it constantly rewards players who want to learn it. Movement becomes a form of expression rather than merely transportation between objectives.
contentBlocks.heading: Mario Has Never Felt Better to Control

contentBlocks.text:
The capture mechanic allows Mario to temporarily control enemies, creatures, and objects, giving each kingdom a different set of verbs. A Goomba can stack with others, a Bullet Bill can cross long gaps, a Pokio can climb walls with its beak, and a Tropical Wiggler can stretch across spaces Mario cannot.

The best captures feel like compact platforming systems. Nintendo introduces a rule, builds several challenges around it, then moves on before the idea loses its novelty. That rhythm keeps the game fresh because Mario is constantly learning a new relationship with the environment.

Not every capture is equally deep. Some exist primarily for a joke, a single puzzle, or a brief visual surprise. But even the shallow ones contribute to the sense that nearly anything in Odyssey might become interactive once Cappy is involved.
contentBlocks.heading: Cappy Turns Every Kingdom Into a Toy Box

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey's kingdoms are not enormous open worlds. They are dense playgrounds built around recognizable landmarks, hidden routes, layered vertical spaces, and enough secrets to make revisiting them worthwhile.

That scale works beautifully. Players can develop a mental map of each kingdom while still discovering alcoves, challenges, characters, doors, and Power Moons long after the main objective is complete. Sand Kingdom feels fundamentally different from Metro Kingdom, which feels different from Luncheon Kingdom, yet all of them are designed around Mario's mobility.

The strongest spaces encourage playful rule-breaking. A visible rooftop or distant ledge becomes a challenge even when the game never explicitly asks the player to reach it. Often, Nintendo has hidden something there anyway.
contentBlocks.heading: The Kingdoms Are Small Enough to Learn and Dense Enough to Surprise

contentBlocks.text:
Power Moons are everywhere. They can be earned through platforming challenges, races, puzzles, exploration, NPC interactions, hidden rooms, minigames, clever captures, or simply noticing something suspicious in the environment.

This abundance makes Odyssey extremely welcoming. Progress rarely depends on solving one specific challenge, so players can follow whatever interests them and still keep moving. The game constantly says yes to curiosity.

The downside is that not every Moon feels important. Some are earned through memorable challenges; others are sitting behind a corner, under a glowing patch of ground, or attached to a very simple interaction. When rewards are this common, the emotional difference between an ingenious discovery and an effortless pickup becomes smaller than it should be.
contentBlocks.heading: Power Moons Make Curiosity Almost Always Worthwhile

contentBlocks.text:
Metro Kingdom is the clearest demonstration of Odyssey's identity. New Donk City combines vertical exploration, movement challenges, characters, secrets, music, and a playful collision between Mario's cartoon logic and a more urban setting.

The kingdom is immediately readable but full of routes. Fire escapes, rooftops, poles, taxis, power lines, and interior challenges turn the city into a platforming space without making it feel like a traditional obstacle course.

Odyssey repeatedly reaches this level of confidence when a kingdom's theme, captures, movement, and presentation all reinforce one another. These are the moments when it feels less like a collection hunt and more like Nintendo discovering another way to make moving through a 3D space delightful.
contentBlocks.heading: New Donk City Captures Odyssey at Its Best

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Odyssey is colorful without becoming visually noisy. Each kingdom has a strong identity, character animation is expressive, and small reactions give both Mario and Cappy enormous personality.

The soundtrack moves comfortably between orchestral adventure, playful regional themes, and vocal set pieces that give major moments a sense of occasion. Nintendo understands exactly when to let nostalgia surface and when to push Mario into something stranger.

The game also treats its own history with warmth rather than reverence. Costumes, 2D sections, references, familiar enemies, and musical callbacks appear throughout the journey, but Odyssey rarely feels trapped by them. It uses Mario's past as another toy rather than a set of rules it must obey.
contentBlocks.heading: Presentation Makes the Adventure Feel Like a Celebration

contentBlocks.text:
Finishing the main story opens a much larger layer of challenges, additional objectives, and reasons to return to earlier kingdoms. For players who love Mario's movement, this is where some of the game's most demanding platforming appears.

It is also where Odyssey's collectible philosophy becomes most uneven. The enormous Moon count gives completionists a long runway, but some objectives are repeated, trivial, or dependent on activities that are more time-consuming than interesting.

The strongest post-game Moons test mastery of movement or ask the player to reinterpret familiar spaces. The weakest feel like numbers added to extend the checklist. Odyssey contains so many great ideas that the filler is easy to forgive, but it still prevents the reward structure from feeling as consistently sharp as the movement itself.
contentBlocks.heading: The Post-Game Is Huge, but Not Every Moon Earns Its Place

contentBlocks.text:
Odyssey rarely tells players there is only one correct way to move through a space. A beginner can follow the obvious path, while an experienced player may chain jumps, cap throws, dives, and captures into a completely different route.

That freedom is the reason the game remains compelling after the story ends. Even when individual Power Moons lose some of their value through overabundance, Mario himself never becomes less enjoyable to control.

Nintendo's best 3D platformers understand that movement should be fun before the reward at the end of the movement is even considered. Super Mario Odyssey follows that principle almost perfectly.
contentBlocks.heading: A Platformer Built Around Joyful Possibility

conclusion:
==Super Mario Odyssey is one of Nintendo's most confident 3D platformers, combining an exceptionally expressive moveset with kingdoms that constantly reward curiosity. Cappy and the capture system give the game a steady stream of mechanical surprises, while Mario's movement is deep enough to make simply crossing a level enjoyable.==

==The huge Power Moon count occasionally weakens the sense of achievement, and not every capture or late-game challenge is developed equally. Those are small imperfections inside an adventure overflowing with creativity. Odyssey succeeds because its greatest reward is not the collectible at the end of a challenge; it is the joy of figuring out how Mario can get there.==

title: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Review: The Definitive Kart Racer
description: Years of additions have turned Mario Kart 8 Deluxe into an enormous, polished celebration of Nintendo’s accessible but surprisingly deep racing formula.
body:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is one of those rare games that makes accessibility look effortless. Almost anyone can understand the basic rules within a race or two, yet the difference between simply driving well and truly mastering its drifting, lines, shortcuts, item timing, and kart combinations is enormous.

That balance is the reason it has lasted so long. Nintendo took the already excellent foundation of Mario Kart 8, rebuilt the package around the Switch, restored a proper Battle Mode, and eventually expanded the track list into something enormous. The result is not the deepest racing game in the traditional sense, but it may be the most complete expression of what Mario Kart is supposed to be: fast, readable, chaotic, competitive, and ridiculously easy to keep playing.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario and other Nintendo characters race across a colorful track in the official Mario Kart 8 Deluxe key art, surrounded by karts, bikes, items, and the series’ signature high-speed chaos.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Mario Kart 8 Deluxe official promotional artwork.

cons: Item randomness can occasionally overwhelm clean racing and strong decision-making
Some Booster Course Pass tracks look noticeably flatter than the best base-game circuits
Single-player progression is relatively light once the cups and unlock goals are exhausted
pros: Responsive handling that is easy to learn and rewarding to master
An enormous and varied course selection
Outstanding local and online multiplayer
Kart customization adds meaningful mechanical depth
Battle Mode and years of updates make Deluxe feel genuinely definitive
reviewMeta.verdict: A brilliantly polished kart racer with exceptional handling, a huge course library, and multiplayer that remains endlessly entertaining, even if item randomness, uneven DLC presentation, and light solo progression keep it from perfection.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review of the Nintendo Switch release and its expanded modern content. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe feels immediately good to control. Steering is readable, drifting is forgiving enough for newcomers, and the speed classes create a natural progression from casual racing to something far more demanding.

The deeper you go, the more the game reveals. Mini-turbo timing, drift angles, racing lines, trick boosts, anti-gravity interactions, shortcuts, and defensive item management all matter. At higher levels, small mistakes become expensive, and players who understand a track can create advantages long before the final lap.

That is the secret behind Mario Kart 8 Deluxe's longevity. It never asks beginners to study its systems before having fun, but it gives experienced players enough mechanical depth to keep improving for years.
contentBlocks.heading: The Handling Is Simple Until You Start Chasing Perfection

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart lives or dies by its tracks, and Mario Kart 8 Deluxe has some of the strongest circuit design Nintendo has ever produced. Courses are colorful and immediately readable, but the best layouts also use elevation, alternate routes, anti-gravity, gliding, underwater sections, moving hazards, and environmental storytelling to give each race its own rhythm.

The base-game circuits remain the visual high point. Tracks such as Mount Wario, Big Blue, Hyrule Circuit, Electrodrome, and the various Rainbow Roads feel less like simple loops and more like miniature theme-park rides built around racing.

With the Booster Course Pass adding 48 more courses to the original selection, the modern package offers an extraordinary amount of variety. Nintendo's own materials confirm that all 48 additional courses were eventually added, effectively doubling the course options available through the expansion.
contentBlocks.heading: The Courses Are Still the Real Stars

contentBlocks.text:
The item system is inseparable from Mario Kart's identity. Shells, bananas, mushrooms, Bullet Bills, lightning, stars, and the infamous Blue Shell make every race unstable enough that players rarely feel completely safe.

That volatility is fantastic in multiplayer because it keeps weaker players involved and gives every lap a story. Good racers still have an advantage, especially when they understand item defense and positioning, but Mario Kart deliberately refuses to become a pure time-trial contest.

The downside is obvious: sometimes the chaos overwhelms the racing. A strong final lap can collapse after several hits arrive in succession, and there are moments where the result feels less connected to the previous two minutes of good driving than it should. That frustration is part of Mario Kart, but it is still frustration.
contentBlocks.heading: Items Create the Chaos — and Sometimes Too Much of It

contentBlocks.text:
Character, kart body, wheels, and glider combinations affect far more than cosmetic preference. Speed, acceleration, weight, handling, traction, and hidden characteristics such as mini-turbo behavior influence how a setup feels across different tracks.

Most players can choose something they like and remain competitive, which is exactly how the system should work. But anyone who wants to optimize can spend a surprising amount of time finding combinations that suit a preferred weight class, drift style, or racing strategy.

The best part is that the system rarely feels mandatory at casual levels. Customization rewards curiosity without turning the game into a spreadsheet before every race.
contentBlocks.heading: Kart Building Adds More Depth Than It First Appears

contentBlocks.text:
One of the most important improvements over the original Wii U release is the return of a proper Battle Mode. Dedicated arenas give modes such as Balloon Battle, Bob-omb Blast, Renegade Roundup, Coin Runners, and Shine Thief enough space to work as their own multiplayer experiences rather than feeling like side activities squeezed onto standard race tracks.

Battle Mode is not the reason most people buy Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, but it matters because it strengthens the party-game side of the package. When a group wants something different from Grand Prix racing, there is a substantial alternative waiting instead of a token extra mode.
contentBlocks.heading: Battle Mode Finally Makes Deluxe Feel Complete

contentBlocks.text:
The Booster Course Pass transformed Mario Kart 8 Deluxe from a large racing game into an enormous archive of Mario Kart history. Nintendo added 48 courses across six waves along with returning characters, bringing back tracks from older console entries and Mario Kart Tour alongside several new interpretations.

From a value and variety perspective, the expansion is excellent. A modern Mario Kart session can jump between decades of track design without leaving the same game.

Visually, however, the quality is less consistent. Several Booster Course Pass tracks use simpler geometry, flatter textures, or less environmental detail than the most elaborate circuits from the base game. Later waves improved considerably, but the contrast never disappears completely. The racing remains strong; the presentation simply is not uniformly luxurious.
contentBlocks.heading: The Booster Course Pass Makes the Package Huge, but Not Perfectly Consistent

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is at its strongest when other people are involved. Local split-screen remains one of the easiest ways to turn a Switch into a party machine, while online racing gives experienced players a much more unpredictable and competitive environment.

Because races are short and the controls are readable, the game has almost no social friction. A newcomer can join immediately, while someone with hundreds of hours can still chase better lines, stronger drifts, and smarter item usage.

That combination is incredibly difficult to design. Many competitive games become less inviting as players improve. Mario Kart gets deeper without losing the ability to make a room laugh when everything goes wrong on the final corner.
contentBlocks.heading: Multiplayer Is the Reason Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Never Really Gets Old

contentBlocks.text:
For all of its content, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe does not offer a particularly rich solo progression structure. Grand Prix cups, time trials, unlocks, mirror mode, and higher speed classes provide plenty to do initially, but there is no substantial career mode or long-form single-player framework tying everything together.

That is not a major problem for a game designed primarily around repeat racing and multiplayer, but it does mean the package can feel less purposeful when played alone for extended periods. Once you have cleared the cups and found the setups you enjoy, motivation becomes self-directed: improve times, chase trophies, master tracks, or simply race because the racing itself is excellent.

Fortunately, the core driving is good enough to carry that weight. It just would have been interesting to see Nintendo build a more ambitious solo structure around it.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Weakest Area Is Long-Term Solo Progression

conclusion:
==Mario Kart 8 Deluxe is difficult to criticize without eventually circling back to how consistently fun it is. The handling is excellent, the course design remains among Nintendo's best, kart building gives experienced players room to experiment, and the modern track selection is enormous. Its chaotic item system occasionally makes strong racing feel irrelevant, some Booster Course Pass tracks cannot match the visual craftsmanship of the original circuits, and solo progression is relatively thin. None of those issues change what the game achieves. As a multiplayer racer, a party game, and a celebration of Mario Kart history, Deluxe remains one of the most complete and replayable games Nintendo has ever released.==

==9.2/10 — EXCELLENT==

title: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild Review: Freedom Redefined
description: Nintendo’s open-air Zelda reinvention remains a landmark adventure built around curiosity, experimentation, and the freedom to make Hyrule your own.
body:
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild does not simply move Zelda into an open world. It rebuilds the series around the idea that curiosity should be enough to pull the player forward.

From the moment Link steps out onto the Great Plateau, Hyrule feels less like a sequence of destinations and more like a place waiting to be understood. Mountains can be climbed, distant ruins can be investigated, weather changes the route ahead, and small environmental details constantly suggest that there may be something worth finding just beyond the next ridge.

That freedom was radical for Zelda in 2017, and it remains the game’s defining strength. Breath of the Wild trusts the player to choose a direction, experiment with its systems, fail without embarrassment, and build a personal journey out of dozens of small discoveries. Even years later, few open worlds make exploration feel this natural.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
imageAlt: Link stands on a sunlit grassy cliff overlooking the vast kingdom of Hyrule, with Hyrule Castle and distant mountains visible beneath a bright blue sky in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.
imageCredit: Nintendo / The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild official promotional artwork.

cons: Limited build variety gives repeat playthroughs less mechanical freshness
Equipment durability can make valuable rewards feel temporary
Shrines become visually and structurally repetitive over a long playthrough
pros: One of the most naturally explorable open worlds ever designed
Exceptional freedom and systemic problem solving
Beautiful art direction and a powerful sense of atmosphere
Discovery feels personal instead of checklist-driven
A bold reinvention that still feels unmistakably like Zelda
reviewMeta.verdict: A landmark open-world adventure whose freedom, atmosphere, and sense of discovery remain extraordinary, even if equipment durability, repetitive shrine structure, and limited build variety reduce its long-term replay appeal.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild’s greatest achievement is how rarely it tells the player that there is only one correct way forward. Once the opening hours establish the basic rules, Hyrule becomes a web of possibilities rather than a chain of objectives.

A tower on the horizon, an unusual rock formation, smoke rising from a distant camp, or a mountain that looks barely reachable can become a self-created objective. The game constantly rewards that instinct. Sometimes the reward is tangible, but just as often it is a new view, an environmental puzzle, a character encounter, or the satisfaction of reaching somewhere that initially looked impossible.

That distinction matters. Many open-world games are enormous because they contain enormous lists. Breath of the Wild feels enormous because the player is allowed to decide what matters. Its map supports exploration rather than replacing it.
contentBlocks.heading: Freedom Is the Real Main Character

contentBlocks.text:
The world itself is designed around observation. Height matters because climbing creates new routes. Temperature matters because the environment can become an obstacle. Weather can interrupt a plan. Physics can turn an ordinary object into part of a solution.

These systems overlap in ways that make Hyrule feel unusually coherent. The game does not need a unique scripted interaction for every situation because its underlying rules are flexible enough to create unexpected outcomes on their own. A puzzle that seems to ask for one solution may accept several. A dangerous area can often be approached from a direction the designers never explicitly point toward.

This is where Breath of the Wild earns much of its reputation. Its freedom is not merely geographical. The player is given room to think, improvise, and occasionally discover a solution that feels almost accidental. That feeling of ownership makes even small victories memorable.
contentBlocks.heading: Hyrule Makes Curiosity Feel Useful

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild gives Link a compact set of core tools early and then spends the rest of the game finding new contexts for them. Instead of repeatedly handing out progression items that unlock one predetermined type of obstacle, Nintendo builds puzzles around systems that can interact with the world in multiple ways.

The result is a game that encourages experimentation. Objects have weight and momentum. Metal reacts differently from wood. Heat, electricity, wind, water, and gravity can become part of a solution. Even when the intended answer is obvious, the possibility of finding another route keeps the player engaged with the rules of the world rather than simply following instructions.

That systemic design also gives combat and traversal a playful quality. Breath of the Wild is often at its best when a plan goes wrong and the player has to improvise. Failure becomes part of discovery instead of something that simply sends you back to the last checkpoint.
contentBlocks.heading: The Physics Sandbox Keeps Zelda Playful

contentBlocks.text:
The shrine system is one of Breath of the Wild’s smartest structural ideas and one of its clearest limitations. Scattering compact puzzle spaces across Hyrule gives exploration a reliable rhythm: spot something unusual, investigate it, solve a challenge, and leave with meaningful progression.
