title: Final Fantasy VII Revelation’s New Story Trailer Puts Meteor and the Weapons at the Center
description: Square Enix brought Final Fantasy VII Revelation to gamescom Opening Night Live with a new story trailer centered on Meteor, the awakening Weapons, and the trilogy’s final confrontation.
body:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation returned during gamescom Opening Night Live with a new story-focused trailer that pushes the remake trilogy toward its endgame. The footage centered on the threat of Meteor and the awakening of the planet’s enormous Weapons as Cloud and his allies move toward the final chapter of Square Enix’s three-part project.

The release window itself is unchanged: Square Enix’s official site lists Spring 2027. Revelation is planned for PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox on PC, Steam, and the Epic Games Store.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Final Fantasy VII Revelation promotional image showing a colossal Weapon rising from the sea near an industrial structure at sunset.
imageCredit: Square Enix

contentBlocks.text: Opening Night Live focused on the escalating stakes around Meteor, the Weapons, and the final confrontation with Sephiroth. Those elements are also reflected in Square Enix’s official description of Revelation, which frames the game as the concluding entry in the remake trilogy.
contentBlocks.heading: The new trailer moves the trilogy toward its endgame

contentBlocks.text: The official game site describes Revelation as the largest adventure in the remake series, with exploration across a broad world by airship and evolved party combat. The ONL story trailer adds narrative pressure without changing that core pitch.
contentBlocks.heading: Square Enix is promising the trilogy’s biggest scale

contentBlocks.text: Square Enix has not narrowed the date beyond Spring 2027. Revelation is scheduled for PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch 2, Xbox Series X|S, Xbox on PC, Steam, and the Epic Games Store, with the company planning a simultaneous multi-platform launch.
contentBlocks.heading: Spring 2027 remains the release window

title: Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons Gameplay Reveals Kaatri’s Pact With Tasha
description: Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons delivered a substantial gameplay reveal at ONL, showing Kaatri mixing forbidden spells and melee combat across the open world of Darkon.
body:
Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons used gamescom Opening Night Live for a substantial gameplay reveal centered on Kaatri, an experienced warrior who becomes a warlock after making a dangerous pact with the witch Tasha.

The official game site describes a 2027 release and an open-world adventure in Darkon where magic is not only a combat tool. Spells and rituals can alter the environment, open routes, reposition enemies, and solve exploration problems.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons promotional art featuring a close-up portrait of Kaatri with dark hair and glowing magical markings.
imageCredit: Wizards of the Coast / Invoke Studios

contentBlocks.text: Kaatri is searching for someone she has lost, and the official premise says that search pushes her into a dangerous pact with Tasha. The journey leads into Darkon, where strange mists and forbidden power define the threat around her.
contentBlocks.heading: Kaatri’s pact drives the story

contentBlocks.text: The official site lists spells including Eldritch Blast, Misty Step, Levitate, Witch Bolt, and Tasha’s Leash. More importantly, those abilities are presented as systemic tools: they can manipulate objects, enemies, traversal, weather, and environmental hazards rather than functioning only as damage buttons.
contentBlocks.heading: Magic is designed for combat and exploration

contentBlocks.text: The official game site currently lists a 2027 release. The project is being developed for PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S, with the ONL gameplay reveal providing the clearest look yet at how its magic-and-melee design works.
contentBlocks.heading: Warlock is coming in 2027

title: HoYoverse Reveals Nodus Fall, a New Co-op Fantasy Action Game
description: HoYoverse used gamescom Opening Night Live 2026 to unveil Nodus Fall, a new cooperative action game built around team battles against enormous fantasy threats.
body:
HoYoverse revealed Nodus Fall during gamescom Opening Night Live on August 25, introducing a new cooperative action game with a darker fantasy tone than the publisher’s best-known releases.

The debut trailer focused on coordinated combat and enormous creatures, but the reveal stopped short of announcing a release date or confirmed platforms. Neural Critic is treating those details as unannounced rather than filling in the gaps from speculation.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Nodus Fall key art showing warriors facing enormous fantasy creatures beneath the game logo.
imageCredit: HoYoverse

contentBlocks.text: Nodus Fall made its public debut during Opening Night Live with a cinematic-and-gameplay presentation centered on a hostile fantasy setting and teams fighting oversized enemies. The reveal establishes the project as a new HoYoverse title rather than an update to one of the company’s existing games.
contentBlocks.heading: HoYoverse introduces a new world

contentBlocks.text: The trailer’s strongest gameplay signal is cooperation. Multiple characters are shown confronting large threats together, making team combat the core idea Neural Critic can verify from the reveal. Beyond that, HoYoverse has not yet provided enough official detail to responsibly characterize progression, monetization, or long-term structure.
contentBlocks.heading: Co-op combat is the clearest hook

contentBlocks.text: No release date, launch window, or platform list was confirmed during the reveal. Those omissions matter: early reports may infer details from HoYoverse’s other games, but Nodus Fall should be treated on its own announced terms until the developer publishes more.
contentBlocks.heading: Release timing and platforms remain unannounced

title: Metro 2039’s New Gamescom Trailer Shows the Stranger Fighting Through Sevastopolskaya
description: 4A Games revealed a new Metro 2039 gameplay sequence at Opening Night Live, showing the Stranger’s combat and movement through Sevastopolskaya Station and the ruins beyond.
body: Metro 2039 returned at gamescom Opening Night Live with a new gameplay trailer titled Renegade. The footage follows the Stranger through another part of 4A Games’ post-apocalyptic Moscow, with Sevastopolskaya Station identified as a key location.\n\nThe reveal is substantial because it shows more of how the new protagonist moves, fights, and survives above and below ground. Deep Silver’s official site continues to frame Metro 2039 as a single-player story blending exploration, survival, combat, and stealth, and now lists the game for February 2027.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Metro 2039 promotional art showing an armed survivor moving through a fiery ruined landscape.
imageCredit: Deep Silver / 4A Games

contentBlocks.text: The new trailer shifts attention back to the Stranger and moment-to-moment survival. It presents movement and combat across ruined environments and underground spaces rather than relying on another cinematic overview.
contentBlocks.heading: Renegade is Metro 2039’s latest gameplay showcase

contentBlocks.text: Official material around the new trailer identifies Sevastopolskaya Station as a crucial location. Metro 2039’s broader setup sends the Stranger back toward the Moscow Metro after the ghosts of his past force him out of exile.
contentBlocks.heading: Sevastopolskaya Station is a major stop in the journey

contentBlocks.text: Deep Silver describes Metro 2039 as a powerful single-player story that combines exploration, survival, combat, and stealth. The new Gamescom footage reinforces that direction without suggesting a change to the series’ core format.
contentBlocks.heading: 4A Games is keeping the series single-player

title: HUMANKIND 2 Announced for 2027 With Deeper Culture Progression and Climate Systems
description: Amplitude Studios revealed HUMANKIND 2 at gamescom Opening Night Live, confirming a 2027 release and a sequel built around deeper cultural progression, climate change, and player-driven civilizations.
body:
Amplitude Studios announced HUMANKIND 2 during gamescom Opening Night Live on August 25, bringing its historical 4X strategy series back for a sequel planned for 2027.

The official Steam listing expands on the reveal with several concrete changes: deeper cultural progression trees, new progression systems, a modernized interface, enhanced visuals, and a world where climate changes can reshape biomes, cities, resources, and long-term strategy.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: HUMANKIND 2 key art showing historical figures before a civilization-spanning cityscape beneath the game logo.
imageCredit: AMPLITUDE Studios

contentBlocks.text: HUMANKIND 2 keeps the original game’s core idea of building a civilization across multiple eras, but Amplitude is pitching the sequel around more continuity and customization as cultures evolve. The studio says each era can unlock culture-specific progression trees that shape the identity of the civilization being built.
contentBlocks.heading: HUMANKIND is getting a full sequel

contentBlocks.text: Amplitude’s official listing says climate changes can transform the strategic map over time, affecting biomes, cities, economies, and access to resources. That gives the sequel a world-state system that can force players to adapt rather than treating the map as a static backdrop.
contentBlocks.heading: Climate is becoming a strategic system

contentBlocks.text: HUMANKIND 2 is currently scheduled for 2027. The Steam listing confirms both single-player and multiplayer support; no more specific release date was announced during Opening Night Live.
contentBlocks.heading: Amplitude is targeting 2027

title: Gears of War: E-Day’s New Story Trailer Brings Marcus and Dom Back to Emergence Day
description: A new gamescom ONL trailer put the relationship between Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago back at the center of Gears of War: E-Day ahead of its October 6, 2026 launch.
body:
Gears of War: E-Day returned during gamescom Opening Night Live with a new story-focused trailer that reinforces The Coalition’s prequel setup: Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago at the beginning of the Locust War.

The release date itself is not new — Xbox already has E-Day scheduled for October 6, 2026 — but the ONL trailer is a meaningful campaign beat because it pushes character and early-war context to the foreground as the game approaches launch.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Gears of War: E-Day key art featuring the series skull-and-cog emblem glowing red beneath the E-Day logo.
imageCredit: Xbox Game Studios / The Coalition

contentBlocks.text: The new presentation leans into Marcus and Dom rather than treating Emergence Day only as spectacle. That matches The Coalition’s established pitch for the prequel: revisiting the beginning of the Locust War while rebuilding the brotherhood that defines the original trilogy.
contentBlocks.heading: The ONL trailer is about the people at the center of E-Day

contentBlocks.text: Xbox describes the game as a prequel set 14 years before the first Gears of War. Players follow Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago as the Locust threat erupts, giving the studio room to show familiar characters before they become the veterans players already know.
contentBlocks.heading: E-Day takes place before the original Gears of War

contentBlocks.text: Gears of War: E-Day launches October 6, 2026 on Xbox Series X|S and PC. Xbox has also confirmed that gamescom attendees are getting the first public hands-on opportunity with the campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: October 6 remains the launch date

title: The 10 Best Open-World Games to Play Right Now
description: From Elden Ring and Breath of the Wild to Red Dead Redemption 2 and Forza Horizon 6, these are Neural Critic’s current picks for the best open worlds in gaming.
body: A great open world is not just a large map. The best ones make movement, discovery, systems, and place feel inseparable from the reason the game works. Neural Critic’s current ranking favors worlds that reward curiosity, support meaningful player choice, and remain worth inhabiting long after the novelty of their size disappears.\n\nThis is a living list focused on what still feels exceptional to play in 2026, not a historical ranking of the genre.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A list of Open-World Games that are memorable

contentBlocks.text: Death Stranding 2 makes distance meaningful. Terrain, weather, route planning, equipment, and the traces left by other players transform movement into the central problem rather than something automated away. Its world can be intentionally lonely, but that isolation makes every sign of another player feel important. The result is an open world where crossing the map is itself the adventure.
contentBlocks.caption: Death Stranding 2 makes the journey across its landscape as important as the destination.
contentBlocks.heading: Death Stranding 2: On the Beach
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Death Stranding 2: On the Beach showcasing its vast terrain and traversal-focused open world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Traversal becomes the story instead of the space between stories

contentBlocks.text: Ghost of Yōtei earns its place through focus. Its landscape is beautiful, but more importantly it supports the rhythm of duels, investigation, travel, and quieter moments rather than becoming a container for disconnected activities. Strong visual guidance and a cleaner mission structure make exploration feel purposeful instead of administrative.
contentBlocks.caption: Ghost of Yōtei uses landscape and visual guidance to make exploration feel purposeful rather than procedural.
contentBlocks.heading: Ghost of Yōtei
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Ghost of Yōtei showcasing the dramatic landscapes and natural scenery of its open world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world strongest when landscape and character point in the same direction

contentBlocks.text: The Witcher 3 remains special because even minor quests often feel connected to people, places, and consequences. Its combat has aged more visibly than its writing, but Velen, Novigrad, Skellige, and the expansions still create one of gaming’s richest senses of regional identity. It remains an easy recommendation for players who want an open world driven by stories rather than map completion alone.
contentBlocks.caption: The Witcher 3 gives its regions identity through stories that make even small detours feel worth taking.
contentBlocks.heading: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt showcasing Geralt within the game’s richly detailed fantasy world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A world remembered as much for its small stories as its main quest

contentBlocks.text: Forza Horizon 6 proves that open-world design does not need quests or character builds to create discovery. Japan’s roads, cities, mountain routes, and racing spaces are interesting because the vehicle changes how the landscape is read. The world constantly gives players reasons to detour, experiment, and keep driving, making it the strongest current open-world racing experience.
contentBlocks.caption: Forza Horizon 6 turns roads, scenery, and speed into their own form of open-world discovery.
contentBlocks.heading: Forza Horizon 6
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Forza Horizon 6 showcasing a high-performance car traveling through the game’s Japanese open-world setting.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world built around the pleasure of movement itself

contentBlocks.text: Night City has always had visual personality, but years of updates helped the systems around it catch up. Build variety, improved progression, stronger combat, and Phantom Liberty’s denser quest design turned Cyberpunk 2077 into a much easier recommendation. Its world remains less physically interactive than the games above it, but few cities in gaming create such a powerful sense of scale and atmosphere.
contentBlocks.caption: Night City remains one of gaming’s most visually distinctive open worlds.
contentBlocks.heading: Cyberpunk 2077
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Cyberpunk 2077 showcasing the dense futuristic architecture, neon lighting, and urban scale of Night City.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Night City finally became as compelling to play as it always was to look at

contentBlocks.text: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II makes its world convincing by refusing to revolve entirely around the player. Reputation, clothing, skills, travel, social position, and local routines all influence how situations unfold. That friction can be demanding, but it gives discovery unusual weight. Few modern open worlds make learning how to exist in a place feel this important.
contentBlocks.caption: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II makes learning how its world works part of the role-playing itself.
contentBlocks.heading: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Kingdom Come: Deliverance II showcasing its grounded medieval landscape and historically inspired open world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A historical world that trusts players to learn how it works

contentBlocks.text: Tears of the Kingdom takes Hyrule and gives players a new way to interpret almost every object inside it. Ultrahand, building, physics, vertical exploration, and the expanded world turn simple traversal problems into opportunities for experimentation. Its enormous scale can become overwhelming, but few games give the player this much freedom to invent a solution rather than discover the intended one.
contentBlocks.caption: Tears of the Kingdom turns Hyrule into a playground for experimentation, construction, and improvised solutions.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom showcasing Link exploring the expansive world of Hyrule.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Building turns the landscape into a giant systems playground

contentBlocks.text: Red Dead Redemption 2 deliberately resists efficiency. Riding, camping, returning to town, caring for a horse, or noticing something unusual beside the road all take time, and that patience gives the world weight. Its controls can feel cumbersome, but few open worlds make routine, landscape, and character feel so closely connected.
contentBlocks.caption: Red Dead Redemption 2 gives its world weight by making travel, routine, and observation matter.
contentBlocks.heading: Red Dead Redemption 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Red Dead Redemption 2 showcasing the expansive wilderness and natural scenery of Rockstar’s American frontier.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A world whose slower pace makes observation matter

contentBlocks.text: Breath of the Wild remains extraordinary because the landscape itself tells players where they might want to go. Climbing, weather, physics, distant landmarks, and the absence of an overwhelming checklist make exploration feel self-directed. Later games expanded many of its ideas, but few match the clarity with which Hyrule teaches players to trust what looks interesting.
contentBlocks.caption: Breath of the Wild still makes curiosity itself feel like the best way to navigate an open world.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild showcasing Link overlooking the vast landscape of Hyrule.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The open world that turned curiosity into navigation

contentBlocks.text: Elden Ring remains Neural Critic’s top open-world recommendation because it preserves mystery at a scale that should have made mystery impossible. Castles, caves, underground regions, distant towers, strange terrain, and major bosses continually create questions before the map explains them. Its build freedom and flexible progression let players respond to difficulty in personal ways, while the world still retains FromSoftware’s deliberate encounter design.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring preserves mystery at a scale that makes every unexplored direction feel significant.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Elden Ring showcasing the Tarnished within the vast and mysterious landscapes of the Lands Between.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Freedom, danger, and authored discovery held together at enormous scale

quickRead: Traversal becomes the story instead of the space between stories
An open world strongest when landscape and character point in the same direction
A world remembered as much for its small stories as its main quest
conclusion: ==Open worlds keep getting larger, but size is no longer impressive on its own. The worlds that endure are the ones where geography changes how players think, move, prepare, or make decisions. That is why this list can include racing, role-playing, and action games without treating the genre as one formula.\n\nNeural Critic will keep updating the ranking as new worlds prove they deserve a place.==
conclusionHeading: A great open world changes how you think about distance

title: The 12 Best Nintendo Games to Play Right Now
description: From Switch 2 showcases to modern versions of Nintendo classics, these are Neural Critic’s current picks for the best Nintendo games to play right now.
body: Nintendo’s current library has an unusual advantage: Switch 2 brings new games, upgraded editions, and better ways to play older favorites into the same ecosystem. That makes “best Nintendo games right now” a much more interesting question than simply listing the newest releases.\n\nNeural Critic’s ranking focuses on games that feel especially worth playing on Nintendo hardware in 2026, whether because they showcase Switch 2, remain exceptional years later, or have returned in newly relevant versions.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Official promotional imagery representing games available across Nintendo Switch and Nintendo Switch 2.
imageCredit: Nintendo / respective publishers · Official promotional artwork

contentBlocks.text:
Star Fox works best when it keeps the player moving, reading threats, and making quick decisions rather than burying the experience beneath unnecessary systems. The 2026 return understands that appeal and gives Nintendo’s space combat series a more immediate modern presentation.

It may not have the enormous scope of the games higher on this list, but that focus is part of the appeal. On Switch 2, Star Fox is a strong reminder that compact, replayable action still has a place beside sprawling adventures.
contentBlocks.caption: Star Fox brings Nintendo’s space-combat series back with a modern visual overhaul.
contentBlocks.heading: Star Fox
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official promotional image from Star Fox on Nintendo Switch 2.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Nintendo’s space combat series returns with a cleaner modern rhythm

contentBlocks.text:
Pokémon Legends: Z-A continues the series’ effort to make catching, movement, and exploration feel like active parts of the adventure instead of transitions between traditional battles. Its structure gives the player more reasons to observe Pokémon behavior and think about the space around an encounter.

The series still carries technical and structural habits that can hold it back, but Legends remains the most interesting direction for players who want Pokémon to feel less rigid. On current Nintendo hardware, it is an easy recommendation for fans looking for something more exploratory.
contentBlocks.caption: Legends: Z-A continues Pokémon’s push toward more active exploration and encounters.
contentBlocks.heading: Pokémon Legends: Z-A
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official promotional image from Pokémon Legends: Z-A, set within the game’s reimagined Lumiose City.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A more exploratory direction for Pokémon’s modern era

contentBlocks.text:
Hades II fits Nintendo hardware almost perfectly because its structure supports both short sessions and long stretches of mastery. Every run can produce new story beats, resources, relationships, or build discoveries even when the immediate attempt ends early.

The combat is fast, readable, and deeply replayable, while Switch 2 gives the game a stronger technical home than Nintendo’s previous hardware could have offered. It is one of the easiest third-party recommendations in the current library.
contentBlocks.caption: Hades II is an especially natural fit for Nintendo’s portable hardware.
contentBlocks.heading: Hades II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Hades II, showcasing Supergiant Games’ hand-painted mythological art direction.
contentBlocks.subtitle: One of the best portable action games you can keep returning to

contentBlocks.text:
Final Fantasy VII Rebirth is enormous, emotional, occasionally excessive, and often brilliant. Its party combat blends real-time movement with tactical decision-making, while its regions give the characters room to exist outside the main plot.

Seeing a game of this scale arrive on Nintendo hardware is part of what makes the Switch 2 era feel different. The appeal is not merely technical novelty: Rebirth remains one of the strongest modern RPGs available anywhere, and its presence materially deepens Nintendo’s third-party library.
contentBlocks.caption: Rebirth gives Switch 2 one of the largest modern RPGs in its third-party library.
contentBlocks.heading: Final Fantasy VII Rebirth
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official promotional image from Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, featuring the game’s expansive world and characters.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A massive RPG finding a surprisingly natural home on Switch 2

contentBlocks.text:
Metroid Prime is strongest when scanning, navigation, environmental storytelling, and combat all feel like parts of the same act of exploration. Beyond preserves that identity while giving the series a more modern technical foundation.

Its deliberate pace will feel very different from a conventional first-person action game, but that difference is exactly why it matters. On Switch 2, Metroid Prime 4 gives Nintendo a first-person adventure with a sense of place few other games attempt.
contentBlocks.caption: Metroid Prime 4 builds exploration around atmosphere, scanning, and Samus’s expanding abilities.
contentBlocks.heading: Metroid Prime 4: Beyond
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, featuring Samus Aran and the mysterious world of Viewros.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Exploration and atmosphere built around seeing the world differently

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy still feels inventive because gravity changes the relationship between Mario and the level itself. Tiny planets, shifting perspectives, transformations, launch stars, and tightly edited challenges constantly change what movement means without making the controls unreadable.

The modern Switch release gives the game improved presentation while Switch 2 support makes it easier to appreciate on current hardware. Its age is visible in a few camera and control decisions, but the level design remains extraordinary.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Galaxy remains remarkable for how often gravity changes the rules of platforming.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario explores one of the gravity-bending worlds of Super Mario Galaxy.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A platforming classic made newly relevant on modern Nintendo hardware

contentBlocks.text: The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales stands out because it treats readability as a strength. Exploration, combat, towns, dungeons, and progression are presented with a compact clarity that recalls older action RPGs without feeling trapped by them.\n\nIts strongest quality is momentum: the game moves quickly between discovery and action, making it especially well suited to Nintendo hardware. In a library full of enormous releases, Elliot earns its place by showing how satisfying a more focused adventure can still be.
contentBlocks.caption: The Millennium Tales combines modern action with the visual clarity of Square Enix’s HD-2D style.
contentBlocks.heading: The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official image from The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales, showcasing its HD-2D fantasy world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A modern action RPG with the clarity of an older adventure

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild remains essential because its world is designed around what the player notices rather than what the interface announces. Mountains, ruins, unusual silhouettes, weather, physics, and climbing combine to make exploration feel like a chain of self-directed questions.

The Switch 2 edition gives that design a more comfortable technical home, but the real reason to return is unchanged: Hyrule still trusts curiosity more than instructions. Few open worlds have aged this gracefully.
contentBlocks.caption: Breath of the Wild still makes curiosity itself feel like a navigation system.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link explores the open landscapes of Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The open world that made curiosity feel like a navigation system

contentBlocks.text:
Mario Kart World earns a second look in this ranking because its greatest strength is not any one mode or technical feature; it is how reliably the game works for different kinds of players. A competitive session, a family multiplayer night, or a few quick races all make sense within the same package.

Its connected world and broader structure give Switch 2 a defining multiplayer experience without sacrificing the immediate readability that has always made Mario Kart special.
contentBlocks.caption: Mario Kart World expands the series beyond individual courses into a connected racing world.
contentBlocks.heading: Mario Kart World
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Official Mario Kart World image showing Nintendo’s racers within the game’s connected racing environment.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Nintendo’s most effortless social game on Switch 2

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy 2 is one of the easiest games on this list to recommend because it wastes almost no time. New mechanics arrive constantly, develop through a handful of clever variations, and disappear before they become routine. Yoshi expands Mario’s movement while gravity continues to let individual stages rewrite the rules.

The Switch release and Switch 2 enhancements make the game newly convenient to revisit, and Neural Critic’s full review found that its concentrated platforming remains exceptional even where the sequel sacrifices some of the first Galaxy’s atmosphere.
contentBlocks.caption: Galaxy 2 delivers new platforming ideas at an almost unreasonable pace.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario adventures through one of Super Mario Galaxy 2’s colorful planetary stages.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Nintendo’s platforming ideas delivered at an almost unreasonable pace

contentBlocks.text:
Tears of the Kingdom takes Breath of the Wild’s trust in player curiosity and adds a construction system capable of turning simple objects into transportation, tools, puzzles, or wonderfully strange experiments. The result is an open world that often feels less like a designed solution and more like a collection of rules waiting to be combined.

Its scale can become overwhelming, but the freedom to approach problems in personal ways keeps the adventure surprising. The Switch 2 edition gives one of Nintendo’s most ambitious games the hardware environment it deserves.
contentBlocks.caption: Tears of the Kingdom turns construction into another way of exploring Hyrule.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link explores Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, where land, sky, and player-built creations shape exploration.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A systems-driven adventure where building becomes another form of exploration

contentBlocks.text:
Donkey Kong Bananza earns the top position because it feels built around discovery at the level of the environment itself. Smashing, digging, climbing, and reshaping spaces turns movement into a form of experimentation, allowing the player to read a level and then physically change how it can be traversed.

It carries the playful clarity of Nintendo’s best platformers while giving Switch 2 a game that feels designed for the new hardware rather than merely improved by it. Right now, Bananza is Neural Critic’s clearest recommendation for someone asking what a Switch 2 can do that feels genuinely new.
contentBlocks.caption: Bananza makes smashing and reshaping the environment part of exploration itself.
contentBlocks.heading: Donkey Kong Bananza
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Donkey Kong explores the destructible underground world of Donkey Kong Bananza.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The game that best explains what a new Nintendo generation should feel like

quickRead: Nintendo’s space combat series returns with a cleaner modern rhythm
A more exploratory direction for Pokémon’s modern era
One of the best portable action games you can keep returning to
conclusion: ==Nintendo’s strongest advantage in 2026 is continuity. New Switch 2 games can sit beside upgraded modern classics and older masterpieces without making the library feel fragmented. That gives players an unusually broad answer to the question of what to play next.\n\nThis list will evolve as Switch 2 grows, but the goal will remain the same: highlight games that feel especially worth experiencing on Nintendo hardware now, not simply the newest releases.==
conclusionHeading: Nintendo’s current library is strongest when old and new reinforce each other

title: The 12 Best Xbox Games to Play Right Now
description: From huge role-playing worlds to racing, shooters, and inventive first-party adventures, these are Neural Critic’s current picks for the best games on Xbox Series X|S.
body: Xbox in 2026 is as much an ecosystem as it is a box beneath the television. Game Pass, Play Anywhere, first-party releases, and an enormous third-party library all shape what makes the platform worth using.\n\nNeural Critic’s current ranking therefore focuses on games that feel especially strong on Xbox Series X|S right now: titles that showcase the hardware, fit naturally into the Xbox ecosystem, or simply remain too good to ignore.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Promotional artwork from Starfield, Cyberpunk 2077, and Indiana Jones and the Great Circle arranged in a three-panel collage, representing several major adventures available across the Xbox ecosystem.
imageCredit: Bethesda Softworks / CD Projekt Red / MachineGames — composite via The Mirror

contentBlocks.text:
Hi-Fi Rush turns timing into a visual language. Attacks, movement, environmental hazards, animation, and music all pulse around the same beat, but the game is smart enough not to punish players who simply want to enjoy its expressive combat.

Its bright presentation and compact structure make it a refreshing counterweight to the enormous games elsewhere on this list. Years later, it remains one of the Xbox generation’s most distinctive surprises.
contentBlocks.caption: Hi-Fi Rush turns rhythm into both a combat system and a visual identity.
contentBlocks.heading: Hi-Fi Rush
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Chai moves through a colorful cel-shaded scene in Hi-Fi Rush, surrounded by the game’s comic-book visual effects and rhythm-driven action.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Rhythm-action that still feels completely unlike anything around it

contentBlocks.text:
Avowed works because Obsidian understands that role-playing does not require a world measured in hundreds of square miles. Its regions are dense, readable, and filled with decisions that reward curiosity without burying the player beneath endless map cleanup.

Combat supports different approaches while conversations and quests keep the experience rooted in character. For Xbox players who want a modern fantasy RPG without committing to an endless checklist, Avowed remains one of the platform’s strongest fits.
contentBlocks.caption: Avowed favors dense, explorable regions over an unnecessarily enormous open world.
contentBlocks.heading: Avowed
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A first-person scene from Avowed showcases one of the game’s colorful fantasy regions, with detailed environments and magical elements visible around the player.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A flexible fantasy RPG that respects the player’s time

contentBlocks.text:
DOOM: The Dark Ages changes the rhythm of modern Doom without losing its momentum. Combat feels heavier and more grounded, asking players to control space, read threats, and keep pushing rather than simply recreating the exact movement language of Eternal.

Its campaign is loud and spectacular, but the real appeal is mechanical. Once its systems click, encounters become exercises in confidence and flow. It remains one of the best showcases for fast, technically polished action on Series X.
contentBlocks.caption: The Dark Ages makes modern Doom feel heavier without sacrificing its forward momentum.
contentBlocks.heading: DOOM: The Dark Ages
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Doom Slayer battles demonic forces in DOOM: The Dark Ages, surrounded by the game’s darker medieval-inspired environments and heavy combat imagery.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Heavy, deliberate action built around relentless forward pressure

contentBlocks.text:
Hades II succeeds because a failed run rarely feels wasted. New conversations, resources, relationships, upgrades, and discoveries continue moving the larger story forward even when the immediate attempt ends early.

Its combat is fast but highly readable, and the enormous range of combinations encourages experimentation instead of forcing one perfect route. On Xbox it is an ideal game for both short sessions and long stretches of repeated mastery.
contentBlocks.caption: Hades II makes every run feel like another step in a much larger journey.
contentBlocks.heading: Hades II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Melinoë fights through a vibrant encounter in Hades II, surrounded by colorful supernatural effects and the game’s hand-painted mythological art direction.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A roguelike sequel that makes repetition feel like progress

contentBlocks.text:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives turn-based combat a physical edge through active dodges, parries, and timing. Party composition and build decisions remain crucial, but the player is never completely passive once an enemy begins its attack.

That mechanical energy is matched by a striking world and emotionally direct story. It remains one of the strongest RPGs in the current Xbox library and a particularly easy recommendation for players who want something familiar in structure but fresh in execution.
contentBlocks.caption: Expedition 33 gives turn-based combat an unusually physical sense of timing.
contentBlocks.heading: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Members of Expedition 33 appear within the stylized fantasy world of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, highlighting the game’s cinematic presentation and distinctive art direction.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based strategy with the tension of an action game

contentBlocks.text:
Halo: Campaign Evolved works because the foundation was already strong. Open combat spaces, readable enemy behavior, vehicle sequences, and the series’ signature encounter rhythm still give the campaign a clarity many modern shooters struggle to match.

The remake’s upgraded presentation and modern refinements make the original Halo easier to revisit without erasing what made it important. On Xbox’s 25th anniversary, it feels less like a museum piece and more like a reminder of why the platform’s identity formed around this series in the first place.
contentBlocks.caption: Campaign Evolved revisits Halo’s original encounter design through a modern presentation.
contentBlocks.heading: Halo: Campaign Evolved
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Master Chief appears in a rebuilt campaign environment from Halo: Campaign Evolved, with modern visuals recreating the science-fiction landscapes associated with the original adventure.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A classic Xbox campaign rebuilt without losing its original rhythm

contentBlocks.text:
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 is messy in ways that are difficult to separate from its appeal. The Zone feels dangerous because the game is willing to let systems collide, plans fail, and exploration produce stories the player was never explicitly sent to find.

Technical improvements have made the experience easier to recommend than it was at launch, while its atmosphere remains its greatest strength. Few Xbox games create such a convincing sense that the world exists independently of the player.
contentBlocks.caption: The Zone remains S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2’s greatest strength: unpredictable, hostile, and strangely inviting.
contentBlocks.heading: S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A lone stalker explores the bleak and dangerous Zone in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl, surrounded by ruined structures and harsh atmospheric scenery.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An unforgiving open world where atmosphere becomes a system

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 remains extraordinary because player choice extends beyond dialogue menus. Positioning, spells, environmental interactions, relationships, exploration, and improvisation constantly create outcomes that feel authored even when the player reaches them in an unexpected way.

The interface naturally feels different from playing with a mouse and keyboard, but the underlying flexibility survives the transition to console remarkably well. It is still one of the strongest long-form games available on Xbox.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur’s Gate 3 turns exploration and improvisation into part of the role-playing itself.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur’s Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A scene from Baldur’s Gate 3 showcases its richly detailed fantasy world and characters, reflecting the game’s emphasis on exploration, interaction, and player choice.
contentBlocks.subtitle: One of the deepest role-playing sandboxes available on console

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring continues to stand above most open worlds because discovery is allowed to arrive before explanation. A distant structure, strange cave, unexpected lift, or difficult encounter can redirect an entire evening without the game needing to turn that detour into a checklist.

Its enormous build variety also gives difficulty more flexibility than earlier FromSoftware games. On Series X, it remains one of the most rewarding worlds to explore and one of the easiest recommendations for players who enjoy learning through experimentation.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring still makes the simple act of choosing a direction feel meaningful.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Tarnished stands within the vast fantasy world of Elden Ring, with the dramatic landscapes of the Lands Between extending into the distance.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A vast action RPG that still makes curiosity feel dangerous

contentBlocks.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 is a dramatically different recommendation today than it was at launch. Updates, system changes, and the Phantom Liberty era reshaped progression and combat while preserving the thing Night City always did best: create a place with overwhelming visual personality.

Its strongest quests combine character writing with choices that feel uncomfortable rather than obviously correct. On current Xbox hardware, the game has finally become the ambitious RPG its world always suggested it could be.
contentBlocks.caption: Night City’s visual identity remains one of Cyberpunk 2077’s greatest strengths.
contentBlocks.heading: Cyberpunk 2077
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A scene from Cyberpunk 2077 showcases Night City’s dense futuristic architecture, neon lighting, and distinctive urban atmosphere.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A troubled launch transformed into one of the generation’s richest RPG cities

contentBlocks.text:
Indiana Jones and the Great Circle understands that playing Indiana Jones should involve more than moving from one action sequence to the next. Exploration, puzzles, stealth, improvised solutions, disguises, and optional discoveries make its locations feel like spaces to investigate rather than corridors between cutscenes.

The first-person perspective initially seems unusual for the character, but it ultimately strengthens the sense of inhabiting the adventure. It is one of the most confidently authored games associated with modern Xbox.
contentBlocks.caption: The Great Circle treats its locations as places to investigate, not merely backdrops for action.
contentBlocks.heading: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Indiana Jones explores an ancient location in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, surrounded by archaeological details and environmental clues.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Adventure design built around curiosity, improvisation, and character

contentBlocks.text:
Forza Horizon 6 earns the top position because it represents almost everything Xbox does well at once: technical polish, immediate accessibility, enormous depth for players who want it, seamless online systems, and a world that constantly gives the player another reason to keep moving.

Its Japan setting gives the series a fresh visual identity while the underlying driving model remains welcoming without becoming shallow. Whether someone wants to tune cars, explore, race seriously, or simply drive for twenty minutes, Horizon 6 makes the Xbox ecosystem feel frictionless in the best possible way.
contentBlocks.caption: Forza Horizon 6 gives the series a fresh visual identity through its Japan setting.
contentBlocks.heading: Forza Horizon 6
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A high-performance car speeds through the Japanese setting of Forza Horizon 6, showcasing the game’s detailed roads, scenery, and automotive presentation.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The clearest current example of Xbox at its most confident

quickRead: Rhythm-action that still feels completely unlike anything around it
A flexible fantasy RPG that respects the player’s time
Heavy, deliberate action built around relentless forward pressure
conclusion: ==The best Xbox games now reflect how broad the platform has become. A racing game can sit beside an old-school role-playing epic, an immersive adventure, a demanding open world, and a rebuilt Halo campaign without any of them feeling out of place.\n\nThis ranking will keep moving as the Xbox library changes. What matters is not whether every game is exclusive, but whether Xbox remains one of the best places to experience it. These twelve currently make the strongest case.==
conclusionHeading: Xbox is strongest when the library feels bigger than one identity

title: The 12 Best PlayStation Games to Play Right Now
description: From generation-defining exclusives to essential third-party adventures, these are Neural Critic’s current picks for the best games to play on PlayStation 5.
body: PlayStation 5 now has the depth of library that makes choosing what to play harder than finding something good. Neural Critic’s current list prioritizes games that either showcase the hardware especially well, define the modern PlayStation library, or remain exceptional places to spend your time in 2026.\n\nThis is not an all-time PlayStation ranking. It is a living recommendation list built around what feels most essential to play right now.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: PlayStation games featured in Neural Critic’s 2026 ranking of the best games to play right now.

contentBlocks.text:
Stellar Blade arrives with immediate visual confidence, but its strongest quality is the way combat gradually opens up. Parries, dodges, counters, burst skills, and build choices create a rhythm that rewards players who learn enemy behavior instead of simply overpowering it.

Its world structure can feel uneven and some of its storytelling is less memorable than its combat, but as a modern PS5 action game it remains one of the clearest examples of spectacle backed by satisfying mechanical progression.
contentBlocks.caption: Stellar Blade
contentBlocks.heading: Stellar Blade
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Stellar Blade artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A sharp action game with more depth than its spectacle first suggests

contentBlocks.text:
Spider-Man 2 succeeds because traversal is entertaining before the game even gives the player an objective. Swinging, web wings, fast travel, and the enlarged New York map create a superhero movement system that makes simply crossing the city feel rewarding.

The campaign can become crowded as it balances two protagonists and a large cast, but its set pieces, accessibility, polished combat, and technical presentation still make it one of the easiest PS5 recommendations for players who want a blockbuster built specifically around the console generation.
contentBlocks.caption: Marvel’s Spider-Man 2
contentBlocks.heading: Marvel’s Spider-Man 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most complete version of Insomniac’s superhero playground

contentBlocks.text:
Death Stranding 2 doubles down on the unusual ideas that made its predecessor memorable while smoothing many of the frictions that once made those ideas difficult to appreciate. Traversal, planning, terrain, weather, tools, and asynchronous cooperation remain central, but the journey feels more flexible and expressive.

It is still deliberately unconventional and will not suit players looking for constant combat. For anyone willing to meet it on its own terms, however, it offers one of the most distinctive large-scale experiences available on PS5.
contentBlocks.caption: Death Stranding 2: On the Beach
contentBlocks.heading: Death Stranding 2: On the Beach
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Death Stranding 2: On the Beach artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A stranger, more confident journey through connection and isolation

contentBlocks.text:
Resident Evil Requiem keeps the series relevant by treating tension as something built through pacing rather than volume. Exploration, resource pressure, dangerous encounters, and carefully staged environments create a campaign that knows when to hold back and when to make the player move.

Its value on PS5 comes from how cleanly it combines cinematic presentation with the intimate uncertainty that defines the best Resident Evil games. It is one of the strongest reasons to revisit survival horror in 2026.
contentBlocks.caption: Resident Evil Requiem
contentBlocks.heading: Resident Evil Requiem
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Resident Evil Requiem artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Capcom’s latest reminder that survival horror still thrives on pressure

contentBlocks.text:
Metaphor: ReFantazio takes familiar social systems, turn-based combat, party relationships, and calendar management and reshapes them around a fantasy world with its own political tension and identity. The result feels recognizable without feeling derivative.

Its strongest quality is momentum. Character growth, dungeon planning, travel, and story progression continually reinforce one another, making a very long RPG feel unusually purposeful. For PS5 players looking for a deep, authored adventure, it remains essential.
contentBlocks.caption: Metaphor: ReFantazio
contentBlocks.heading: Metaphor: ReFantazio
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Metaphor: ReFantazio artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A huge role-playing journey with unusual confidence and momentum

contentBlocks.text:
God of War Ragnarök is at its best when combat, spectacle, and character drama are allowed to support each other. Kratos has a flexible set of weapons and abilities, encounters reward aggressive control of space, and optional fights provide some of the game’s strongest mechanical tests.

The story occasionally tries to carry too much at once, but the production quality, performances, accessibility, and combat depth still make Ragnarök one of the defining PlayStation adventures of this generation.
contentBlocks.caption: God of War Ragnarök
contentBlocks.heading: God of War Ragnarök
contentBlocks.imageAlt: God of War Ragnarök artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Blockbuster craftsmanship with real weight behind its characters

contentBlocks.text:
Saros builds on Housemarque’s talent for demanding arcade-like action without simply repeating Returnal. Fast movement, escalating enemy patterns, run-based tension, and the strange world of Carcosa create a game that feels immediately readable and consistently dangerous.

What earns it a place this high is the way failure continues to produce knowledge. Each attempt sharpens the player’s understanding of movement, weapons, and encounter rhythm. It is one of the most convincing current demonstrations of PS5-focused action design.
contentBlocks.caption: Saros
contentBlocks.heading: Saros
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Saros artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Housemarque turns repetition into forward momentum again

contentBlocks.text:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 combines turn-based decision-making with active defensive timing in a way that gives every encounter physical tension. Party composition, builds, and resource choices still matter, but dodges and parries ensure the player never completely disengages after selecting a command.

Its visual identity and emotionally direct storytelling give the journey personality beyond its combat. On PS5 it remains one of the strongest modern RPG recommendations because it feels both traditional and genuinely new.
contentBlocks.caption: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.heading: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based combat made dramatic, reactive, and personal

contentBlocks.text:
Final Fantasy VII Rebirth is massive, but its best moments are often surprisingly intimate. Character interactions, regional exploration, combat experimentation, and side activities give the party a sense of life that carries the game through even its most excessive stretches.

Its action combat remains one of Square Enix’s strongest hybrids, allowing real-time pressure and tactical menu decisions to coexist naturally. Rebirth is messy in the way ambitious games often are, but its ambition pays off often enough to make it indispensable on PlayStation.
contentBlocks.caption: Final Fantasy VII Rebirth
contentBlocks.heading: Final Fantasy VII Rebirth
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Final Fantasy VII Rebirth artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An enormous RPG that somehow keeps finding room for personality

contentBlocks.text:
Ghost of Yōtei succeeds by understanding that an open world feels strongest when the landscape supports the character rather than distracting from them. Exploration, duels, quiet environmental moments, and larger confrontations create a journey with a strong sense of place.

It also benefits from the lessons learned across the generation: faster navigation, more flexible combat options, and tighter mission pacing make the experience feel more deliberate than a traditional icon-clearing open world. It is one of PS5’s strongest first-party adventures.
contentBlocks.caption: Ghost of Yōtei
contentBlocks.heading: Ghost of Yōtei
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Ghost of Yōtei artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A focused open-world adventure built around place and purpose

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring remains one of the easiest games to recommend on PS5 because its freedom continues to feel meaningful. Builds, exploration routes, optional regions, summons, weapons, spells, and boss order allow players to create genuinely different journeys through the Lands Between.

The game can still be uneven in its late stages, but few worlds reward curiosity this consistently. Years after release, it remains a reference point for how open-world scale and authored encounter design can coexist.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Elden Ring artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most liberating large-scale action RPG on the platform

contentBlocks.text:
Astro Bot earns the top spot because almost every part of it is designed around immediate joy. Movement is precise, levels introduce ideas quickly, DualSense features are integrated rather than decorative, and the game constantly finds new ways to turn familiar PlayStation history into playful mechanics.

More importantly, it understands editing. Ideas arrive, develop, and disappear before they become routine. That concentration of invention makes Astro Bot both one of the best games on PS5 and one of the best demonstrations of what the console itself can uniquely contribute to play.
contentBlocks.caption: Astro Bot
contentBlocks.heading: Astro Bot
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Astro Bot artwork featured in Neural Critic’s PlayStation ranking.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The purest showcase of why playing on PS5 can still feel special

quickRead: A sharp action game with more depth than its spectacle first suggests
The most complete version of Insomniac’s superhero playground
A stranger, more confident journey through connection and isolation
conclusion: ==The best PS5 library is no longer defined by one kind of game. First-party showcases, ambitious RPGs, survival horror, action games, and unusual experiments now sit beside one another without needing to compete for the same audience.\n\nThat is why this list is designed to change. New releases will enter, older games will fall away, and some will remain because the experience they offer continues to be difficult to replace. For now, these twelve represent the strongest places Neural Critic would tell a PS5 owner to start.==
conclusionHeading: The PlayStation library is deep enough to keep changing

title: The 12 Best PC Games to Play Right Now
description: From enormous RPGs to brilliant puzzle games and fresh 2026 releases, these are the PC games Neural Critic recommends playing right now.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A selection of standout games representing Neural Critic's best PC games to play right now.
imageCredit: Neural Critic / game imagery

contentBlocks.text:
Big Walk is built around the kind of multiplayer moments that are hard to manufacture on purpose. Its island gives groups simple objectives, but the real entertainment comes from trying to communicate, getting separated, improvising a plan, and turning small mistakes into stories.

It is new enough that its long-term staying power still has to be earned, but right now it captures the playful side of PC co-op unusually well.
contentBlocks.caption: Big Walk turns communication, wandering, and small mistakes into the point of the adventure.
contentBlocks.heading: Big Walk
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A group of players exploring the colorful island in Big Walk.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The freshest reason to get a few friends into the same voice chat

contentBlocks.text:
Forza Horizon 6 does not reinvent the series, but it understands why the formula remains easy to return to. The Japan setting gives its road trips a strong identity, while the structure moves comfortably between exploration, events, collecting, and harder races.

On PC, that polish matters. It can be a gorgeous showcase for a powerful system, but the bigger strength is how quickly it gets out of the way and lets the player drive.
contentBlocks.caption: Forza Horizon 6 pairs a Japan setting with the series' familiar mix of freedom and accessible racing.
contentBlocks.heading: Forza Horizon 6
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A sports car racing through the Japanese setting of Forza Horizon 6.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A polished open-road showcase that makes PC hardware feel worthwhile

contentBlocks.text:
Resident Evil Requiem earns its place by showing how effective a focused single-player game can feel in a year full of enormous releases. Capcom builds tension through space, sound, limited information, and careful pacing rather than relying only on scale.

It is also one of the more convincing technical showcases on PC in 2026, with detailed environments and strong lighting supporting the atmosphere rather than replacing it.
contentBlocks.caption: Resident Evil Requiem uses modern presentation to reinforce a tightly controlled horror campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: Resident Evil Requiem
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A tense interior environment from Resident Evil Requiem.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A current-generation horror showcase with confident pacing

contentBlocks.text:
Blue Prince becomes more interesting the less someone explains before you begin. Its shifting mansion turns room placement, observation, memory, and deduction into parts of the same puzzle, and progress often means understanding a rule rather than simply unlocking a door.

PC suits that style beautifully because it is the kind of game that encourages notes, theories, screenshots, and a growing mental model of how its strange house behaves.
contentBlocks.caption: Blue Prince makes the layout of its mansion part of the puzzle itself.
contentBlocks.heading: Blue Prince
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The shifting rooms and hallways of Mount Holly in Blue Prince.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A puzzle box that keeps revealing another puzzle underneath

contentBlocks.text:
Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is compelling because ordinary decisions matter. Clothing, reputation, preparation, conversation, travel, and combat all belong to the same simulation, so role-playing comes from how the player behaves as much as which dialogue option they choose.

It can create friction, but that commitment is also why the world feels unusually reactive. Dense RPG systems like these have always felt at home on PC.
contentBlocks.caption: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II makes everyday decisions part of its role-playing systems.
contentBlocks.heading: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Henry traveling through the medieval world of Kingdom Come: Deliverance II.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Role-playing that commits to the messy details of inhabiting a world

contentBlocks.text:
Silksong succeeds because Hornet does not feel like a replacement for the original game''s hero. Her movement is faster, more acrobatic, and more assertive, which changes how exploration and platforming are designed around her.

Pharloom is dense without feeling like a copy of Hallownest, and the climb through its regions gives the adventure a clearer sense of direction while preserving the pleasure of being distracted by a suspicious path.
contentBlocks.caption: Silksong builds a new identity around Hornet's faster movement and the vertical journey through Pharloom.
contentBlocks.heading: Hollow Knight: Silksong
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Hornet exploring the kingdom of Pharloom in Hollow Knight: Silksong.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A long-awaited sequel that justifies the wait through movement

contentBlocks.text:
Hades II takes a structure that already felt unusually complete and finds meaningful room to expand it. Melinoe''s weapons, magic, upgrades, relationships, and routes create more possibilities without turning each run into administrative work.

The reason it remains so easy to recommend is the connection between repetition and storytelling: another attempt still moves relationships and knowledge forward instead of feeling like simple repetition.
contentBlocks.caption: Hades II expands the first game's replayable structure without losing its narrative momentum.
contentBlocks.heading: Hades II
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Melinoe using magic during a run in Hades II.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Supergiant's loop is deeper, broader, and still remarkably focused

contentBlocks.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 belongs on a 2026 list because the game people can play today is dramatically stronger than the one that launched. Years of updates reshaped progression and quality-of-life systems, while Phantom Liberty added some of the game''s strongest missions and character work.

PC remains the version that best expresses Night City''s technical ambition, and its modding scene gives returning players more reasons to experiment.
contentBlocks.caption: Cyberpunk 2077's current PC version finally matches much more of Night City's original ambition.
contentBlocks.heading: Cyberpunk 2077
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Night City illuminated at night in Cyberpunk 2077.
contentBlocks.subtitle: One of PC gaming's roughest launches became one of its best showcases

contentBlocks.text:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 became one of the defining RPGs of 2025 because it treats turn-based combat as a foundation rather than a limitation. Players still plan around party composition and abilities, but dodges, parries, and timed inputs keep encounters physically engaging.

Its larger achievement is cohesion: the art direction, music, performances, and melancholy premise all point toward the same emotional identity.
contentBlocks.caption: Expedition 33 mixes deliberate party strategy with real-time reactions and a distinctive visual identity.
contentBlocks.heading: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Members of Expedition 33 traveling through the game's Belle Epoque-inspired world.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Turn-based combat made immediate without abandoning strategy

contentBlocks.text:
Stardew Valley keeps earning its place because almost nothing else balances routine, freedom, and long-term attachment this gracefully. A day can be spent farming efficiently, exploring, fishing, decorating, talking to neighbors, or ignoring productivity entirely.

PC adds another layer through years of community creativity and an enormous modding ecosystem, but the base game remains the reason people stay.
contentBlocks.caption: Stardew Valley remains one of PC gaming's most durable examples of player-directed routine and progression.
contentBlocks.heading: Stardew Valley
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A colorful farm and town scene from Stardew Valley.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A decade later, PC still gives this small farming game an enormous life

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring remains extraordinary because the Lands Between keeps creating questions. A distant tower, a suspicious cliff, or a ruined structure can redirect an entire session without an interface announcing that something important is nearby.

Its demanding combat is balanced by unusual freedom: explore elsewhere, change a build, experiment with a new tool, or return later with a different plan. Years after launch, it is still one of the strongest arguments for getting lost on purpose.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring turns curiosity into the main navigation system of a vast action RPG.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooking the Lands Between in Elden Ring.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Open-world freedom without turning discovery into a checklist

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur''s Gate 3 stays at number one because its greatest strength has aged into an even bigger advantage: possibility. Quests, conversations, character abilities, environmental systems, and tactical encounters constantly overlap, letting players solve problems in ways that feel discovered rather than selected from a menu.

PC is also where that design feels most at home, with mouse-and-keyboard controls and a huge modding community extending an already remarkably reactive RPG.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur's Gate 3 remains the benchmark for reactive role-playing and systemic player choice.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur's Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A party of adventurers preparing for an encounter in Baldur's Gate 3.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The PC RPG standard is still the easiest recommendation to make

quickRead: The freshest reason to get a few friends into the same voice chat
A polished open-road showcase that makes PC hardware feel worthwhile
A current-generation horror showcase with confident pacing
conclusion:
==A list called “the best PC games right now” should be allowed to change. New releases arrive, older games receive transformative updates, communities move, and sometimes a game that seemed permanent simply stops being the thing we would recommend first.==

==That is why this is a living Neural Critic ranking rather than a one-time verdict. The goal is to answer a practical question as clearly as possible: if someone has a PC and wants something excellent to play today, where should they start?==

title: Take-Two’s GTA 6 Leak Hunt Expands Across Microsoft, Discord, X and YouTube
description: Take-Two’s effort to identify people linked to unauthorized GTA VI material now spans four DMCA subpoena proceedings involving Microsoft, Discord, X and Google/YouTube, as the CyberLeek campaign continues and key questions about attribution remain unresolved.
body:
Take-Two Interactive’s response to the Grand Theft Auto VI leak campaign has grown from takedown efforts into a multi-platform attempt to identify people connected to the unauthorized distribution of Rockstar Games material. Public court-record reporting now shows four separate DMCA subpoena proceedings involving Microsoft, Discord, X Corp. and Google/YouTube.

The filings do not establish who CyberLeek is, how the material was obtained, or whether every account named or swept into a records request participated in the original leak. They are identification tools under the DMCA, not findings of liability. The procedural status also matters: a court order directing a clerk to issue a subpoena is not the same thing as a platform being served, producing records, or Take-Two successfully identifying a person.

The investigation has continued alongside the leak campaign itself. Rockstar publicly described the unauthorized releases as heartbreaking before its August 27 Extended Look, while CyberLeek subsequently escalated into reported story material and cashed out substantial proceeds connected to the $CYBERLEEK token. None of those developments has yet produced a verified public identification of the person or group behind the campaign.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Official Grand Theft Auto VI artwork from Rockstar Games.
imageCredit: Rockstar Games / official artwork

contentBlocks.text:
Take-Two’s legal effort is broader than the Microsoft and Discord requests that first brought the investigation into public view. Court-record reporting shows **four separate Section 512(h) DMCA proceedings**, directed at **Microsoft, Discord, X Corp. and Google/YouTube**.

The Microsoft-related request seeks records connected to accounts and services that Take-Two believes may help trace the distribution chain. The Discord request is unusually broad, seeking identifying and device-related information associated with users in specified servers during the relevant period. Separate filings involving X and Google/YouTube target accounts or uploads that Take-Two believes may be connected to the unauthorized material.

The important distinction is that these proceedings are designed to obtain identifying information. They are **not lawsuits against the platforms**, and the existence of a request does not prove that every account or community referenced in it participated in the original leak.
contentBlocks.heading: The leak hunt now spans four major platforms

contentBlocks.text:
The procedural language around the subpoenas requires care. Judges can sign orders directing a court clerk to issue a requested DMCA subpoena, but that step should not be described as proof that a platform has already been served or has handed records to Take-Two.

Discord made that distinction explicit on August 24, when marketing director Ryan K. Rigney said the company **had not yet been served** and would evaluate the validity and scope of a subpoena before responding. Reporting on the four proceedings has likewise cautioned that no resulting user-data handover had been publicly established at the latest verified stage.

That leaves several separate milestones to watch: issuance, service on the provider, a provider response, any production of records, and finally whether those records actually help establish attribution. None of those later steps should be collapsed into a claim that CyberLeek has been identified.
contentBlocks.heading: What the court process actually confirms

contentBlocks.text:
Rockstar Games publicly addressed the unauthorized footage ahead of its official August 27 presentation, describing the situation as **heartbreaking** for the team and emphasizing that the leaked material was not how it wanted players to experience the game. The studio nevertheless went ahead with its Extended Look, which is now officially available.

The leak campaign did not stop. Reporting says CyberLeek subsequently released a roughly **4-minute-38-second unauthorized sequence described as part of Lucia’s prologue**, pushing the incident from gameplay and systems footage into potentially significant story material. Neural Critic is not reproducing, linking to, or describing the leaked story content.

That escalation matters to this investigation because it shows that Take-Two’s legal pressure and Rockstar’s public response had not, at that point, ended the releases.
contentBlocks.heading: Rockstar spoke out, but the leaks kept escalating

contentBlocks.text:
The campaign also developed a financial dimension. On-chain reporting on August 27 indicated that the creator behind the **$CYBERLEEK token** cashed out roughly **$250,000–$270,000** connected to the token. CoinDesk reported that proceeds were distributed across fresh wallets and that part of the trail appeared to reach a KYC-verified exchange account.

That could become relevant to attribution because regulated exchange records can connect activity to verified account information. But the public evidence does **not** currently establish that a named person behind any exchange account is CyberLeek, and there has been no confirmed announcement from Take-Two, an exchange or authorities identifying the leaker through the token activity.

For now, the financial trail is an investigative lead rather than a solved identity.
contentBlocks.heading: The $CYBERLEEK money trail may become another lead

contentBlocks.text:
The CyberLeek incident is now reaching Take-Two’s investor narrative as well as its legal response. On August 31, Investing.com reported that Take-Two shares fell about **7.2% in morning trading**, with the continuing GTA VI leak situation cited as a factor weighing on sentiment.

BofA Securities nevertheless reiterated a **Buy** rating and a **$368 price target** on Take-Two. More importantly for the leak itself, the firm said details in the unauthorized footage appear consistent with access to a **genuine playable build**, while finding **no clear evidence that a distributable copy of GTA VI exists** at this stage.

That distinction matters. Access to an internal, development or otherwise restricted playable build is not the same thing as possessing a complete copy that can be distributed publicly. CyberLeek has created the impression of broad access, but the public evidence still does not verify possession of a full distributable game. Until Rockstar, Take-Two, investigators or independently verifiable evidence establishes otherwise, claims that CyberLeek has the ‘full game’ should remain treated as unproven.
contentBlocks.heading: The leak is now reaching investors — but a full distributable build remains unproven

contentBlocks.text:
The confirmed picture is now substantial: unauthorized GTA VI material circulated under the CyberLeek name; Take-Two opened four DMCA subpoena proceedings spanning Microsoft, Discord, X and Google/YouTube; Rockstar publicly condemned the leaks; the campaign continued into reported story material; and on-chain reporting documented a large $CYBERLEEK token cash-out.

What remains unresolved is just as important. There is still **no verified public identification of CyberLeek**, no confirmed public explanation of how the material was obtained, and no verified announcement that Discord, Google, X or Microsoft records have unmasked the source. Accounts appearing in filings or online discussions should not be treated as the original leaker without evidence.

Neural Critic will continue separating those confirmed events from speculation and will not redistribute the unauthorized footage.
contentBlocks.heading: What is confirmed — and what remains unknown

contentBlocks.text:
The next meaningful development will be procedural or evidentiary rather than another rumor: confirmation that one of the providers has been formally served, confirmation that records have been produced, a new court filing, an official Take-Two or Rockstar statement, or reliable evidence identifying the source.

The reported **September 4** production date associated with the early requests remains an important point to watch. Any provider response around that window could materially change the investigation.

Rockstar’s August 27 Extended Look is now a separate official-news story. This article will remain focused on the leak investigation, the legal process and verified changes in the effort to identify those responsible.
contentBlocks.heading: What happens next

conclusion: Take-Two’s GTA VI leak investigation is no longer a two-platform story. The documented effort now reaches Microsoft, Discord, X and Google/YouTube, while a separate crypto trail and continued unauthorized releases add new potential leads. But the central question remains unanswered: there is still no verified public identification of CyberLeek. Until a provider response, court filing or official statement changes that, Neural Critic will treat attribution claims as unconfirmed and keep the investigation separate from Rockstar’s official GTA VI coverage.

updates.note: Take-Two says its GTA VI leak investigation is "rapidly evolving." In new August 31 court filings, the company sought a second, more targeted Discord subpoena and asked to keep the identifying details under seal to avoid tipping off the people being investigated. Take-Two also withdrew its Google/YouTube subpoena request after determining that the requested information was no longer needed. There is still no verified public identification of CyberLeek or confirmed public disclosure that provider records have unmasked the source.
