title: Super Mario Galaxy 2 Review: Platforming Ideas at Full Speed
description: Nintendo takes the gravity-bending foundations of Super Mario Galaxy and turns them into a faster, denser, more demanding celebration of 3D platforming.
body: Super Mario Galaxy 2 begins with an unusual advantage: it does not need to prove that spherical worlds and shifting gravity can work. The original already did that. Instead, the sequel treats those ideas as a foundation and immediately starts asking what else Mario can do with them. The result is a game with less interest in ceremony and more interest in momentum. Galaxies arrive quickly, mechanics evolve rapidly, and individual stars often feel like compact design experiments built around one strong idea. Where the first Galaxy often inspires awe, Galaxy 2 frequently inspires a different reaction: how did Nintendo think of this many platforming setups and make nearly all of them readable?
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario rides Yoshi through a colorful cosmic scene in Super Mario Galaxy 2 promotional artwork.
imageCredit: Nintendo / official game imagery

cons: Less atmospheric and emotionally distinctive than the original Galaxy
The streamlined hub sacrifices some sense of place
A few motion-controlled sequences still feel tied to their hardware era
pros: An extraordinary density of creative level ideas
Yoshi adds meaningful new movement and traversal mechanics
Sharper challenge design without sacrificing control clarity
Fast pacing makes the campaign exceptionally replayable
reviewMeta.verdict: A relentless showcase of 3D platforming craft that trades some of the original Galaxy’s atmosphere for denser ideas, sharper challenges, and astonishing mechanical variety.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review of the original Nintendo Wii release. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
The original Super Mario Galaxy spends meaningful time establishing the Comet Observatory, Rosalina, and the strange emotional calm of its journey through space. Galaxy 2 is much more direct. Starship Mario becomes a compact hub, the map pushes the player toward the next challenge almost immediately, and the game rarely lingers between ideas.

That shift changes the tone, but it also gives the sequel remarkable pacing. New mechanics appear with very little friction. A level can introduce a gravity switch, a disappearing platform route, a drill, a cloud power-up, or a moving obstacle pattern and reach its most interesting variation within minutes.

The game feels edited around play rather than atmosphere. Something is lost in that exchange, especially for players who loved the first game’s sense of place, but the reward is one of Nintendo’s most concentrated platforming campaigns.
contentBlocks.caption: Galaxy 2 wastes little time between ideas, moving quickly from one playful obstacle setup to the next.
contentBlocks.heading: Galaxy 2 Trades Wonder for Momentum
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario moves through a bright grassy obstacle course inside a transparent bubble in Super Mario Galaxy 2.

contentBlocks.text:
Galaxy 2 has an almost unreasonable density of ideas. Many games would reuse their strongest mechanic across an entire region. Nintendo often builds one memorable star around an idea, develops it just enough to make the player understand its possibilities, and then moves on.

That confidence keeps the adventure unpredictable. Some stages revolve around rhythm and timing. Others focus on navigation, transformation, momentum, gravity, moving architecture, or increasingly precise jumps. Even familiar concepts from the first game are frequently remixed into harder or faster variations.

The important part is that novelty rarely replaces clarity. The game can become visually busy, but the player usually understands what the level is asking. That balance between surprise and readability is one of Galaxy 2’s greatest achievements.
contentBlocks.caption: The sequel constantly escalates familiar mechanics into faster, stranger, and more spectacular challenges.
contentBlocks.heading: Every Level Arrives With a New Trick
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario and Yoshi launch through the air as an explosion erupts beside a floating grassy planetoid in Super Mario Galaxy 2.

contentBlocks.text:
Yoshi is the sequel’s most important addition because he changes how Mario interacts with space rather than functioning as a simple bonus character. His flutter jump adds hang time, his tongue can grab enemies and objects, and different fruit abilities temporarily rewrite the rules of movement.

Dash Yoshi turns stretches of a level into speed challenges. Blimp Yoshi introduces vertical control. Bulb Yoshi reveals hidden routes and asks the player to think about visibility as part of traversal. None of these abilities dominate the entire game, which keeps them feeling special.

More importantly, Yoshi fits Galaxy 2’s design philosophy: introduce a mechanic, communicate it quickly, push it toward an interesting variation, and leave before it becomes routine.
contentBlocks.caption: Yoshi expands Mario’s movement vocabulary with new traversal tools, temporary abilities, and playful routes.
contentBlocks.heading: Yoshi Turns Movement Into a Second Language
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario rides Yoshi across a bright beach area with water, flowers, and tropical scenery in Super Mario Galaxy 2.

contentBlocks.text:
Galaxy 2 is noticeably more willing to test the player. Later stars ask for cleaner movement, faster decisions, and better understanding of mechanics that earlier missions only introduced. Comet challenges and optional content can turn familiar stages into much stricter tests.

That difficulty works because Mario remains predictable. Long jumps, spins, wall jumps, ground pounds, and mid-air corrections still give the player enough control to recover from imperfect approaches. When Galaxy 2 becomes demanding, it usually feels like the level is asking for better execution rather than fighting the controls.

The game is still welcoming enough to finish without mastering everything, but players who want to chase its harder stars will find some of the sharpest platforming Nintendo produced on the Wii.
contentBlocks.caption: Later stars demand cleaner movement and quicker decisions without sacrificing the game’s readable controls.
contentBlocks.heading: Challenge Stars Push the Formula Harder
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario clings to a small spherical planetoid while Bowser attacks against a vivid red space backdrop in Super Mario Galaxy 2.

contentBlocks.text:
The sequel’s biggest weakness is closely connected to its greatest strength. By stripping away much of the first game’s atmosphere and narrative texture, Galaxy 2 becomes easier to replay and faster to navigate, but it can also feel less emotionally distinct.

Starship Mario is charming, yet it never develops the same quiet identity as the Comet Observatory. The soundtrack remains excellent and the visual imagination is extraordinary, but fewer moments pause long enough to create the same sense of wonder or melancholy that defined parts of the original.

That does not make Galaxy 2 a lesser platformer. In pure mechanical terms it may be even more accomplished. It simply means the two games excel in slightly different ways: Galaxy feels like an adventure through space, while Galaxy 2 feels like Nintendo turning that adventure into an almost nonstop sequence of brilliant platforming problems.
contentBlocks.caption: Even at its most streamlined, Galaxy 2 keeps its stages visually playful and mechanically distinct.
contentBlocks.heading: A Leaner Adventure With Fewer Emotional Peaks
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario faces a giant Piranha Plant boss on a small rocky planetoid surrounded by Star Bits in Super Mario Galaxy 2.

conclusion: ==Super Mario Galaxy 2 is Nintendo working with the confidence of a studio that already solved the hardest problem. Gravity no longer needs to be the headline, so the sequel can spend nearly every level bending, combining, and accelerating the ideas that made its predecessor special. It loses some of Galaxy’s emotional atmosphere in the process, but what replaces it is an extraordinary concentration of platforming craft. For players who value mechanical invention, replayability, and level design that keeps finding new ways to surprise, Galaxy 2 remains one of the genre’s clearest high-water marks.==

title: Super Mario Galaxy Review: A Platforming Masterpiece Among the Stars
description: Nintendo turned gravity, movement, music, and constant invention into one of the most imaginative 3D platformers ever made.
body:
Super Mario Galaxy begins with a familiar promise: run, jump, collect stars, and rescue Princess Peach. Then Mario steps onto a tiny planet, gravity bends beneath his feet, the horizon curves around him, and one of Nintendo’s most recognizable formulas suddenly feels new again.

Released for the Nintendo Wii in 2007, Galaxy remains remarkable because its biggest ideas are never treated as one-off spectacle. Gravity, spherical worlds, launch stars, transformations, motion controls, and orchestral music all serve the same goal: make movement itself feel surprising. Nearly two decades later, very few 3D platformers are this confident about introducing an idea, exploring it fully, and moving on before it becomes routine.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Mario leaping between small planets in the gravity-bending worlds of Super Mario Galaxy.
imageCredit: Nintendo / Super Mario Galaxy

cons: A few motion-control sequences have aged less gracefully
The camera can occasionally make spatial judgment harder
Minor hub traversal friction when revisiting specific stars
pros: Gravity mechanics constantly reinvent familiar platforming ideas
Exceptional level variety with very little filler
Precise, readable movement across wildly unconventional spaces
One of Nintendo’s most memorable orchestral soundtracks
reviewMeta.verdict: A masterclass in 3D platforming whose gravity-bending level design, precise movement, orchestral presentation, and relentless invention still feel extraordinary.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review of the original Nintendo Wii release. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
The defining idea is gravity, but Galaxy succeeds because Nintendo treats gravity as a design language rather than a visual trick. Mario can sprint around spheres, leap between tiny planetoids, cling to surfaces that would be ceilings in another game, and launch across space without the controls becoming unreadable.

That clarity is an enormous achievement. A stage may twist the camera, reverse the apparent direction of “down,” or ask Mario to cross a structure hanging in open space, yet movement usually remains intuitive. The player learns to trust the game’s rules even when the geometry stops behaving like a traditional platforming level.

The result is a type of 3D platforming that feels playful at the level of physics itself. Galaxy does not merely place obstacles in front of Mario. It keeps changing the relationship between Mario, the ground, and the space around him.
contentBlocks.caption: Galaxy pairs its cosmic scale with a warm, playful sense of place from the very beginning.
contentBlocks.heading: Gravity Turns Platforming Into a Playground
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario stands beside a glowing Luma in a flower-filled area of Super Mario Galaxy.

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy is almost reckless with ideas. One mission might be built around climbing a mountain of moving platforms, another around navigating a toy box, racing a shadow version of Mario, balancing on a rolling ball, using Bee Mario to reach fragile surfaces, or crossing a level that reforms beneath every step.

Most games would build an entire chapter around one of these concepts. Galaxy frequently introduces a mechanic, develops it through a handful of escalating challenges, and then leaves it behind. That editing discipline keeps the adventure moving and gives individual stars a strong identity.

There are recurring structures, but the game rarely feels repetitive because the context is always changing. Even revisiting the same galaxy can reveal a substantially different objective, route, hazard, or transformation. The player is not simply clearing a map. They are moving through a catalogue of platforming experiments.
contentBlocks.caption: New mechanics and transformations constantly give each galaxy its own rhythm and identity.
contentBlocks.heading: Every Galaxy Feels Like a New Idea
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Bee Mario moves through a colorful flower-filled planetoid with coins and small platforms in Super Mario Galaxy.

contentBlocks.text:
Mario’s moveset is smaller than in some later 3D entries, but nearly every action has a clear purpose. Long jumps, backflips, wall jumps, ground pounds, spins, and careful mid-air corrections give players enough control to express themselves without turning each level into a technical obstacle course.

The spin attack is especially important. It provides a small amount of aerial correction, activates environmental objects, attacks enemies, and creates a rhythm that separates Galaxy from earlier 3D Mario games. It also makes the Wii Remote feel integrated into the design rather than used only as a novelty.

Not every motion-controlled interaction has aged equally well. Pointer-based collection and a few tilt-focused sequences can feel less natural today than Mario’s core movement. But these moments are brief, and the fundamental platforming remains remarkably responsive.
contentBlocks.caption: Precise movement keeps unusual gravity and shifting perspectives readable even when the world bends around Mario.
contentBlocks.heading: Movement Stays Precise When the World Turns Upside Down
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario balances on a wooden platform beside a large windmill structure suspended above space in Super Mario Galaxy.

contentBlocks.text:
Galaxy’s visual design understands that outer space can be both enormous and intimate. A level can open on a tiny floating island and then send Mario through launch stars toward planets, mechanical structures, gardens, lava fields, ghost houses, or impossible architecture suspended against a star-filled sky.

The orchestral score gives those transitions emotional weight. Triumphant themes make major galaxies feel adventurous, while quieter pieces give the Comet Observatory and Rosalina’s storybook sequences a sense of melancholy that is unusual for Mario. The soundtrack is not simply decoration; it helps define the scale and personality of each space.

Rosalina and the Observatory also provide the game with a stronger sense of place than a basic level-select screen would have offered. The hub is compact enough to navigate quickly, but memorable enough to make returning between adventures feel like coming home.
contentBlocks.caption: Strong visual composition and memorable set pieces make even compact challenges feel theatrical.
contentBlocks.heading: Music and Presentation Make Space Feel Magical
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario stands in a bright circular grass arena surrounded by Piranha Plants in Super Mario Galaxy.

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy is not completely untouched by age. The camera occasionally chooses an angle that makes a jump harder to read, some motion-control challenges feel more like hardware demonstrations than timeless mechanics, and repeated trips through the Observatory can add a little friction when chasing specific stars.

Those weaknesses stand out partly because the rest of the game is so carefully edited. Galaxy spends very little time on filler. Its best stages introduce a premise immediately, build toward a satisfying twist, and end before the idea loses its energy.

What remains is an adventure whose imagination is matched by discipline. Plenty of games can surprise the player once. Super Mario Galaxy keeps doing it for dozens of hours while maintaining the precision and readability expected from Nintendo’s best platformers. That is why it still belongs near the very top of any conversation about the medium’s greatest games.
contentBlocks.caption: A few aging control quirks remain, but the fundamental joy of moving through Galaxy still shines through.
contentBlocks.heading: A Few Old Frictions Cannot Dim the Adventure
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario performs a spin attack as colorful Star Bits scatter across a grassy planetoid in Super Mario Galaxy.

conclusion:
==Super Mario Galaxy remains one of the finest examples of Nintendo at its most imaginative. Its gravity-bending worlds, precise platforming, orchestral score, and constant stream of new ideas make nearly every galaxy feel memorable. A few motion-control quirks and occasional camera frustrations show its age, but they barely diminish an adventure that still feels joyful, inventive, and remarkably polished. More than fifteen years later, Super Mario Galaxy is not simply a great Mario game — it is one of the defining 3D platformers ever made, and an easy recommendation for anyone who values creativity, movement, and pure game design.==

==9.8/10 — MASTERPIECE==

title: Neural Critic’s 10 Best Games of All Time
description: From landmark design breakthroughs to modern masterpieces, these are the ten games Neural Critic believes best represent what the medium can achieve.
body:
Any list claiming to name the best games of all time has to admit one thing immediately: there is no objective formula for greatness. Sales, review scores, influence, technical ambition, and personal attachment all measure different things.

For Neural Critic’s first all-time canon, we are prioritizing five ideas: design influence, quality of execution, longevity, replayability, and how clearly a game’s ideas still communicate today. This is not a list of the most important games ever made, nor a ranking of our favorite memories. It is our current editorial answer to a harder question: which games best demonstrate the possibilities of the medium?
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: The most memorable and influencial games ever created

contentBlocks.text:
Portal 2 is the rare sequel that expands almost every part of its predecessor without losing the elegance that made the original work. Its portal mechanics remain immediately understandable, but Valve keeps combining them with momentum, gels, lasers, light bridges, and environmental timing in ways that constantly reframe what the player thinks is possible.

Its writing is just as important to the experience. Comedy, level design, performance, and pacing reinforce one another instead of competing for attention. Even after the solutions are known, Portal 2 remains a masterclass in teaching complicated spatial ideas without drowning the player in explanation.
contentBlocks.caption: Portal 2 turns a tiny set of rules into one of gaming’s most inventive puzzle campaigns.
contentBlocks.heading: Portal 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Chell navigating one of Aperture Science’s portal-based test chambers.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A puzzle game that never stops finding new ideas

contentBlocks.text:
Super Metroid helped define an entire vocabulary for exploration games. Doors, terrain, enemy placement, ability gates, and tiny environmental details quietly teach the player how Zebes works. Progress feels earned because new abilities do more than unlock doors—they change how familiar spaces are understood.

What makes the game endure is restraint. It rarely needs lengthy dialogue or explicit navigation markers because its world is built to communicate through shape, sound, and possibility. Modern games continue to borrow that language, but Super Metroid still feels unusually confident in how little it needs to say.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Metroid remains one of the clearest examples of world design teaching the player through exploration.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Metroid
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Samus exploring the interconnected caverns of planet Zebes.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Exploration design that still teaches without speaking

contentBlocks.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2 is deliberately slower than most blockbuster open worlds, and that patience is exactly what gives it weight. Riding into a town, caring for a horse, returning to camp, or noticing a stranger at the side of a road can feel meaningful because the world is allowed to exist at a human pace.

Its simulation is sometimes excessive and its controls can be cumbersome, but few games create such a convincing relationship between character, landscape, and routine. Arthur Morgan’s story works because the enormous world around him is not just scenery; it becomes evidence of a life that is changing faster than he can accept.
contentBlocks.caption: Red Dead Redemption 2 uses detail and pacing to make its world feel inhabited rather than assembled.
contentBlocks.heading: Red Dead Redemption 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Arthur Morgan riding through the American frontier.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world built around observation and consequence

contentBlocks.text:
Half-Life 2 made physics, environmental storytelling, scripted spectacle, and first-person combat feel like parts of one continuous language. The Gravity Gun is still one of the medium’s great design tools because it is simultaneously a weapon, a puzzle mechanic, and an invitation to experiment with the world.

Its greatest achievement is pacing. City 17, Ravenholm, the coast, and the Citadel all feel distinct, yet the campaign rarely breaks its sense of forward movement. Many games have surpassed individual pieces of Half-Life 2, but very few combine so many ideas with this much clarity.
contentBlocks.caption: Half-Life 2 made physics and environmental interaction central to the rhythm of a shooter campaign.
contentBlocks.heading: Half-Life 2
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Gordon Freeman moving through the occupied streets of City 17.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A first-person campaign with almost no wasted motion

contentBlocks.text:
Minecraft’s greatest strength is not any single adventure, boss, biome, or crafting recipe. It is the way a small collection of readable rules can support building, survival, engineering, exploration, role-playing, multiplayer communities, education, and forms of creativity its original design never explicitly demanded.

Few games have given players this much ownership over what playing means. Its blocky world is instantly understandable, but the possibilities inside it are almost impossible to exhaust. That flexibility has made Minecraft less like a conventional release and more like a permanent piece of gaming culture.
contentBlocks.caption: Minecraft endures because its basic rules can support thousands of different kinds of play.
contentBlocks.heading: Minecraft
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A player-built landscape in Minecraft made from colorful blocks.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A ruleset simple enough to become almost anything

contentBlocks.text:
Baldur’s Gate 3 makes an enormous role-playing game feel reactive at a scale that once seemed unrealistic. Conversations, combat arenas, character relationships, quests, and environmental systems overlap constantly, allowing the player to solve problems through persuasion, violence, stealth, magic, improvisation, or wonderfully bad judgment.

Its real achievement is not that every possibility has a bespoke answer. It is that the game is willing to let systems collide and then support the consequences. That generosity makes repeated playthroughs feel less like revisiting content and more like testing a different version of the same world.
contentBlocks.caption: Baldur’s Gate 3 makes player choice feel systemic rather than decorative.
contentBlocks.heading: Baldur’s Gate 3
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A party of adventurers preparing for a choice-driven encounter in Baldur’s Gate 3.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Choice-heavy role-playing without sanding away the chaos

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls changed the language of action RPGs by making uncertainty part of the design. Combat asks for patience, death turns knowledge into progression, and Lordran’s looping geography transforms exploration into a form of mastery. A shortcut is not merely convenient—it changes the player’s mental map of the entire world.

Its influence is obvious, but influence alone would not earn this position. Dark Souls still works because its combat, level design, atmosphere, multiplayer ideas, and storytelling all reinforce the same philosophy: pay attention, accept failure, and learn how the world fits together.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls made knowledge, spatial memory, and persistence inseparable from progression.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Chosen Undead crossing one of Lordran’s interconnected environments.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A world where challenge, discovery, and geography become one system

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild reimagined open-world structure around what the player can see, wonder about, and physically reach. Mountains are not decorative barriers, distant landmarks are invitations, and a flexible physics-and-chemistry sandbox turns simple environmental problems into opportunities for experimentation.

The game’s most important innovation is trust. It is willing to give players major abilities early, let them approach objectives in unexpected orders, and accept improvised solutions that would break more rigid adventures. That freedom helped redefine what exploration could feel like in a modern open world.
contentBlocks.caption: Breath of the Wild made curiosity itself the main navigation system.
contentBlocks.heading: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link overlooking the open landscape of Hyrule in Breath of the Wild.
contentBlocks.subtitle: An open world that trusts curiosity more than instructions

contentBlocks.text:
Super Mario Galaxy treats gravity as a toy. Tiny planets, shifting perspectives, spherical spaces, launch stars, transformations, and constantly changing objectives let Nintendo reinvent platforming rules from one stage to the next without losing the immediate pleasure of simply moving Mario around.

That variety could have made the game feel scattered. Instead, its controls, music, visual clarity, and tightly edited level design create remarkable cohesion. Few games are this generous with new ideas, and even fewer know exactly when to stop using one and move to the next.
contentBlocks.caption: Super Mario Galaxy combines constant invention with exceptionally readable platforming.
contentBlocks.heading: Super Mario Galaxy
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Mario leaping between small planets in a gravity-bending galaxy.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Movement, level design, and imagination in near-perfect balance

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring takes ideas that once depended on tight, hostile corridors and proves they can survive at enormous scale. The Lands Between is open, but it rarely feels like a checklist. Sightlines, ruins, terrain, enemy placement, and architectural silhouettes keep creating questions that exploration can answer—or replace with even stranger questions.

Its achievement is the balance between freedom and authorship. Players can wander, overlevel, summon help, specialize into wildly different builds, or throw themselves at a challenge far earlier than intended, yet the world still retains the danger, surprise, and deliberate encounter design associated with FromSoftware’s best work. For Neural Critic’s first all-time list, no game better combines modern scope with uncompromised identity.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring expands the Souls design philosophy into a world built around curiosity and player choice.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooking the Lands Between in Elden Ring.
contentBlocks.subtitle: FromSoftware’s design philosophy expanded without losing its mystery
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S

quickRead: A puzzle game that never stops finding new ideas
Exploration design that still teaches without speaking
An open world built around observation and consequence
conclusion:
==A canon should never be permanent. New games will challenge these choices, older games will be rediscovered, and the qualities we value in interactive design will continue to change.==

==That is why Neural Critic’s Best Games of All Time is intended to be a living editorial franchise rather than a list carved into stone. The important part is not pretending that ten positions can settle decades of gaming history. It is making the case clearly enough that readers can argue with it—and perhaps discover something worth playing along the way.==

title: Elden Ring Review: A Monumental Open World Worth Getting Lost In
description: FromSoftware transforms its demanding action-RPG formula into a vast, mysterious adventure where curiosity is rewarded at nearly every turn.
body:
Elden Ring takes the foundations FromSoftware refined across the Souls series and gives them room to breathe. The Lands Between is enormous, but its scale rarely feels empty because distant landmarks, hidden paths, and unexpected encounters continually invite exploration.

Its greatest achievement is not simply creating a large world. It is making discovery feel personal. Two players can follow completely different routes, meet different characters, find different tools, and still feel as though the game deliberately guided them toward a memorable story.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooks the expansive Lands Between beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring.

cons: Some late-game enemies and encounters feel repeated
Performance can be inconsistent on PC
Several questlines are unnecessarily difficult to follow
pros: A world that constantly rewards curiosity
Exceptional build and combat variety
Memorable bosses, regions, and visual direction
Player freedom without excessive hand-holding
reviewMeta.verdict: A towering action RPG whose freedom, atmosphere, and build variety outweigh its occasional repetition and technical roughness.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Reviewed on PC using a personally purchased copy of the game.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring understands that an open world becomes exciting when players can make meaningful decisions about where to go. The map presents striking landmarks without immediately explaining them, encouraging players to choose their own objectives and investigate at their own pace.

Exploration frequently produces something valuable: a new weapon, spell, character, dungeon, shortcut, or piece of environmental storytelling. Even when a discovery is not useful for a particular build, the journey often delivers a memorable encounter or a better understanding of the world.
contentBlocks.caption: Leyndell is one of many distant landmarks that gradually becomes a destination.
contentBlocks.heading: The Lands Between Makes Exploration Feel Personal
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished rests near the outskirts of Leyndell in Elden Ring.

contentBlocks.text:
The combat remains deliberate and demanding, but Elden Ring offers more ways to approach difficulty than any previous FromSoftware action RPG. Heavy weapons, fast blades, shields, bows, sorceries, incantations, spirit summons, and weapon skills can reshape the rhythm of an encounter.

This flexibility makes experimentation part of the adventure. A difficult enemy may become manageable after changing equipment, exploring elsewhere, upgrading a summon, or discovering an ability that complements the player's strengths.
contentBlocks.caption: Incantations and weapon skills give players many ways to control a battle.
contentBlocks.heading: Combat Supports Remarkably Different Playstyles
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished summons a lightning incantation during combat in Elden Ring.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring's strongest major encounters combine mechanical pressure with unforgettable presentation. Learning attack patterns, choosing safe moments to respond, and adapting a build creates a satisfying progression from uncertainty to control.

The quality is not perfectly even. Some repeated enemies and late-game difficulty spikes can weaken the sense of discovery, but the finest battles remain among FromSoftware's most ambitious achievements.
contentBlocks.caption: Difficult encounters reward preparation, observation, and experimentation.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Best Battles Turn Challenge Into Spectacle
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished uses a fire incantation during an Elden Ring battle.

conclusion:
==The game trusts players to interpret its world through item descriptions, architecture, character dialogue, and environmental clues. That restraint gives the Lands Between an unusual sense of history and makes community discussion part of the experience.
==
==However, the same approach can make character quests difficult to follow. Important steps may depend on returning to an unexpected location or speaking to someone after an unclear trigger. Mystery strengthens the atmosphere, but clearer ways to review conversations would improve accessibility without removing discovery.==
conclusionHeading: Mystery Is Both a Strength and a Frustration

title: FromSoftware's Soulsborne Games Ranked From Easiest to Hardest
description: From the freedom of Elden Ring to the precision demanded by Sekiro, we rank seven landmark FromSoftware adventures by the difficulty of a normal first playthrough.
body:
Difficulty in a FromSoftware game is never just about enemy damage. Level design, boss speed, healing systems, build freedom, checkpoints, and the amount of help available all shape how demanding a first playthrough feels.

This ranking considers each base game in its standard form. It assumes a blind or lightly guided first run, allows the tools each game naturally provides, and does not factor in challenge runs, downloadable expansions, or deliberately overpowered late-game builds. Individual experience will still vary—and that is part of what makes this debate fun.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: FromSoftware's Soulsborne Games Ranked From Easiest to Hardest

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring contains some of FromSoftware’s most demanding individual encounters, but its open structure gives players more control over when and how they face them. If a boss feels overwhelming, the Lands Between almost always offers another cave, quest, weapon, upgrade, or region to explore first.

Spirit Ashes, multiplayer summons, powerful status effects, and an enormous range of builds create multiple answers to the same obstacle. That accessibility does not make the game easy; it makes difficulty more adjustable than in the studio’s earlier, more linear adventures.
contentBlocks.caption: Elden Ring lets players leave a difficult encounter and return with a stronger build.
contentBlocks.heading: Elden Ring
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooking the vast landscape of the Lands Between.
contentBlocks.subtitle: The most flexible path through the formula
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PS4, PS5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X|S

contentBlocks.text:
Demon’s Souls is mechanically slower and more limited than the games that followed it. Many bosses are built around a readable trick or environmental idea, so discovering the intended solution can matter more than mastering a long sequence of reactions.

The real pressure comes from the journey. Long runs back to bosses, scarce healing early on, World Tendency, and levels filled with traps can punish carelessness severely. Once its systems are understood, however, its combat challenges are generally more manageable than those of later FromSoftware games.
contentBlocks.caption: Demon’s Souls often places its harshest challenge between the player and the boss arena.
contentBlocks.heading: Demon's Souls
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A lone warrior exploring the ruined kingdom of Boletaria.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Simpler combat wrapped in unforgiving level design

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls rewards caution more than raw speed. Shields are extremely effective, enemies usually telegraph their attacks clearly, and a careful player can control most encounters one opponent at a time. Its connected world also allows knowledge to become a powerful advantage on later attempts.

What makes the first journey difficult is uncertainty. Important mechanics are barely explained, routes can lead into areas meant for later, and a poor choice of equipment can make progress feel much harder. The game becomes dramatically easier once the player learns how its world fits together.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls is demanding at first, but knowledge steadily turns Lordran into familiar territory.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls Remastered
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Chosen Undead crossing one of Lordran’s interconnected environments.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A deliberate test of patience and observation
contentBlocks.platforms: PC, PS4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls II is not always the fastest game in the series, but it constantly tests positioning and resource management. Groups of enemies, long combat spaces, limited early healing, weapon durability, and the Adaptability stat can make the opening hours especially uncomfortable.

Scholar of the First Sin also rearranges encounters and frequently places pressure on players from several directions. Its enormous build variety eventually provides strong solutions, but reaching that point requires learning a slightly different rhythm from the rest of the trilogy.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls II frequently increases difficulty through enemy placement and sustained pressure.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Bearer of the Curse facing multiple threats in the kingdom of Drangleic.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Attrition, ambushes, and the danger of being surrounded

contentBlocks.text:
Dark Souls III keeps the familiar stamina-based foundation but dramatically raises the speed of its major encounters. Bosses chain attacks together, delay their timing, transform between phases, and punish healing attempts more aggressively than in the earlier Dark Souls games.

The game is more linear and its controls are highly responsive, which reduces some confusion outside combat. Even so, the late-game boss roster demands reliable dodging, careful stamina use, and the ability to adapt when a familiar pattern suddenly changes.
contentBlocks.caption: Dark Souls III combines clear controls with some of the trilogy’s fastest and most complex bosses.
contentBlocks.heading: Dark Souls III
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The Ashen One confronting one of Lothric’s towering enemies.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Faster bosses leave less room to breathe

contentBlocks.text:
Bloodborne removes the comfort of a strong shield and asks players to fight at close range. The regain system can restore recently lost health through immediate counterattacks, while firearms reward precise parries. Both mechanics push the player toward danger instead of allowing them to wait safely.

Its opening area is a severe introduction, healing items must be replenished, and several bosses combine speed with unpredictable movement. Players who adapt to its aggressive rhythm may eventually find it liberating, but the transition from defensive Souls habits can be brutal.
contentBlocks.caption: Bloodborne turns forward pressure and quick reactions into essential defensive tools.
contentBlocks.heading: Bloodborne
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Hunter moving through the gothic streets of Yharnam.
contentBlocks.subtitle: Aggression is not optional—it is the survival system

contentBlocks.text:
Sekiro is the hardest FromSoftware game on this list because it offers fewer ways to avoid learning its central skill. Character builds, summoned allies, and traditional level grinding cannot replace the need to deflect attacks, manage posture, read perilous moves, and control the pace of a duel.

The result is a steep but unusually honest learning curve. Major opponents act like examinations of mechanics introduced throughout the game, and progress often depends on changing the player’s habits rather than improving a statistic. Once its rhythm clicks, Sekiro can feel remarkably precise—but earning that confidence is the toughest first-playthrough challenge FromSoftware has created.
contentBlocks.caption: Sekiro’s hardest encounters demand mastery of deflection, posture, and attack recognition.
contentBlocks.heading: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice
contentBlocks.imageAlt: The shinobi Wolf in a fierce sword duel.
contentBlocks.subtitle: A focused combat system that demands true mastery

quickRead: The most flexible path through the formula
Simpler combat wrapped in unforgiving level design
A deliberate test of patience and observation
conclusion:
==No FromSoftware difficulty ranking can be universal. A player who thrives on aggressive combat may find Bloodborne more forgiving than Dark Souls, while someone who enjoys exploration and build crafting may have a smoother journey through Elden Ring.
==
==What makes these games memorable is not simply how often they defeat the player, but how clearly they teach persistence, observation, and adaptation. Sekiro earns the hardest position here because it demands the narrowest form of mastery—but the most difficult FromSoftware game will always be the one whose lessons challenge your natural playstyle.==

title: Why Dark Souls Remastered Still Defines Interconnected World Design
description: Years later, Lordran remains a masterclass in spatial storytelling, meaningful shortcuts, and exploration built on player memory.
body:
Dark Souls Remastered preserves a world whose greatest achievement is not its size, but its structure. Lordran folds back on itself through elevators, locked gates, hidden paths, and distant landmarks that gradually become familiar.

The result is an adventure where **learning the world feels as important as mastering combat**. Its design still influences how modern action RPGs create tension, discovery, and a lasting sense of place.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: An armored wanderer overlooking the interconnected ruins of Lordran

contentBlocks.text:
Lordran rarely explains its structure directly. Instead, the player learns by recognizing towers, bridges, gates, and routes seen from different angles. **Navigation becomes knowledge**, and that knowledge makes the world feel increasingly personal.

Returning to an earlier location through an unexpected doorway creates a powerful realization: places that seemed far apart were connected all along.
contentBlocks.caption: Lordran uses visible landmarks to help players build a mental map.
contentBlocks.heading: A world that teaches through geography
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A wide view of Anor londo

contentBlocks.text:
A shortcut in Dark Souls is more than convenience. Opening a gate or activating an elevator permanently changes the rhythm of an area. A threatening journey becomes manageable because the player has understood and reshaped the route.

**Progress is measured through access**, not only through statistics or equipment.
contentBlocks.caption: Unlocking a shortcut transforms both navigation and the player’s confidence.
contentBlocks.heading: Shortcuts that change how progress feels
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A wide gate that opens to a memorable but sad boss fight

contentBlocks.text:
Encounters reward patience, spacing, and attention to the environment. Enemy placement, narrow corridors, and open courtyards communicate different risks before a fight begins.

The game can be demanding, but its strongest moments encourage the player to **observe first and act with purpose**.
contentBlocks.caption: Level layout and enemy placement turn observation into a core skill.
contentBlocks.heading: Challenge built around observation
contentBlocks.imageAlt: One of the first hurdles that may challenge new players

contentBlocks.text:
Many later games expanded the scale of action-RPG worlds, yet Lordran remains memorable because almost every path has a structural purpose. Its compact design creates surprise without relying on a huge map.

Dark Souls Remastered proves that **an interconnected world can feel larger than its actual boundaries** when every discovery changes the player’s understanding.
contentBlocks.caption: The strength of Lordran comes from density, connection, and deliberate placement.
contentBlocks.heading: Why Lordran still matters
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A panoramic map showcasing the interconnected level design of the entire world

contentBlocks.text:
Take the long route once, because the shortcut feels better when you understand what it replaces. Read item descriptions when curiosity strikes, revisit suspicious doors, and never underestimate an elevator.

Most importantly, do not rush to turn Lordran into a checklist. **Its best stories are the routes you slowly learn for yourself.**
contentBlocks.heading: And the rest

title: How Elden Ring Reinvented Open-World Exploration
description: Elden Ring transformed FromSoftware’s demanding action-RPG formula into an open world built around mystery, danger, and unforgettable discovery.
body:
When Elden Ring opened the gates to the Lands Between, it offered something very different from the familiar open-world formula. Its map was enormous, but the game rarely treated exploration like a list of errands waiting to be completed.

Instead, FromSoftware used distant landmarks, hidden paths, environmental clues, and carefully placed challenges to make curiosity the player’s most important guide. The result was an open world that felt mysterious without becoming directionless—and one that rewarded attention at almost every turn.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooks the expansive Lands Between beneath the glowing Erdtree in Elden Ring.

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring rarely begins by telling players exactly where they should go. Instead, the Lands Between uses castles, glowing trees, distant towers, and unusual terrain to create **visual invitations** that naturally pull the player forward.

A ruined structure might conceal a merchant. A narrow path may lead to an underground region. Even something that appears decorative can become the beginning of an unexpected journey. The map is not merely a space between objectives—it is **part of the storytelling itself**.
contentBlocks.caption: The Lands Between uses striking landmarks to guide players naturally instead of relying entirely on objective markers.
contentBlocks.heading: 1. A map that rewards observation
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished overlooks the vast Lands Between, with distant castles, cliffs, and the glowing Erdtree guiding exploration.

contentBlocks.text:
Many open-world games reveal activities through icons before the player has seen them. Elden Ring takes the opposite approach: **the discovery usually comes first**, and the map marker comes later—if the player decides to place one at all.

That creates a simple but powerful exploration loop:

- Notice something unusual in the distance.
- Work out how to reach it.
- Discover a location, character, item, or entirely new route.
- Leave with another mystery to investigate.

The question driving the adventure is rarely *“Which marker should I clear next?”* It is *“What is over there?”*
contentBlocks.caption: Discoveries appear through observation and exploration before players decide whether to mark them on the map.
contentBlocks.heading: 2. Discovery without a checklist
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A lightning Incantantion being summoned

contentBlocks.text:
The game’s challenge also changes the meaning of exploration. When one route feels overwhelming, the world quietly encourages players to **leave, grow stronger, and return with a new plan**.

Exploration therefore becomes a form of progression. A newly discovered weapon, upgrade material, spirit summon, or useful spell can completely change how a difficult encounter feels. The open world is not a distraction from the game’s challenges; it gives players more ways to prepare for them.
contentBlocks.caption: A Tarnished rests near a Site of Grace while considering different routes through the surrounding region.
contentBlocks.heading: 3. Difficulty gives exploration a purpose
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished using a fire Incantantion

contentBlocks.text:
The Lands Between contains vast open fields, but it also preserves the intricate level design for which FromSoftware is known. Places such as Stormveil Castle and Leyndell behave like enormous **legacy dungeons**, filled with interconnected routes, shortcuts, vertical spaces, and secrets.

Moving between free-form exploration and tightly designed locations gives the journey its rhythm. The open world provides freedom, while the major dungeons create focused tests of everything the player has learned.
contentBlocks.caption: When one path becomes too difficult, the open world offers new places, equipment, and opportunities to prepare.
contentBlocks.heading: 4. Legacy dungeons inside a seamless world
contentBlocks.imageAlt: A Tarnished rests near the outskirts of leyndell

contentBlocks.text:
Elden Ring understands that curiosity becomes more powerful when the game does not immediately explain what the player will find. Sometimes a suspicious cliff leads to treasure. Sometimes an innocent-looking lift keeps travelling far longer than expected. And sometimes a small doorway somehow becomes the start of an evening-long detour.

That unpredictability gives the Lands Between its personality. **The world feels memorable because discoveries belong to the player**, not to a checklist prepared in advance.

You may begin with a clear destination in mind. Ten minutes later, you are underground, slightly confused, carrying three mysterious items, and wondering how you travelled so far from the original plan. In Elden Ring, that is not a failure of navigation. *That is the adventure.*
contentBlocks.heading: And when curiosity wins…

title: How Breath of the Wild Changed the Open-World Genre
description: Breath of the Wild transformed Hyrule into a world driven by curiosity, experimentation, and player freedom. These are the design ideas that helped reshape the modern open-world genre.
body:
When The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild arrived in 2017, it challenged many conventions associated with open-world games. Instead of filling the map with instructions and prescribed activities, Nintendo built an interconnected world that encouraged players to observe, experiment, and choose their own path.

Its individual ideas were not all completely new. Climbing, physics systems, survival mechanics, and nonlinear exploration had appeared elsewhere. What made Breath of the Wild remarkable was how naturally these elements worked together. The result was an adventure where exploration felt driven by the player rather than by a checklist.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Link overlooks the expansive landscape of Hyrule in The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

contentBlocks.text:
From the opening moments on the Great Plateau, distant mountains, unusual structures, towers, and patches of light constantly invite investigation. The game rarely needs to place a mission marker in front of the player because the landscape itself provides ==direction==.

This makes exploration feel personal. Players travel somewhere because it looks interesting, not simply because the interface tells them to go there. Even small discoveries—such as a ==hidden Korok==, an abandoned camp, or an unusual rock formation—reward the habit of paying attention.
contentBlocks.caption: Hyrule’s distinctive landmarks naturally encourage players to choose their own destinations.
contentBlocks.heading: 1. A world designed around curiosity
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link overlooks the expansive landscape of Hyrule from a high viewpoint, with mountains and landmarks visible in the distance.

contentBlocks.text:
After leaving the Great Plateau, players can travel toward almost any visible destination. ==The four Divine Beasts== can be completed in different orders, large portions of the world can be ignored, and experienced players can even head toward Hyrule Castle unusually early.

This freedom changes the relationship between the player and the story. Instead of following one tightly controlled route, every player creates a different journey through Hyrule. The game still provides objectives, but it rarely dictates how or when they must be completed.
contentBlocks.caption: After leaving the Great Plateau, players are free to explore Hyrule and pursue its major objectives in almost any order.
contentBlocks.heading: 2. Freedom to approach the adventure in any order
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link observes several regions of Hyrule from an elevated location, illustrating the scale and openness of the world.

contentBlocks.text:
The ability to climb almost any surface fundamentally changed how players navigated an open world. Mountains, ruins, towers, and cliffs were no longer decorative barriers—they became possible routes.

Climbing also reduced the need to search for the one path intended by the designer. If players could see a destination and had enough stamina, they could often create their own way there. Later open-world games increasingly adopted similar traversal systems because of ==how effectively they turned the environment into part of the gameplay.==
contentBlocks.caption: The ability to climb almost any surface transforms mountains and ruins into possible routes rather than barriers.
contentBlocks.heading: 3. Climbing transformed the landscape
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link climbs the side of a steep mountain, tower, or ancient structure above the surrounding landscape.

contentBlocks.text:
Fire spreads through dry grass, metal attracts electricity, wind carries objects, temperatures affect Link, and different materials react to forces in predictable ways. Because these systems follow understandable rules, players can combine them to produce solutions the game never explicitly teaches.

A metal weapon can conduct lightning. A fire can create an updraft. A heavy object can become a weapon when moved with Magnesis. These interactions make Hyrule feel less like a static collection of missions and more like a world players can manipulate.
contentBlocks.caption: Interconnected systems allow players to combine tools, physics, weather, and environmental elements in unexpected ways.
contentBlocks.heading: 4. Systems that encourage experimentation
contentBlocks.imageAlt: Link uses fire, wind, electricity, or a Sheikah Slate rune to interact with objects in the environment.

conclusion:
==If Breath of the Wild teaches us anything, it is that the best plan is often the one you invent five seconds after your original plan goes completely wrong. A thunderstorm interrupts your climb? Find another route. Your weapon breaks during a fight? Pick up whatever is nearby. Notice something suspicious on top of a distant mountain? You already know you are going to climb it.==

==That unpredictability is what makes Hyrule so memorable. Its systems do not simply give players more activities—they create small, personal stories. Two people can visit the same location and leave with completely different memories of what happened there.==

==And perhaps that is the game’s greatest contribution to the open-world genre: it trusts curiosity more than instructions. It gives players a landscape, a collection of interconnected tools, and just enough encouragement to ask, “I wonder if this will work?”==

==Most of the time, it does. And when it doesn’t, the result is usually even more entertaining.==
gameKey: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
